items.title: Lammy urges Burnham to take UK back into the EU
paragraphs: David Lammy has urged Andy Burnham to take Labour into the next general election with a pledge to rejoin the European Union.
The former deputy prime minister's intervention comes as Burnham prepares to reopen a debate on the long-term relationship with Europe in the wake of a summit in Brussels this Friday.
It makes him the latest senior Labour figure to publicly support a future reversal of Brexit, after ex-chancellor Rachel Reeves said she believed Britain's future lies in the bloc.
Burnham confirmed on Tuesday he plans to set out options for a future relationship next month, alongside his blueprint to boost the British economy over the next decade.
The prime minister has held out the possibility he could ask to rejoin at some stage, whilst ruling out major changes before the next election.

In an article earlier this month, Reeves said she believed "Britain's future lies in the European Union", without specifying a timeframe for the move and insisting it was important to "get the next steps right".
But Lammy has now gone further, calling for Burnham to advocate rejoining at the next election, paving the way for a negotiation on a deal to return.
Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, he added that the public should then be given a vote on whether to accept the new membership deal.
Returning to the bloc's customs union, in which EU member states charge the same taxes on imported goods, would not deliver "enough" economic growth, he said.
He added that rejoining Europe's single market from the outside was "not a runner" as it would mean applying swathes of EU law without a say on the content.
Another cabinet minister under Sir Keir Starmer, Peter Kyle, has also backed this approach, writing on Substack, external that a "complex halfway option" would be "the worst of all worlds".
He added that a promise to rejoin at the next election, followed by a renegotiation and a referendum on the final terms, was the "only way through I see".
He added: "How would I vote? Well, I would want to see the deal before deciding. I want Britain back in the EU, but not at any cost."
Lammy, who is also a former foreign secretary, argued the UK would be able to rejoin the EU whilst staying outside the passport-free Schengen travel zone and without committing to adopt the euro.

But he appeared to concede that Britain's EU budget rebate, first negotiated in the 1980s, could become less financially generous, adding that a "different formula" for financial contributions would be "up for negotiation".

He also revealed he had made an unsuccessful attempt to persuade Sir Keir to "tear up" his red lines on Europe towards the end of his two-year premiership, but the former prime minister had encountered resistance from within his cabinet.
Labour's 2024 election manifesto committed the party to "make Brexit work" whilst ruling out rejoining either its customs union or single market.
Any move away from those red lines by Burnham would set up a huge dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK at the next election.
But Lammy argued the prime minister's status as a former mayor from the north of England meant he was "uniquely placed" to convince the public of the need to reverse the decision to leave.

It comes as Burnham prepares to travel to the Brussels this Friday for an EU summit at which both sides hope to unveil new agreements on food, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime.
The prime minister inherited negotiations on those deals from his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, who kicked off talks on the agreements last year.

But he has also started a broader discussion over the UK's long-term relationship with Europe, which has been welcomed by some within his own party but seen him accused by critics of betraying the result of the 2016 decision to leave.
Burnham's Conservative predecessor Lord Cameron, who resigned as prime minister after losing the 2016 Brexit referendum, has urged the Labour leader not to start a renewed debate over EU membership.
Speaking last week, he warned a fresh debate over the issue would be "long and painful" and could harm attempts to improve upon the exit deal negotiated under the Conservatives.
He added: "The EU countries will just think: 'Well, these guys are gonna rejoin anyway, so what's the point in giving them a good partnership deal'."

items.title: Ivan Toney loses bid to avoid Euro 2028 court clash
paragraphs: A bid to move the date of England striker Ivan Toney's assault trial to avoid a clash with Euro 2028 has been refused.
The 30-year-old footballer is accused of headbutting and punching Saber Da Silva during a confrontation at a nightclub in Wardour Street, central London, on 6 December.

Toney denied assault occasioning actual bodily harm at a court hearing last month and a date for a three- to four-day trial was fixed for 12 June 2028, which is three days into the Uefa Euro 2028 tournament.
He represented England at this summer's World Cup and has made 10 international appearances and scored one goal.

At a hearing at Southwark Crown Court on Wednesday, where Toney did not appear, his barrister Mozammel Hossain KC said: "It came to our attention that… there may be potentially a football match called the European Championship in 2028 between 9 June and 9 July."

Hossain proposed a trial date in August that year, adding: "We ask you please that the matter be put back to then for a trial so that if the defendant is included in this football tournament he can play.
"My knowledge of football is very limited but I am told he was included in the last one in 2024 and the England squad for the World Cup."
Judge Tony Baumgartner called it a "speculative" application.
He refused the request, saying: "It does not seem to me to be in the interest of justice to disturb the date that was already fixed."
The judge said the application could be made again if Toney is selected for the England squad.
Toney missed out on the latest squad for the country's Nations League ties.
Toney started his football career with Northampton Town and played for teams including Wigan Athletic and Peterborough United before signing for Brentford in 2020.
He scored 72 goals during four years with the Bees before making a surprise switch in 2024 to Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli.

items.title: Brain cancer patients demand public inquiry into chemotherapy scandal
paragraphs: Becky Jones who had 11 years of chemotherapy for a cancer she did not have said treatment was "handed out like sweets"
ByDavid Lumbin CoventryShehnaz Khan and Oprah FlashWest Midlands
Brain cancer patients who were given years of unnecessary chemotherapy are calling for a public inquiry, after a review found people were severely harmed under an NHS trust's care.
Some were misdiagnosed while others were told if they stopped temozolomide (TMZ) treatment they would die, despite this not being true.
The Royal College of Physicians (RCP) investigated 20 cases at University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW) NHS Trust.

The drug is typically meant to be taken for six months but in one case a patient of Prof Ian Brown was given more than 100 cycles of chemotherapy over a period of 13 years. They later developed leukaemia as a side-effect of too much chemotherapy.
Becky Jones, who had 11 years of the treatment for a cancer she did not have, has told the BBC she was "absolutely disgusted" that "chemotherapy was dished out like it was sweets".
University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire NHS Trust has apologised
"I have two young children and to think once upon a time I might not have been there for their future kills me every day and it's all down to one person," the 35-year-old added.
She is one of more than 40 patients taking legal action against the NHS Trust. The mum-of-two was 21 when she was told she had a grade 4 glioblastoma and six to 12 months to live.
After more than 100 cycles of chemotherapy it was found she had never had a brain tumour and that her imaging was consistent with tumefactive demyelination, a less serious lesion.
She said of the report: "The findings are worse than I ever expected them to be.
"A national inquiry needs to happen and things need to be tightened up so it can't happen to anyone else.
"I don't think I'll ever find closure until the trust accept what they have done wrong and are held accountable. I would like answers."
The review, released on Wednesday, was commissioned by the trust following the retirement of one of its doctors.
Brown, referred to as Dr Y in the RCP's report, did not take part in the review and refused to comment when approached by the BBC at his home.
University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW) NHS Trust has apologised for "failures" within its neuro-oncology service under the care of the retired clinical oncologist.

Chief executive Professor Andy Hardy and trust chair Sue Noyes said in a statement: "This is far below the standards our patients deserve and that we expect. We let you down, and for that we offer our sincere apologies."
Prof Ian Brown, who retired in 2024, is referred to as Dr Y in the review
Brown was employed there from 1996 to 2024 and concerns over his practice were raised by colleagues when his patients were handed over upon his retirement in December 2023.
Medics found people on long-term repeated cycles of TMZ, against standard practice and national guidelines.
Some patients had also been left on treatment despite their cancer progressing, when moving to the best supportive care for their symptoms would have been a better choice.

TMZ, a chemotherapy drug that is sometimes used for glioblastoma and astrocytoma brain tumours, should usually be taken post radiotherapy for six cycles, usually over six months, but some patients have told the BBC they received it for many years.
The review warned there may be many more affected patients, with 83 receiving extended TMZ treatment between 2017 and 2023.
Overall, the RCP examined 20 cases of care under Brown, though the number of patients affected is higher - including those who have since died.

Working to strict definitions of harm, the review team concluded six patients had suffered severe harm, five moderate harm and eight low levels of harm. In the final case, the review team could not reach a judgement on moderate or severe harm.
Among other recommendations, the RCP said that any wider review of patients who received the treatment and have since died should be discussed with the Department of Health and Social Care.
"There is a large cohort of deceased patients who have received this non-standard chemotherapy regime, who may potentially have come to harm," the report said.

"To review every patient would be a significant and costly undertaking. The Trust should determine whether such a step is appropriate, and if so, discuss with the DHSC and/or NHS England how such a review would proceed."
After 10 years of treatment, Mark Poulton found out he had been wrongly diagnosed

Father-of-three Mark Poulton, from Redditch, Wocestershire, said he had been left in "constant pain" with spells of depression after undergoing chemotherapy for a decade, only to discover two years ago that he had been misdiagnosed.
The 54-year-old told the BBC: "I feel angry that I've gone through 10 years of TMZ that I probably shouldn't have done and the report backs that.

"You get a cancer diagnosis of any sort and you feel you will collapse, then you go to a hospital and you're in the right place, you feel safe, only to find out 10 to 12 years later that you were abused by the system that failed me and the other patients involved.
"More needs to be done, it can't end here with this review. We need action so it doesn't happen again."
In 2014 he was told he had oligodendroglioma, an aggressive brain tumour, but found out in 2024 that he actually had astrocytoma, a different type of cancer.
The review also highlighted patients who were exposed to a "significant lifetime risk" of developing secondary cancers and other health problems after several years of non-standard chemotherapy.

One, who received the drug for 10 years, experienced "significant toxicity", including ongoing fatigue, nausea and a "severe episode" of ophthalmic shingles and galactorrhoea caused by a drug prescribed to treat chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.
The review also referred to a Mr N, who the BBC understands to be clinical nurse specialist Ian Edwards.
Some patients were advised implicitly and explicitly that stopping treatment would be harmful, the review said.
There was also evidence in some cases of patients being given misleading information.

The review team heard in interviews that a small number of patients had requested discontinuation of their treatment, which Edwards then discussed with Brown and acted upon, however no evidence of this was seen in the cases reviewed.
"In one case when the patient questioned their treatment, they were told by Mr N (Edwards) that Dr Y (Brown) was 'legally bound' to continue it," they added.
Edwards has also since retired from the trust, UHCW confirmed, adding it had made a formal regulatory referral to the Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) regulator.
Becky Addison of law firm Brabners said the report was "thorough" but patients still need answers
Legal firm Brabners, which represents more than 40 patients and is calling for an independent public inquiry, said cases had been referred to the police but no action had yet been taken.
Becky Addison, from the firm, said: "Now is the opportunity that everyone needs to sit up and look at how important this is for patients that they get the answers that they deserve.

"They've had their lives taken away from them in unimaginable ways and all that they need at the moment is answers, transparency and accountability and that will come by way of a statutory public inquiry."
All living patients receiving TMZ at the trust have already had their care reviewed again internally to ensure it aligned with expected standards, the UHCW trust has said.
A "comprehensive independent external clinical review process" will also evaluate all living patients who received over 12 cycles of TMZ under Brown.

The trust added: "We have initiated discussions with the NHS England regional director of patient safety to establish clear requirements and methodology for reviewing the cohort of deceased patients who received non-standard chemotherapy regime."

items.title: Trump shakes hands with Putin and Xi ahead of historic talks in China
paragraphs: Watch: BBC correspondents discuss historic Trump, Xi and Putin meeting
ByOlivia Ireland and Laura BickerChina correspondent
Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met for the first time in over a year on Wednesday, as the pair prepared for landmark talks in China with Xi Jinping.

The US president was greeted off his plane by the Chinese leader as he arrived in Shenzhen for a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders, which will culminate in a closely-watched meeting between the pair and the Russian president.
After a carefully choreographed handshake and hug between Trump and Xi on the tarmac, the US president later greeted and exchanged pleasantries with Putin ahead of a reception.
Trump and Putin are expected to hold one-on-one talks on the sidelines of the summit on Thursday, in which the conflict in Ukraine could be discussed.
However the main focus during the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (Apec) will be on the US-China-Russia talks on Thursday - the first time the trio of leaders have met together in person.

A full agenda has not been made public but there have been various hints about what could be discussed, including the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran, nuclear proliferation, trade tensions and developments in artificial intelligence.
After a lavish reception from Xi, the leaders of the US and Russia shook hands ahead of a reception
It was not clear on Wednesday what form separate Trump-Putin talks would take, though a Kremlin spokesperson indicated short informal talks may happen without large delegations in the room.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has raised fears of a plan to end the war being discussed in the absence of representatives from Kyiv or Europe.

Wednesday's handshake was the first in-person meeting between Trump and Putin since August 2025, when the Russian leader travelled to Alaska for talks on the Ukraine war which failed to deliver a breakthrough.
Xi's personal reception for Trump at the airport mimicked a similar move by the US president when the Chinese leader visited Washington in September, a gesture Xi described as "special".
A red carpet was rolled out in front of Air Force One for Trump, with a cheering crowd, honour guard, military flyover and flowers presentation all in place to welcome him.
Chinese state-run news agency Xinhua quoted Xi as saying he wanted to pursue a "constructive strategic and stable relationship based on respect, fairness, and equality".
Xi's greeting will be seen as a diplomatic gesture designed to begin the week's talks with his American counterpart on a cordial note.
A lavish welcome ceremony was laid on for Trump's arrival
The Apec summit is being held in Shenzhen, south-east China, a booming for manufacturing and advanced tech.

It comes against the backdrop of the ousting of Nvidia chief executing Jensen Huang, who admitted to having an affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of spying for Beijing - a claim dismissed as a "smear" by China.
Trump has pursued warmer relations with China but the incident points to ongoing tensions between the two powers.
Several hours before Trump's arrival, Putin landed in Shenzhen and held around two hours of talks with Xi, with whom he has pressed for closer economic and defence relations.
Xi said both countries would "move forward steadily and boldly" and that the relationship was "stable as a mountain, unshaken by storms".

items.title: Apec summit live: Xi welcomes Trump on China visit as Putin claims Europe in ‘humiliating decline’
paragraphs: Xi hails Shenzhen's transformation in Apec banquet speech
Trump and Putin shake hands ahead of Apec welcome banquet
Putin and Trump could meet informally during Apec summit, Russia state media reports
Xi says he hopes to build 'stable' China-US ties with Trump - state media
Xi hails ‘unshaken’ China-Russia ties after talks with Putin
Trump welcomed by Xi as he arrives for summit
Carney challenges Putin's claim that sanctions no longer work
Trump arrives in Shenzhen for Apec summit, Chinese state media reports
Trump announces new trade deal with Philippines as he heads to China
Taiwan sends representative to Apec summit
Xi Jinping calls for freer trade, greater cooperation on AI
Here is more of Xi’s speech (as per Xinhua):

double quotation markAt tomorrow’s Leaders’ Meeting, we will discuss measures to expand mutual openness, explore pathways for innovation-driven growth, broaden opportunities for pragmatic cooperation in various fields, and promote the implementation of more outcomes. I look forward to discussing the grand plan for Asia-Pacific cooperation and jointly advancing the cause of Asia-Pacific development with you all.
Now, I propose that we raise a glass together.
For the common prosperity of the Asia-Pacific region,
For the success of this informal leaders’ meeting,
For the health of all guests and their families,
China’s state news agency Xinhua has published the text of Xi Jinping’s welcome speech at tonight’s Apec banquet in Shenzhen.
In his remarks, Xi praised the city’s transformation into an international economic and innovation hub, describing it as a symbol of China’s development.
Here are a few passages from his address:

double quotation markThis evening, the shores of the South China Sea are aglow with lights, and autumn is in full swing here in Shenzhen, the City of the Phoenix. As the 33rd Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting is about to commence, I would like, on behalf of the Chinese Government and the Chinese people, to extend a warm welcome to all our distinguished guests.

I have often said that to see a thousand years of China, one should visit Xi’an; to see five hundred years of China, one should visit Beijing; and to see a hundred years of China, one should visit Shanghai. Today, I would like to say to you all: to see fifty years of China, come to Shenzhen.

Shenzhen is a place with a rich history. In 1978, when I first came to Shenzhen, it was still a small fishing village. More than 40 years have passed in the blink of an eye, and now it is filled with high-rise buildings and bustling traffic. The changes are truly remarkable.”
US president Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian president Vladimir Putin, as China’s Xi Jinping looks on, ahead of the welcome banquet at the Apec summit in Shenzhen, China:
Donald Trump has arrived at the welcome banquet with Xi Jinping:
The newswires are carrying pictures of world leaders arriving for the welcome banquet at the Apec summit, including Russia’s Vladimir Putin:
Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump could have several opportunities to speak during the Apec summit in China, according to Russia’s state news agency, Tass.
Citing Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov, Tass reported that the two leaders could exchange words informally at various points during the summit.
They will communicate “on their feet, on the steps, in chairs”, Ushakov reportedly said, suggesting their interactions need not be limited to a formal sit-down meeting.

Xi Jinping told Donald Trump he hoped their talks would help advance a “constructive, strategic and stable relationship” between China and the US, based on “respect, fairness and reciprocity”, according to China’s state news agency Xinhua.
Xi also recalled Trump’s personal welcome at the airport during his visit to the US in September, saying China’s own welcome for the US president reflected its tradition of reciprocity.
Xinhua reported the following remarks by the Chinese president:
double quotation markWhen I visited the United States in September this year, president Trump and his wife made a special trip to the airport to welcome me, and a grand welcoming ceremony was held.

China is a nation of courtesy, with a tradition of reciprocity. I welcome you back to China and look forward to exchanging in-depth views with you on major issues concerning China–US relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation and the global landscape, so as to advance a constructive, strategic and stable relationship between China and the US based on respect, fairness and reciprocity.”
Chinese state media have released a readout of Xi Jinping’s earlier meeting with Vladimir Putin.

In it, Xi is quoted as saying China-Russia relations are “unshaken by storms and steady as a mountain”, and have set “an example of a new type of major-country relationship characterised by equality, mutual respect, trustworthiness, and win-win co-operation”.
Xi also urged closer political and military ties between the two countries.

He said “the two sides should leverage the mechanisms for exchanges between the two countries’ governments, legislative bodies, militaries and political parties, ensuring that the consensus reached by the two countries’ heads of state is effectively implemented”, according to the readout.
In a notable gesture, Xi personally greeted Trump on the airport tarmac in Shenzhen, reciprocating the welcome the US president extended to the Chinese leader during his visit to the US in September.

As a reminder, Ukraine carried out a major strike on the Kerch Bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia, destroying its central road section in an operation involving two strikes over consecutive days.

The attack earlier this week dealt a significant blow to a key transport link and a symbolic project for Vladimir Putin, as the Russian president sat down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for talks at the Apec summit.
My colleague Jakub Krupa has the latest on the Ukraine conflict over on our Europe live blog here:
While we await Trump to disembark Air Force Once, we have this report from our China correspondent Rebecca Bailey in Shenzhen:
Canada’s Mark Carney has hit back at Vladimir Putin’s earlier assertion that sanctions no longer work in this day and age.

“Mr Putin can ask his financial institutions, he can ask his oligarch friends, he can ask his hockey players whether or not sanctions are a thing of the past. I think he’ll find out that they’re very real, they’re biting,” Carney told reporters.

In his address to the summit this morning, Putin had said that “the traditional tools of economic dominance and de facto coercion have largely run their course, having ⁠lost much of their intimidating power”.

Speaking at an outdoor press conference as purple clouds lingered ominously in the background, Carney said: “Not for the first time, Vladimir Putin is lying about the situation on the ground. Sanctions are very real and they’re going to continue to increase as long as this war goes on.”

Carney had previously said he would not boycott a group photo with Putin out of respect for hosts China. But he said if he were to find himself next to the Russian president, he would make Canada’s position clear.

Carney met China’s president Xi Jinping on Tuesday, with the two countries announcing remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.
The two men also discussed AI, Carney said Wednesday, adding he had taken the opportunity to share Canada’s views on a model for global governance.

“The absence of any global governance around AI is an enormous risk,” he said. “It’s an enormous economic risk but it’s a biohazard risk, and it’s a risk to democracy, human dignity, other factors... So it is past time to develop global governance frameworks for these sectors.”
Carney is due to meet Donald Trump later today, he said, where they would discuss efforts to reach a trade deal.
“We have been making progress... Two steps forward, one step back type thing,” he said.
He said he fully respected Trump’s engagement with China.

“I’m going to say something positive here about the initiative around denuclearization, the trilateral meeting that is going to happen,” he said. “Guess what? Canada’s in favor of denuclearization. If the relationship can be used towards that end, we’re very much supportive of it.”
Donald Trump has arrived in Shenzhen, China, for the Apec summit, Chinese state media reported.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto 6 is a masterpiece, say critics
paragraphs: After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.
Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?
According to the first reviews, it's a resounding yes.
Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100, external - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.
Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.
They have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN, external branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".
Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building.
"The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote, external, but he added "there are also nits to pick".
For The New York Times, external one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors.
Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action.
But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.

The graphics of the game were hotly anticipated and so far have not disappointed critics, with The Guardian, external describing Leonida, the setting inspired by Miami, as "so lifelike that at times it beggars belief".
And the relationship between the lead characters, Jason and Lucia, has also stunned critics.
"They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim," The Guardian's Keza MacDonald wrote, adding: "I found it impossible not to care for them".
Writing for Forbes, external, Paul Tassi said: "I can't say I've ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share".
The Washington Post, external said GTA 6 "raises the bar at every level", while Bloomberg, external's Jason Schreier called it a "masterpiece" in his five star review.
"It's hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here," he wrote. "There's nothing else like it.
"While playing this game, I often found myself wondering how it even exists."
Rockstar hasn't revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (£760m).

items.title: Mary Peltola flips Alaska's Senate seat. And, Nvidia won't reinstate Jensen Huang
paragraphs: Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-154145/nx-s1-mx-6045399-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, according to The Associated Press. Her victory gives Democrats 56 senators in the upcoming Congress. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting for its general election, but Peltola secured a majority of first-place votes, eliminating the need for ranked-choice calculations. Her win flips a Senate seat in a state that President Trump won by 13 percentage points in 2024. The race's final days were tumultuous due to allegations that Peltola's team tried to recruit another candidate to the race to siphon votes from the incumbent. Peltola's campaign denied any involvement.
Mary Peltola looks on during a campaign rally at the Alaska Aviation Museum on October 30, 2026 in Anchorage, Alaska. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images hide caption

Trump has arrived in the Southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, where he is set to meet with China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday. This will mark the third time these two leaders have met this year. They are expected to discuss trade, investment and tariffs, which are currently on hold.

Nvidia board chairman Harvey Jones said in an earnings call yesterday that the board does not intend to reinstate former CEO Jensen Huang. Huang "voluntarily resigned" on Nov. 12 after disclosing "personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct," according to Jones. Huang acknowledged he had been unfaithful to his wife. News reports have tied him to a woman who U.S. intelligence officials say was recruited by China's spy agency. The board unanimously accepted his resignation. Earlier yesterday, Huang said he would return as CEO if the board permitted it and agreed to testify before Congress regarding national security issues surrounding the company.

Major organizations have been experiencing widespread crashes of computer and online systems. Apple reported significant outages yesterday, and the U.S. National Security Agency also experienced a breakdown. As of this morning, no major disruptions seem to be occurring. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there is no evidence that these incidents are related to one another or involve a malign actor or cybercriminal.

Kratom and related 7-OH products are widely available at gas stations, smoke shops, liquor stores and online. As early as Friday, the federal government could make some of the products illegal. Mindy Schauer/MediaNewsGroup/Orange County Register via Getty Images hide caption
Mindy Schauer/MediaNewsGroup/Orange County Register via Getty Images

In recent years, highly concentrated products containing 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) have emerged online and at smoke shops, liquor stores and gas stations. These products, available as tablets, gummies, tonics and chocolates, contain one of the major psychoactive ingredients in kratom. Unlike kratom leaf products, 7-OH acts more like an opioid in the human brain. Some people use kratom to maintain long-term recovery from opioid addiction. Others say it helps them feel energized or focused. Users of 7-OH and kratom can show signs of addiction, and unclear product labeling makes it hard to determine the quantities consumed. Over the past decade, the U.S. government has tried to restrict these products, but public opposition has kept them legal. Recently, this situation has started to change.
Family physician Mara Gordon answers reader health questions monthly for NPR's special series Real Talk with a Doc. Send in your question to thrive@npr.org.

Artificial intelligence scribes help doctors take notes in various settings, from gynecologist visits to emergency rooms. Dr. Gordon says the technology saves time and allows her to focus entirely on her patients without the distraction of multitasking. But she also understands why patients might feel uneasy about new technology, and says she shares their concerns about privacy. Here's what Dr. Gordon says you should know about AI scribes:
A selection of different flavored manoushe. Jawad Rizkallah hide caption

items.title: Stormont department failing to protect wild birds, oversight body finds
paragraphs: A parallel investigation is looking at the same issues involving Defra and Natural England, and they have also been issued with decision notices.

In Northern Ireland, the OEP's Chief Regulatory Officer Helen Venn acknowledged that "positive steps" had been taken, but added that delays in meeting legal obligations had played a part in the significant decline of wild birds in Northern Ireland.

"SPAs are important for achieving the Executive's commitments in relation to nature, such as the strategic outcome of thriving, resilient and connected nature and wildlife in the Environmental Improvement Plan.
"This is in addition to the Executive's international commitment to protect at least 30% of land and seas for nature's recovery by 2030.

"This is why it is important for Daera to carry out its legal responsibilities in a reasonable timeframe to deliver nature recovery and in relation to the classification and adaptation of SPAs on land."
The agriculture and environment minister Andrew Muir said there was "a moral and legal obligation" to protect wild bird habitats and welcomed continuing engagement between his officials and the OEP.

"The OEP has recognised in their investigation longstanding and concerning failures to implement recommended actions to protect wild bird habitats and populations by successive administrations both in England and Northern Ireland.
"While we have a long way to go to reverse current trends, there are signs of hope and clear examples of nature recovery in action.
"However, the scale of challenge requires greater levels of support from across government to provide the necessary resources and funding to address the nature crisis."
And he said the recently-published Nature Recovery Strategy and the Farming With Nature support package "reinforces" the department's commitment to nature restoration.
Sherwood said the group had been highlighting failing for decades.
"Today's findings from the OEP confirm what conservation organisations have been saying: action has been delayed for far too long.

"The focus must now move to delivery, with the Executive leading the way, and Daera and NIEA being resourced to take urgent action to put these protections in place and help reverse the decline of our most vulnerable bird populations.
"We hope today's OEP report will be the catalyst needed."

items.title: Minister criticises media for 'amplifying' Russell Brand's prison message
paragraphs: Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell has criticised media organisations for broadcasting a message from the wife of jailed rapist Russell Brand on his behalf.

Laura Brand read out the message on the disgraced comedian's YouTube channel on Sunday, in which he said he was not guilty of the offences for which he is serving a 10-and-a-half year prison sentence.
The message has prompted an official investigation into whether Brand broke prison rules.

The clip of Laura Brand has been played on outlets including BBC Radio 4's Today programme, ITV's This Morning, Sky News, LBC and the News Agents podcast. On Wednesday, Education Secretary Powell said the media should not have "amplified" his words.
"I was appalled at that [message] and actually I think mainstream media shouldn't have transmitted that either," she told LBC on Wednesday.
"It's a platform I don't think should have been amplified, to be honest."
Powell went on to describe Russell Brand as "someone who's not showing a jot of remorse, a jot of any sensitivity at all to their victims".
She continued: "This is somebody who's been convicted and found guilty of very, very serious offences and rape."
In a statement, the BBC said the Today programme had played the Laura Brand clip "in error, due to miscommunication within the team", and had since removed it from catch-up service BBC Sounds.
BBC News has asked the other outlets named above for a comment, as well as YouTube's parent company Google about its policy.

In 2023, after a media investigation revealing allegations about Brand, YouTube suspended his channels from making money from adverts for "violating" its "creator responsibility policy". But they are still available to view.
Brand's social media accounts on Meta platforms - which owns Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - were disabled last week.
Earlier this week, Downing Street officials described Brand's message to his followers as "clearly appalling", adding that it was being urgently investigated,
No 10 said it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules.

Asked about the message, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.
"Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments."

items.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 probe is now one light-day away
paragraphs: is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

After traveling through the void of space for 49 years, Voyager 1 has hit a momentous milestone: the spacecraft is now officially one light-day away from Earth, which is, as NASA put it, “very, very far.” The probe crossed the milepost on Wednesday at 5:16AM ET, and is now 16.094 billion miles away from our planet — equal to the distance that light travels in 24 hours.

It’s the furthest that any human-made object has ever traveled, and Voyager 1’s journey isn’t over yet. It’s been heading towards a star called Gliese 445 in the Ursa Minor constellation since completing its primary objectives to conduct flybys of Jupiter and Saturn in 1980. That star is 17 light-years away, meaning Voyager 1 won’t pass by it for around 40,000 years, despite traveling at nearly 38,000 miles per hour.

The light-day milestone is a remarkable feat alone, but especially so when you consider that Voyager 1 is still operational. NASA has done well to keep it functioning, and it can continue to send back readings on plasma waves, magnetic fields, and space-bound particles, though it now takes radio signals an entire day to travel between Earth and the spacecraft. Voyager 2, which launched 16 days before its twin, is also expected to reach a distance of one light-day away from Earth, but not until 2035.

items.title: Does GTA VI live up to the hype? Our games editor has played it – ask her anything
paragraphs: After more than a decade and a reported billion dollars in the making, Grand Theft Auto VI is finally released on Friday. It’s one of the most anticipated games of all time.

The Guardian’s games editor, Keza MacDonald, is one of the first people in the world to have played it. Last month she visited Rockstar North’s headquarters in Edinburgh to go behind the scenes, and she’s now been playing a review copy.

So does it live up to the hype? What’s it like to play as Lucia and Jason, the series’ first double act of protagonists? How big is the new Vice City, and does it really feel alive? And are the radio stations as good as ever?
Keza will be here at 4pm today to answer your questions about the graphics, the open world, the characters, the story and anything else you want to know before you play, without spoilers.
Post your questions in the comments below or email conversations@theguardian.com

items.title: Cotswolds barn renovation by ConForm creates a "dialogue between old and new"
paragraphs: London studio ConForm Architects has transformed a former cattle barn into a multifunctional space for a working farm in the Cotswolds, contrasting its original red-brick and timber structure with zinc and black-timber additions.
Named Open Byre, the 124-square-metre barn has been adapted into a flexible space for meetings and gatherings, with the first floor containing a standalone apartment for guests.

ConForm Architects‘ design responds to the dual nature of the barn’s surroundings – with traditional red-brick farm structures to the east and more contemporary agricultural barns to the east – combining restoration with a new contrasting palette of stone, metal and timber.

“The design centres on a dialogue between old and new. Rather than blending the interventions into the existing fabric, we wanted each to remain legible and reinforce the other,” studio partner Ben Edgley told Dezeen.
“The building sits between two distinct parts of the farm: the older red brick buildings around the formal front farmyard and the more recent, industrial agricultural structures beyond,” he added.
“The design responds to both, retaining the brickwork and slate roof at the front while using zinc and blackened timber at the rear to reference the newer farm buildings.”

A defining feature of the barn’s new rear facade is a projecting volume wrapped by gabion walls, filled with locally-quarried stone and punctured by a large window illuminating a cross-laminated timber (CLT) staircase.

In the ground floor’s flexible office and arts spaces, the idea of material contrasts continues, with original red-brick walls and repaired timber ceilings accompanied by joinery including desks, storage and a bathroom pod in black through-coloured MDF.
Above, the guest apartment is tucked beneath the exposed beams of the barn’s roof, with its own dedicated living room, kitchen-diner and bathroom finished in matching black timber.

“The central CLT stair is the defining gesture. It brings together structure, circulation and spatial organisation, drawing the eye from the entrance through the building towards the trees beyond,” said Edgley.
“Its scale and material presence establish a clear contrast with the existing brickwork and timber frame,” he added.
“The clients were closely involved in the process, undertaking much of the timber repair alongside local craftsmen. Their commitment to retaining the original fabric was central to the project.”
ConForm Architects was founded in 2017 by Edgley alongside Eoin O’Leary.
Previous projects by the studio include a terraced home in London with perforated metal floors to filter daylight and a green-terrazzo flat extension modelled on bay windows.

items.title: Cosimo I de’Medici review – up close and personal with a Renaissance godfather
paragraphs: Mounting a “store-cupboard” exhibition – choosing items from existing collections to make a new, contained display – can be a cheap and easy way for a museum to make something out of its existing resources, without the faff of securing loans or collaborating across the industry. In the case of the Wallace Collection, however, the store cupboard is so embarrassingly rich and diverse that strong displays such as this on Cosimo I de’Medici can be drawn from only a handful of its objects.

The 19th-century collection of Sir Richard Wallace holds a notable number of medieval objects, but their display can seem – at least to contemporary eyes – like a cacophony of applied arts, armour and paintings, not to mention a ton of gilt. This Medici display is part of a new enterprise drawing out histories from the noise for singular focus, sensibly repurposing what was once the cloakroom (a previously wasted bit of prime real estate) as a new dedicated space.

The Medici family history itself is more labyrinthine than can be captured in a single exhibition, even for diehard historians (or, I dare say, bingers of the 2016 Italian-British TV series), and the Wallace eschews dense background reading here. It has a dual obligation to impart the artwork’s historical significance in relation to its existence in the Wallace Collection, which is perhaps why it omits significant details regarding Cosimo’s role in founding the Uffizi Gallery and expanding the Pitti Palace in Florence. We get the key grounding, however, in that in 1537, the 17-year-old Cosimo was elected as the new duke of Florence. This followed swiftly after the assassination of the last male heir of the senior branch of the Medici family, Alessandro, leaving a power vacuum at threat from republicanism.

And, crucially, it demonstrates that it is not necessarily the most “beautiful” works that are the most compelling. It’s always secretly thrilling to encounter a fresco that’s been hacked off the wall (removal videos are nail-biting stuff), and a 1464 fresco of the young Cicero reading taken from a Milanese branch of the Medici bank even has chunks at its base missing, the snap-lines used to mark out its design in wet plaster clearly visible up close in raking light, and somewhat hilariously mounted in an incongruous wooden frame. Among its usual Wallace location the clunky fresco medium would usually pale next to its fine art neighbours – now it shines in the spotlight.

We are told how the statesman Cicero was a model of civic virtue and morality and hence adopted as a symbol of the Florentine republic. He is envisaged here (in a commission by Cosimo the Elder, not Cosimo I as is the case for every other piece – pay attention at the back!) as a studious young figure with a sense of industry and success, implying similar connotations for the benefacting Medici family.

The varying amount of iconographic content – ie, the visual symbolism deliberately used by Cosimo I for dynastic purposes – does highlight the limitations of working within Wallace’s collection. Certainly, a parade helmet (c1550) and sword (1546-69) bear a plethora of imagery and were inventoried in the Medici armouries as alluding to Hercules, who was commonly said (by Florentines) to have founded Florence. Cosimo’s heraldry sits next to an Order of the Golden Fleece, of which Cosimo was a member, and topped by a ducal crown, despite his only becoming grand duke in 1569. In short, the iconographic picture and dynastic assertion is bright and clear.

Yet the show’s (literal) centrepiece, a 1574 earthenware wine cooler, bears only Cosimo’s personal emblem, a turtle with a sail, alluding to the motto festina lente (make haste slowly), which was itself pinched from Roman emperor Augustus. The rest of the glazed iconography is a combination of fanciful mythological whimsy, satyrs and monstrous figures. It bears a naval battle which it is noted can only with certainty be linked to its purpose for holding liquid. Unlike the armour for which its display purpose – and audience – was obvious, we can only speculate on the audience for such an object other than banqueting and revelry. Perhaps we can – only half-jokingly – look to the glaringly formidable testes of the carved monsters supporting the bowl for further declaration of dynastic strength and rigour.

Such a sparse but precise display is welcome as a contrast with the Wallace’s visual overwhelm, using close and precise old-school art historical analysis to draw out one strand of its many contained histories. Even the choice of terracotta wall colour instantly imparts a Florentine flavour – a smart touch. Its limitations remind us that the collection is based on personal, not curatorial choice, : we don’t even have a portrait of Cosimo himself in the collection, despite Bronzino having churned out dozens of them. Yet hopefully there will be more studies like this to enjoy.

items.title: Suno now lets you make AI videos for your AI music
paragraphs: Suno has introduced image and video generation in its latest effort to expand beyond being an AI music platform. The new feature, called “Visuals,” allows users to turn Suno songs into AI-generated video clips that automatically lipsync to lyrics, or make images via prompt descriptions that can be used as thumbnails and album artwork.

Visuals is available on web, iOS, and Android. The exact layout differs across Suno’s desktop and mobile interfaces, but users will find a new Visuals tab under Create mode on each version. Web users can also access Visuals by selecting the three dot menu on a song in their library. From there, users can select which section of the track to use, up to a maximum of 15 seconds, and select a reference image to build the generated video clip.

There are three options available for the starting image reference: selecting one of the original character presets provided by Suno, uploading your own photo or artwork, or generating the image directly on Suno using descriptive prompts. The image generation capabilities also allow users to select specific aspect ratios, optimizing results for landscape or portrait modes and online platforms.

For video generation, users can select whether the reference image is used as the start or end frame, making it easier to edit the 15-second clips together. There’s a toggle to automatically lipsync vocals to the generated video, and tools for adjusting aspect ratio and clip length. Visuals also includes a dedicated video editing timeline for assembling clips into longer videos, and adding customizable song lyric text.

The H3 Move AI model is being used to power Visuals, based on H3 from MiniMax. Suno says the AI has been “optimized for our community including adding additional protections and safeguards,” which include a “suite of new text and visual filters” designed to block people from using or generating the likeness of specific artists, public figures, copyrighted works and IP. Visuals also uses its own “Visuals credits” to generate videos and images, which are distinct from the song credits used to make AI music, meaning Suno users will have additional expenses to pay in order to use this new feature.

The Visuals launch follows Suno introducing a Speech feature in October for generating spoken words and voiceovers. Adding video capabilities is another attempt to diversify the platform after Suno’s music generator attracted a number of high-profile lawsuits, though it seems some users would rather the company focus on improving those song-generating capabilities. In the YouTube video for the Visuals launch, one user says “FIX AUDIO BEFORE ADDING CRAP NOBODY ASKED FOR” — a sentiment that other commenters are echoing.
