items.title: Meet Linde Freya Tangelder, Nendo's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years
paragraphs: Nendo has selected Linde Freya Tangelder for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler. In this interview, the Dutch designer explains why she doesn’t find design inspiring.
Insofar as she creates furniture and lighting, Tangelder is technically a designer, but only just.

“How I think is not typical design,” she told Dezeen. “So I’m never thinking about function in the first place. The whole process is very intuitive, it’s just a cloud of connections in my head – more about concepts or stories that I want to tell rather than making a functional piece.”
“I’ve never been so inspired by design in general,” she added. “It’s a skill that fits very well to me, but I’d rather connect it in inspiration to art, to architecture, or another discipline.”
With a highly sculptural style, Tangelder also sometimes refers to herself as an artist – a label she says she wouldn’t have dared use when starting out.
She has made a name for herself through pieces that often play with unexpected juxtapositions of materials and use traditional methods of production to create an unmistakably contemporary aesthetic.
“I like to use poor materials, rich materials, and fuse them,” she explained. “For me, it’s sort of a synonym for how I think culture should be.”
In 2019, she was identified by Dezeen as a young designer to watch after exhibiting at Collectible, as well as winning that year’s Biennale Interieur designer of the year award.
Explaining the studio’s decision to select her as a 20×20 nomination, Nendo praised Tangelder’s approach for being “both remarkably gentle and quietly bold”.
“Driven by a playful curiosity to take architecture apart and put it back together, she reveals qualities in familiar materials that we have long overlooked,” the studio told Dezeen.
Referencing buildings in the medium of furniture has become something of a calling card for Tangelder.

Notable examples include the Bolder Chair, which recalls architectural columns, the Windows of Bo Bardi table, which mimics the shape of windows on the SESC Pompéia Factory in São Paulo, and Brick’s Reflection Chair with its terracotta backrest (pictured left).
These propensities are reflected evocatively in the name of Tangelder’s studio – Destroyers/Builders – though recently, she tends to work more under her own name.
“I’m inspired by architecture, things I see in buildings,” she said. “I think it’s just really interesting to scale it down to the field of artistic design, or limited-edition design.”
“In the history of architecture there’s so much to tell,” she continued. “For me it’s more diverse and also less superficial than the history of design, and I think that’s what interests me so much.”
“And also that it feels more essential, I think that is maybe the core. I just like brick. I like simple materials that are used for construction rather than smooth finishes just for decoration.”

Not that she is completely opposed to smooth, decorative finishes – as evidenced by the fact that an entire room in the home-slash-studio that she shares with her landscape-architect partner is used exclusively for lacquering.
In fact, most of the house, which is in a leafy area outside Brussels, is taken up by Tangelder’s atelier space.
She moved to Belgium shortly after graduating from Design Academy Eindhoven in 2013, and has become part of an increasingly rich design scene in the country over the past decade.

“I moved to Belgium because I really like the culture, the art scene, architecture as well,” said Tangelder. “The design scene I thought was actually quite minimal, or I didn’t really see a lot of studios at that time. But I liked that as well, it felt a little bit more new for me.”
“I think it developed a lot, the landscape in design in Belgium over the last 10 years,” she considered. “There’s a lot happening right now.”
It has certainly been a productive decade for Tangelder, whose back-catalogue is impressively extensive considering she has only ever employed a very small number of assistants.
Part of that has been made possible thanks to collaborations with the healthy network of craftspeople across Belgium that Tangelder has established to help with production.
“That has been super important for me,” she said. “Each material that I really love, I have a partner now.”

But moreover, the chunky portfolio is a reflection of a huge amount of hours spent working in the studio. Though she says her work-life balance is improving, Tangelder works almost every day including weekends, and has been known to go years without a holiday.
“I really like it, so for me it’s the best way to spend my time,” she said, before pausing.
“I should think about it more as fun time, because of course it’s also a struggle. You’re always struggling over all the decisions that have to be made.”
Like many independent designers, Tangelder has had to battle to earn a living from her discipline.

“In the first years it was quite a struggle to start from out of nothing,” she remembered. “Just to survive and make it happen, and to earn a project back – there’s so much investment in each project.”
Over time, she says she has acquired a reasonably good sense of which pieces are likely to prove more lucrative, though she has resisted the temptation to focus her energies entirely on these.
“I think when you decide to only continue projects that you know will have commercial success, then it will be less experimental,” she explained.
“So that means you take risks all the time,” she added. “It’s maybe more intense, but also more fun.”
Most of Tangelder’s work involves one-off or limited-edition pieces for galleries, but she has also partnered with brands.
A big moment came in 2022 when she was commissioned by Cassina to produce a collection of side tables and pouffes, and she has continued to work with the Italian brand each year since.
This year she was able to put on a solo exhibition at Milan design week supported by Cassina, showcasing a combination of her independent pieces and products created for the brand.
It was an unusual example of small-scale making and larger-scale production design being displayed side-by-side.
Far from being a barrier to creative expression, Tangelder has found that these commissions can be an enabler by providing up-front revenues, unlike solo work.
“So it gives less pressure, I would say, which is very good for the creative process,” she said.

But you can have too much of a good thing, and while she enjoys the more collaborative experience of working for a brand she limits this type of work to two projects per year to ensure she has plenty of time for her own pieces.

Tangelder’s current obsession is cast and oxidised metal, so she reports spending a lot of time these days in a foundry in Antwerp. Her most recent piece is a grungy take on a conventional desk lamp, in white bronze.
“I just think the material is very me,” she remarked. “That desk light tells a lot about how I like to see objects. It’s really in between a sculpture and a functional object.”
Looking to the future, she is interested in working more with fashion, having previously designed a chair for Dior.
And, she would like to work on a larger-scale installation – perhaps an outdoor sculpture, she suggests.
In a world where for various reasons the boundary between design and art is increasingly blurred, Tangelder is undoubtedly at the forefront.
She is an interesting 20/20 choice from Sato, who is typically associated with minimalist, highly functional product design.
For her part, Tangelder sees her work as partly an indirect response to the Sato approach – a continuation of a conversation.
“I have, of course, quite a different form language, but I think it’s also a reaction to what he’s done,” she said.
“He’s so clear in the decisions that he makes, he’s a master in it, and I’m really grateful that he sees what I’ve been doing.”

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.

items.title: Banned player says whole Australia team knew about sandpaper cheating plot
paragraphs: Cameron Bancroft has claimed the whole Australia team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot in explosive revelations that will heap pressure on current captain Pat Cummins.

In a detailed testimony, published by the West Australian,, external batter Bancroft - the player caught with the sandpaper during the Test match against South Africa - has given arguably the most complete account of the events in Cape Town eight years ago.
"In 2018 not the entire truth was told," said Bancroft. "I have never been completely honest about what happened."
For the past two weeks, Australian cricket has been embroiled in a debate over the ball-tampering saga following the publication of Usman Khawaja's autobiography.
Khawaja wrote that the whole Australia team knew of the plot, claims supported by David Warner and Chadd Sayers. Cummins described Khawaja's account as "wrong" and "nonsense".
On the day Cricket Australia announced a forum into the sandpaper episode, Bancroft published his account, explaining he was motivated by the news conference given by Cummins.
"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference," said Bancroft.
"It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone.

"What I saw, experienced and lived with - not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa - is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time."
Opener Bancroft was given a nine-month ban for his part in the plot.
Steve Smith was stripped of the Australia captaincy and given a year-long ban, the same suspension given to vice-captain Warner. No other players or coaches were punished.
In his more than 4,000-word piece, Bancroft has claimed:
Sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa – the match before Bancroft was caught
Bancroft had conversations with the Australia seamers – Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether the ball was "swinging enough"
Before the third day of the second Test, the entire playing group and staff had "celebrations" about the effect of the sandpaper
When Bancroft was caught during the third Test, then Australia coach Darren Lehmann told 12th man Peter Handscomb to "get the sandpaper off Bangers now"
Bancroft found the publication of a joint-statement by the Australia bowlers in 2021 "deeply painful".
Khawaja's autobiography and the subsequent claims made by Warner and seamer Sayers have reopened old wounds related to the sandpaper saga.
Still, those connected have remained true to the accounts they have presented during the intervening eight years.
The most significant denial came from Cummins, who rebuffed Khawaja's account in an extraordinary 68-minute address to the media in Sydney. Lehmann and Starc have also reiterated their denials.
Now, it is the extensive detail provided by Bancroft that could shed a whole new light on the controversy and lead to further questions for Cummins, Lehmann and Cricket Australia.
Cummins is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand on 9 December.
A statement released on behalf of Cummins said: "Whilst we feel for Cam and everything he's been through there's nothing in the statement that hasn't been answered by Pat in his press conference."
A Cricket Australia statement said: "We respect that Cameron Bancroft has told his story, and we will take time to consider his comments.
"We expect that there will be many dimensions to the events of 2018, which is why we have established the forum for individuals to give their version of events.
"We are finalising the terms of reference and will commence the process as soon as possible."
In his account, Bancroft said: "I have spent eight years speaking about accountability, honesty and the lessons I learned from one of Australian cricket's darkest moments.
"However, in 2018 not the entire truth was told. I have never been completely honest about what happened.
"It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team.
"When I was questioned during Cricket Australia's investigation, I did not give a complete and truthful account.
"I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others.
"I did this to protect Cricket Australia's investigation and not implicate others around me."

Bancroft said his actions were "discussed" and "acknowledged" by the entire playing group at the end of the second day and before the beginning of the third day. He said he was encouraged by Saker, who has since worked as a consultant with England.
The only person within the camp to express unease at the ball-tampering, according to Bancroft, was media manager Kate Hutchison.
"I received wraps and encouragement from members of the playing and coaching staff, especially David Saker," said Bancroft.
"Our media manager, Kate Hutchison, expressed her objection to what was happening.
"I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion.
"I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up.
"Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it."

Bancroft identifies Saker as the coach Khawaja claimed encouraged him to work harder on the ball during the third Test in Cape Town. The 33-year-old said he took "feedback" from all the bowlers and wicketkeeper Tim Paine, who took over the captaincy when Smith was sacked.
In Cape Town, Bancroft was confronted by the umpires when TV cameras showed him concealing the sandpaper in his trousers. He claimed Lehmann sent a message to him via Handscomb.
"Peter Handscomb ran out at the drinks break after I'd been caught and shoved the sandpaper down my pants," wrote Bancroft.
"He said to me: 'I think it's time I take that off you now.' And Pete was doing his job after Boof [Lehmanm] shouted to him on the walkie talkie "get the sandpaper off Bangers [Bancroft] now".
"If he didn't know he wouldn't have said that. And if it wasn't clear enough before, then it was obvious now."
In 2021, Bancroft was playing county cricket with Durham and gave an interview to The Guardian in which he said the bowlers' involvement in the plot was "self-explantory".
In response, Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and spinner Nathan Lyon released a joint-statement denying any knowledge that ball-tampering had taken place.
"Reading that statement was deeply painful," said Bancroft.
"I had memories of conversations on the field in Port Elizabeth and Newlands, feedback about the ball and shared celebrations that made the statement difficult for me to digest."
For almost two weeks, Australian cricket has been at war with itself over the revelations in Usman Khawaja's autobiography.
But there has been an absence of a smoking gun. Without tangible, new, hard evidence, all that was left was claim and counter-claim.
Naturally, the spotlight fell on Pat Cummins because of his role as a bowler in Cape Town and his elevation to Australia captain in the years since.
His performance last week in front of the media, on live television, was extraordinary. For 68 minutes he took all questions and appeared plausible in his answers.
In being so robust in his denial of Khawaja's account - Cummins called it "nonsense" - the skipper also left himself open to the consequences if it was later revealed he was not telling the truth.
Crucially, it was Cummins' press conference that compelled Cameron Bancroft to speak out.
It must be stressed that Bancroft's account is not the open-and-shut evidence that convicts Cummins or anyone else in the dressing room at Newlands in 2018.

But it is certainly the most complete account we have heard from anyone involved, walking step-by-step through the genesis of the plot, the execution and the fallout. Bancroft has named names: Cummins, the other bowlers, Tim Paine, coach Darren Lehmann and assistant coach David Saker. It is, potentially, the decisive intervention that shifts this whole saga in a new direction.

Whether by accident or design, it came on the day Cricket Australia (CA) announced its forum for evidence into the sandpaper controversy. Before Bancroft's account CA's action felt an unsatisfactory halfway house - not an investigation, with no guarantee outcomes will be published.

What now? Will CA go further? How will those implicated by Bancroft respond? How can Cummins lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand? Could Steve Smith break a silence he has held since the publication of Khawaja's book?
Throughout the past fortnight, there has been a sense that Australian cricket hoped the sandpaper debate would eventually go away. Cummins even said he never wanted to speak about it again.
Instead of fading, the thirst for the truth grows, now fuelled by Bancroft's extraordinary story.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto VI has arrived
paragraphs: More than a decade after Grand Theft Auto V was first released, its sequel is finally launching. On November 19th, GTA VI will be available on both the PS5 and Xbox Series X / S, and it’s quite possibly the most anticipated video game launch of all time.

Part of this has to do with the success of its predecessor, as GTA V sold more than 230 million copies over the last 13 years. Some of it has to do with the sheer length of time between releases, a period that was plagued by leaks and a handful of delays that made the wait even harder for fans.

But GTA VI is now a real thing you can play, and you can also keep track of all of the important post-launch information right here. That includes our own review and interviews with the development team, as well as news on just how the game ends up resonating with players.

Grand Theft Auto VI isn’t just the biggest GTA game to date; it’s also the most romantic. Though the series is well known for its sordid assortment of criminal leads, GTA VI switches things up by starring a pair of thieves who also happen to fall in love after meeting while stealing a car. It’s still an open-world action game full of chaos and mayhem. But many players will also be attempting to nurture the budding relationship in between heists. The sprawling game is designed to support both audiences.

“It’s a risk,” explains Rob Nelson, producer on GTA VI and co-studio head at developer Rockstar North. “It’s a real change for Grand Theft Auto. You can still play it the old way, you can reject all of this stuff. But for people who do engage, it’s meaningful — you’re earning it, you’re working at it, just like in a normal relationship.”
If you want to play GTA VI on PS5 tonight, download yesterday’s firmware update first.

Sony has confirmed the 1.267GB download is mandatory to play the new Grand Theft Auto when it launches at midnight tonight. As with most PlayStation firmware patches, we don’t know what it does though, beyond “some security fixes to the system software.”
GTA VI’s voice actor for Lucia was revealed by… The Game Awards.
Rockstar hasn’t publicly said who is playing the two leads in GTA VI, but The Game Awards’ nominee video says that Manni L. Perez has been nominated for Best Performance for her work in the game.

Arion Kurtaj, a member of the Lapsus$ cybercrime group who leaked 90 videos of Grand Theft Auto VI in 2022 and hacked other big companies, pleaded guilty on Monday, according to the UK’s Crown Prosecution Service (CPS).

Kurtaj, who is now 21, hacked BT/EE sometime between August and November 2021, and starting in early November of that year, the company “noted a marked increase in unauthorised SIM swaps of their customers mobile phones.” He was charged for those offenses and moved to a hotel for his “own protection” in September 2022, but “breached his bail conditions to carry out further hacks on major companies using a mobile phone, the hotel TV’s Wi-Fi and a firestick,” including hacks on Rockstar Games, Uber, and Revolut, the CPS says.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
paragraphs: In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it.

For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) At the start, Lucia is incarcerated and Jason is making a go of things in the sunbeaten Keys, working for a dodgy guy down on the marina and renting a run-down house on stilts with a jetty round the back and a pet snake. When Lucia gets out of prison, the two of them try to make some kind of life for themselves – but before long they get caught up with the wrong people and have to flee the cosy life they’ve just started building.

For a long time you really are two-bit criminals on the run, getting in with every dirtbag petty thief and drug-runner you come across in order to scrape some cash together and stay under the radar. You meet hillbilly pill-heads and biker gangs, friendly conspiracy theorists, a shady doctor, Lucia’s former prison friends and their lowlife boyfriends. By the time I actually got to Vice City – a glitzy den of sin, the centre of all Leonida’s pleasures and all its most extravagant criminality, where the gangbangers hustle on social media and even the narcos are obsessed with their Instagram clout – I had been playing for 30 hours. It took me 70 hours to finish the game and I could have taken longer.

Leonida is so lifelike that at times it beggars belief, so vast that it feels overwhelming, and outside the story missions you can do whatever you please. There are nightclubs, gyms, flea markets, malls, restaurants, clothes shops, basketball courts, shooting ranges, aircraft hangars, projects and mansions, places to hunt and fish or go kayaking, gas stations and thousands of individuals engaged in conversation as you pass by. Interesting things are always happening in your peripheral vision. You might witness the cops chasing someone down to plant drugs on them, or overhear an interesting confrontation, or see a car speeding away and wonder where it’s going – though interesting things always seemed to happen when I was driving a stolen car at high speed towards a discerning buyer, or otherwise unable to stop and follow my nose. Thankfully, another opportunity would always present itself.

I often felt that the only thing messing up Rockstar’s perfect simulation was me. All this detail and realism comes with some disadvantages, namely complex controls and a tendency for the game’s systems to collide with my intentions in unexpected and sometimes annoying ways. Here I am, driving at high speed through the city before clipping the kerb and flipping my car, causing a massive pile-up. Here I am pressing the wrong button and accidentally punching a random passerby rather than greeting them as intended, kicking off a ridiculous skirmish in which I have to knock out half the customers at a restaurant before running from the cops. Here I am again pressing the wrong button at a bike rack and ending up pinned beneath a tumbling row of bicycles. Missions can go south very quickly and for reasons that aren’t always obvious. In every street race I wiped out spectacularly by crashing into something I couldn’t properly see, while my opponents magically recovered from every collision and sped ahead. This can be a frustrating game at times: unpredictable, laborious, unwieldy and, occasionally, unfair. That is because you are not the master of the game world. You simply exist within it.

Like most compelling crime fiction, Jason and Lucia’s story involves an escalating series of messy events that pull them further and further from where they started, and have you constantly wondering how on earth they’re going to get out of the newest trouble they’re in. To avoid spoilers, substantive discussion of this story can only happen in the coming weeks. But I will say that I was rooting so hard for Jason and Lucia by the end that I felt quite sick with worry about what was going to happen to them, pacing back and forth in front of my TV throughout the final missions. Among all the expectations I had for GTA VI, I did not expect it to make me so emotional.

The key to this is the bond you form with Jason and Lucia. After tens of hours in their company, watching them together – how she smiles fondly at him when they dance together, their playful banter, the stick-ups they pull off as a duo, their resilience and faith in themselves and each other in the face of escalating disaster – I found it impossible not to care for them. They are our avatars in GTA VI’s world but they are not blank stand-ins for the player: you decide their actions but not their personalities. They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim. It made me care about them much more. When the story gave me opportunities to decide what would happen next, what came to mind for me was what they would do, not what I would do.

This is indicative of a tonal shift for Grand Theft Auto that became more obvious the more I played. This series is famous for its violence, misanthropy and pitch-black humour. I have been invested in its characters before, have even rooted for some of them, but I have rarely liked them or related to them. This is the first GTA that wants to encourage some measure of empathy alongside its trademark violent chaos. I was astonished to discover that the game offers you small incentives for acts of kindness, such as texting your partner a selfie, doing your neighbour a favour or throwing your rubbish in the bin rather than dropping it on the ground. Jason and Lucia are not extravagant caricatures, but two people trying to make it in a world totally stacked against them. Pretty much everyone in this Floridian fever-dream is a total crook, on the take or mixed up in some bullshit scheme. It’s so easy to get away with crime in this city, and so difficult to do things the right way. The events of this game might be totally outlandish but these characters and their motivations keep things at least somewhat grounded.

If you thought this newfound heart might tone down GTA’s 18-rated provocativeness, however, you would be very wrong. The protagonists may be surprisingly relatable but they exist in a world that is absurdly foul-mouthed, filthy and over-the-top offensive in every imaginable way. I have never played a game that has more thoroughly earned its 18 rating. Barely a half-hour ever goes by without someone snorting coke off a knife blade, or some full-frontal nudity. There are missions set inside a pornographer’s mansion and a small-town strip club; you can visit those clubs and get a private dance (as either Jason or Lucia, for what it’s worth, or together). At one point Lucia opens the wrong hotel room door to see a woman in a corset wielding a golf club, thwacking balls at a guy’s testicles. On the in-game TV there is a reality show about horny geriatrics. It does not so much push the boundaries of taste as ignore the existence of taste. It contains every perverted scenario you could imagine and several more that would never occur to you.

Sometimes it is a little jarring to emerge from a really pivotal and moving scene between Jason and Lucia into a virtual city where the billboards read things like “WANTED for shitting everywhere: THE SHIT BEAST.” But I found these two sides of GTA’s personality surprisingly easy to accommodate. It’s not as though the story is without its many moments of absurd levity and humour, too: at one point I was taking a bunch of terrifying gang leaders with face tattoos on a real-estate tour, where they sincerely admired the outdoor space with brick pizza oven, and another time I was chasing a man wearing nothing but an alligator thong through a well-to-do suburban neighbourhood. A game this huge can accommodate both pathos and lewdness, and much more.

I did find, however, that Lucia – Grand Theft Auto’s first female protagonist – changed how a lot of this landed for me. GTA has never been particularly kind to women (or men, for that fact, but in past games it has exclusively been the women who were sexualised). There is still a lot of sexism in GTA VI’s world, but now we have Lucia to react to it. This is the first GTA in which I have felt the women are treated as people, not only Lucia but also the many other female characters in the story, from up-and-coming rappers to Lucia’s mother, from a jaded strip-club worker to a badass middle-aged drug-runner whose custom purple carbine rifle is her prized possession. This is a game in which women can be as violent, visibly tough and deeply messed-up as the men. And without wanting to give too much away: there are male strippers in Leonida, too.

I am not about to make a case for GTA VI as a feminist game – there is much to be offended by here, if you are so inclined – but I will say that as a woman who has played and enjoyed every GTA game while also often rolling my eyes at their casual sniggering misogyny, GTA VI hits different for me. I liked it more because the women aren’t always the butt of a joke. Also for the first time, I did not find the violence gratuitous or overblown, despite the fact that this is a story about crime and criminals. There is nothing here like GTA V’s infamous torture mission, which made me feel sick. It says a lot that of all the immoral opportunities afforded to me in Vice City, the only thing I straight-up said “no” to was getting involved in a metaverse scam. THAT would be going too far.

I keep reaching for something that sums up GTA VI, as much as it’s possible to sum up a game as vast as this, and the closest I come is the nightclubs. These show GTA VI at its most extravagant: hundreds of virtual people under the pulsing lights, all dressed up to go out, dancing to a fastidiously curated soundtrack featuring some of the real world’s most famous artists as the controller pulses to the bassline in your hands. These big nights out are an opportunity for both Vice City’s sleaziest denizens and Rockstar’s developers to flash their cash: they are the game’s most ostentatiously expensive and showy scenarios. But at the centre of it all, there are Jason and Lucia, dancing together, focused on each other in the midst of all this chaos and excess.
Keza is one of the first people to have played GTA VI. Ask her anything in our live Q&A at 4pm today. Join here.
Grand Theft Auto VI is out 19 November; £69.99 / €79.99 / A$159.95 / $79.99

items.title: Joanna Page says male actor made 'awful' and 'inappropriate' comments to her on set
paragraphs: Joanna Page has said she was subjected to "really inappropriate" and "awful" comments from a fellow actor while on set.
The Swansea-born actress, 48, told campmates on ITV's I'm a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here! that the unnamed male actor had whispered "awful stuff" in her ear before a scene.
"He just spent the whole time just sort of making up this song and chanting about what he was going to do to me, and nobody said anything," she told fellow campmate Mariella Frostrup.
Page has previously described feeling forced to laugh off being groped while filming with a "handsy" TV presenter.

Page spoke of the inappropriate comments during Tuesday's episode of the reality show, as fellow celebrities, broadcaster Frostrup and model Leomie Anderson, discussed navigating male-dominated work environments in their careers.
Page said the actor had come up to her "before you were going to do a take or something".
"And it was just, like, really inappropriate, awful stuff."

items.title: Greetings from a Berlin square, where an artist's statue watches over children at play
paragraphs: Berlin's Käthe Kollwitz statue watches over children at play Children frolic around the ever-watchful and calm Käthe Kollwitz cast in bronze, in a square named after the German artist, whose work often depicted children in the wake of World War I.

If you were listening to this, you'd hear what isn't pictured: the whoops and wails of children playing on the swings and slides behind me, all under the watchful eye of Käthe Kollwitz cast in bronze. The German expressionist lived just off this square in Berlin — named after her, Kollwitzplatz — and, at the turn of the 20th century, her children probably played here, too.

In the wake of World War I, Kollwitz's lithographs, woodcuts and sculptures fixated on the suffering and futility of war. They depict undernourished, wide-eyed children in the protective arms of mothers whose anguish is etched into their faces. Her statue, The Grieving Parents, stands in Belgium where her son Peter died at the front, aged 18.

As I turn my back briefly on the playground and aim my camera at Kollwitz, a boy jumps into the shot, up onto the statue's plinth. Playing hide and seek, he conceals himself behind Kollwitz. His friend finds him quickly and the two boys chase each other around the statue, inadvertently embracing Kollwitz like she does her own boys in her lithograph renderings.

The Kollwitz statue's presence is calm. She sits, charcoal in hand, poised to draw the happy hubbub of children growing up in a city that is safe. But with wars not so far away and Germany bringing back military service for a new generation, I feel a sudden urge to wrap my arms around my own child, just as Kollwitz did.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto VI is a grounded love story, a gonzo crime thriller and a gaming triumph
paragraphs: Grand Theft Auto VI protagonists, Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, against the backdrop of the Miami-inspired Vice City. Rockstar Games hide caption

I want to tell you about the time I saw Bigfoot. I want to tell you about sitting in the rain on a city street in a muscle car and prepping to rob a bank while lightning split the sky between high-rise condo towers in the distance and the drum fill from In The Air Tonight played on the radio. I want to tell you about gunfights and fistfights, the perfect satire of radio commercials and how the sunrise looks over Ocean Beach. But more than any of that, I want to tell you about the time an alligator bit my mom.

It happened in the backyard of an abandoned house with a rotting inground pool. My mom, Mia Caminos (mother of Lucia Caminos, one of the two leads in Rockstar Games' Grand Theft Auto VI, probably the most highly anticipated video game sequel of all time), was thrilled by the pool. Standing there, amid the artfully rendered weeds and trash, she spread her arms and told me to use my imagination, to see her vision for this ruin of a house with its upmarket water feature, in a scabby neighborhood on the outskirts of Vice City. She speaks in tones of increasingly frantic desperation because she has already put money down on this house, sight unseen. All of her money, actually, in hopes of flipping it and selling it fast to keep her startup real estate business afloat.
Lucia begins her epic as a petty criminal. Rockstar Games hide caption
The pool is still half full of water. There's a dirty, sodden mattress floating in it. And as if this is the main thing standing between her and success, Mia is fixated on getting it out of the pool.

And, dutifully, I do. Playing as Lucia, I grab hold, mash buttons, help my mom drag away the wet, heavy, stinking mattress. And just as we get it up and over the lip of the pool that's going to be the thing that makes this wreck of a house suddenly desirable – that's when the alligator lunges out of the murky water, grabs my mom by the arm and tries to drag her back in.

This is a story about folly, fixation, unrealistic expectations of success at the ass-end of late capitalism, and the vicious, whip-crack cruelty of predators who lie in wait for anyone trying to improve a terrible situation.

But then I shoot the alligator in the head before it can eat my mom. Because this is also a story about violence, and how sometimes (maybe all the times), the loud, cathartic rip of gunfire is the only solution left for people who have already lost so much and can't bear to see one more thing taken from them.
It's a story about my mom and an alligator, sure.
Grand Theft Auto VI returns to Vice City and its Florida-inspired environs. Rockstar Games hide caption

But let's back up a little. For anyone who has somehow missed the shrieking, neon-and-swamp-water marketing onslaught over the past several days, weeks, months and years, Grand Theft Auto VI is the newest release from Rockstar Games. It is a Bonnie and Clyde love story, a knife-edged satire of modern American culture and politics, an unapologetic murder simulator, a love letter to 50 years of crime movies, and a thoughtful, emotional meditation on the sacrifices, small and large, that we make for family. A massive open world game set in the fictional state of Leonida (based on the very real state of Florida), it represents a return to a location that Rockstar hasn't visited in-depth since its 2002 release of GTA: Vice City, and is the first new game in the franchise since GTA5 launched in 2013. According to estimates, it already earned over $1.5 billion in pre-sales and will likely make a total of $3 to $5 billion in its first week, which could make it the largest single entertainment product launch ever.

Fans have been waiting years for it. They have created libraries worth of lore and theories and dissected trailers frame-by-frame. To discount the overheated environment into which this singular work of art is being released would be doing a disservice both to it and the legions of salivating prognosticators who have made guessing the number of bird species included in-game, or speculating on the square mileage of its map, their entire personalities.
While Vice City remains the game's hub, most of its map is actually rural or wild. Rockstar Games hide caption

Now, though, they know it all. We all do. We know that GTA6 is expansive, covering everything from the Keys (where the game starts) to the hilly, forested north, with Vice City in all its grimy, pastel-colored splendor at the beating heart of it. It is a playground, equal parts gorgeous and maniacal, and in all that space the developers have given us a thousand different things to do. You can rob a bank or take a bike ride, go fishing, hunt trophy animals, visit strip clubs, rob random civilians, street race, fly drones, eat a sandwich, work out, manage your family savings account, jump a sports car off the top of a building, steal a plane, punch out a convenience store clerk, fight a bear or, yes, just wander out toward the horizon and study the birds. And while some of that is fun and all of it is diverting (at least for a little while), none of it is the ostensible point. The game-y part of the game — the hundred extras and time-wasters that players have come to expect from open-world projects in general, and GTA specifically — is not what makes it matter.

What matters is Mia and the alligator, Lucia and the gun. It's the multi-pronged, exquisitely balanced narrative about poverty and rigged systems that makes it hard to turn away from GTA while you're playing and impossible not to think about when you're away.
Jason and his pal, Cal, shoot pool. Rockstar Games hide caption

Lucia is an ex-con, a car thief and a small-time criminal who got caught trying to rob a payday loan joint and starts the game in jail. Her partner, Jason Duval, is a veteran, dishonorably discharged, now making a living flying loads for a local coke dealer down in the Keys and living rent-free in one of his properties. Jason skims a little on the coke deals, wears flip-flops and drinks beer in the sun, and goes fishing with his best friend Cal (played with genius-level goofy, drunken paranoia and dopey bravado by Bobby Moynihan). Jason and Lucia have a kid, Tomás, who is currently living with Lucia's family, and every plan they have is about getting right by the law, making a few bucks and grabbing a chance at finally being a family.

Only there are complications — surprisingly banal ones at first (like not being able to open a checking account because of their bad credit) — that slowly ramp up into huge ones across 60-odd hours of main story gameplay that see Jason and Lucia (both of whom are playable characters) graduate from knocking over liquor stores in a beat-up El Camino, to pulling off elaborate heists in the middle of Vice City which will have you dangling from a net suspended from a cargo helicopter hauling 200 tons of cocaine. It goes from Badlands to Die Hard with the speed of a muscle car, all bright chrome and barking straight pipes. From True Romance to Heat like that's just the natural arc of any American love story.

And what's remarkable about the whole bloody delight is that it remains, until its final operatic moments, so surprisingly grounded. This is a somewhat more mature GTA than its predecessors, trading aliens, cannibal cultists and whacked-out drug trips for wellness influencers, local politics and the music industry. Jason and Lucia's relationship is the superstructure around which the entire narrative is built, and it's a dynamic thing that must be maintained in a dozen little ways — making coffee in the morning, opening doors for each other, date nights (even if that means robbing a jewelry store together), or holding hands as you walk toward yet another betrayal by someone you thought you could trust. You can switch freely between them, or just call the other one to come drive the getaway car. Let their relationship dwindle and the narrative shifts, flattens. But when they're together, the two of them talk and talk: In bed, in the car, by the pool. They reveal pieces of themselves in quiet moments, joke, tease, flirt, make plans for a future that always seems right around the next corner. And you love them for it. You can't help but love them for it, and root for them, and want good things for them, because they're just two hard-luck kids trying to do right in a world where "right" sometimes means petting a dog or helping a farmer spray manure all over his boss's house, and sometimes means stealing $10 million from South American drug lords.
The couple that robs together, stays together. That's the hope, anyway. Rockstar Games hide caption

In so many ways GTA6 is an example of inspired synthesis. Rockstar made a killing with the sunlit beauty and craziness of GTA5 more than a decade ago, a game built on deconstructing Hollywood myths and male friendships. Then it made art with a slow-burn meditation on loyalty, death and obsolescence in Red Dead Redemption 2. And this? It is the middle path charted between those two bright stars. It has seriousness and weight and something to say. And also, you accidentally end up starring in a porno movie. Through mechanical tweaks and narrative railroading, the game trades abject chaos for consequences that force you to actually live in its world rather than just murder your way through it, but then makes the dullest, most quotidian chores (like going grocery shopping or answering your mom's texts) feel like a long, slow breath taken between gasping moments of panic.

Yes, you have to sleep. Yes, you have to eat. Yes, you have to work out and put gas in the (stolen) car. But after a while, I found myself actually wanting to do those things because doing them felt like roleplaying; like added opportunities to fully exist within the fiction of Jason or Lucia's world. And in what will no doubt enrage a million over-testosteroned 15-year-olds who want nothing more out of GTA6 than a shinier, brighter, higher-resolution playground in which to jack a Lambo and mow down pedestrians, certain mechanical adjustments in the game (like cars that exist without the tools immediately available to steal them, or how you no longer carry every gun you've ever touched, but store them in the trunk of your ride) have made it harder to jump right in and create mayhem from hour one.

Plus, the police response has been overhauled. Commit brazen crimes and cameras will capture your appearance. Witnesses will describe your clothes or getaway car. Wanted levels now measure not just the size of the armed response, but its sophistication, so speed and stealth become vital. Do a job cleanly, destroy the evidence, get out fast without tripping alarms or blowing stuff up and you're golden. Go loud and cops will search whole regions for you, using helicopters and canine units. They'll hunt you until you change your appearance, swap cars, or simply flee.
Do your best to evade or overcome the police in GTA6. Rockstar Games hide caption

To call the game a masterpiece seems like a cheap, throwaway declaration because after years of development and hundreds of millions of dollars spent, a masterpiece feels… expected, right? Like if it wasn't a masterpiece, that would feel somehow personally insulting. Like they just didn't try hard enough. But the truth is, these things can go wrong so easily. They are enormous, unwieldy, lumbering projects that can fall apart for any number of reasons — and do all the time.

But this one didn't. There is a gloss on it that feels like love. A polish so fine that if you're not looking for it, you might not even notice the way the palm fronds move in the wind when there's weather coming in, or the light on the edge of a storm; how Lucia hangs her head out of a convertible when Jason is driving, or the way the sound of your tires changes depending on whether you're cruising on macadam or blacktop. Does it drag a little in the third act? Sure. Are there NPC glitches, targeting hang-ups and moments where you have to stop to puzzle out exactly who is betraying whom and how they're all connected? Absolutely. But at almost any point, you can walk away from the narrative for a while, call your better half, hop in your car and just drive. Everywhere you go, Leonida is alive around you in a way that no game has ever been before. There are a million stories here just waiting to be discovered or created. Pick one. See where it leads you.

But remember Mia and the alligator. Because at its core, GTA6 will always be a story about predators and prey. And no matter where you go or how powerful you think you are, you can never, ever be sure which one you are.

Jason Sheehan knows stuff about food, video games, books and Star Blazers. He's the restaurant critic at Philadelphia magazine, but when no one is looking, he spends his time writing books about giant robots and ray guns. Children of the Flying City is his latest book.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto VI does something impossible — it lives up to the hype
paragraphs: How do you follow a game like Grand Theft Auto V? Thirteen years ago, Rockstar’s crime-fueled epic went on to redefine what an open-world game could be and became an enormous success, selling more than 230 million copies across three generations of game consoles. It sits just behind Tetris and Minecraft on the list of the best-selling games of all time, and its lucrative online mode has helped it remain popular for well over a decade.

That level of success has allowed Rockstar to take its time with a sequel, which has further increased the hype around the next GTA. A series of major leaks and delays only exacerbated this. At a time when much of the video game industry is struggling, the next edition of GTA stands alone, a cultural moment so big (almost) everybody has been forced to get out of the way. The buildup to Grand Theft Auto VI’s launch is unlike anything the game industry has ever seen.
Even more remarkable? The game was actually worth the wait.

At this point I’ve spent nearly 80 hours in Leonida, GTA VI’s fictional take on Florida. And what I’ve experienced is a game that combines the wide-open freedom offered in GTA V with the remarkable level of immersion from the studio’s 2018 release Red Dead Redemption 2, while also improving on both qualities. At the same time, it’s also the most mature GTA game Rockstar has ever made, merging the criminal antics and absurdist humor the series is known for with a love story that gives you new ways to interact with the world and new reasons for wanting to push forward. This is the GTA game the studio has been building toward for its entire existence.

Let’s start with that new premise. GTA V introduced the idea of multiple protagonists to the series, and VI takes that concept in a different direction. It’s a Bonnie and Clyde-inspired story about Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, two small-time criminals who meet while, of course, stealing a car. It’s the most GTA-possible meet-cute. The idea is that you can play as both characters individually and also build their relationship over the course of the game. Things start out relatively slow. At the outset, Lucia is in prison, and you play solely as Jason, getting things ready for when she gets out. You can fix up your ramshackle house — that involves actually nailing down new stairs and rolling out paint on the walls — and also start building up a nest egg through means that are not exactly legal.

Jason and Lucia’s relationship grows naturally over the course of the game, but it’s also a slow buildup to becoming the inseparable pair they were by the end of my playthrough. GTA VI approaches most of the experience with confident and deliberate pacing. Even when you control them individually, the characters are often together, either just hanging out or partnering for a crime. And being able to play as both is one of the game’s standout features. But I didn’t get to that point in the game until almost 17 hours in. Before that, you play as both leads mostly solo, learning who they are as people, before you’re given free rein to switch between the two.

What’s great about the premise is how seamlessly it fits with what you’re actually doing in the game. There’s some bigger-picture stuff that I won’t spoil, but generally speaking, the main goal in GTA VI is to make a lot of money so that Jason and Lucia can get out of the criminal life for good and retire somewhere comfortably. And outside of the big story missions, you’re largely free to choose how you go about that. You can rob jewelry stores, steal cars, raid drug dens, or even search for hidden treasure at the bottom of the sea. Over the course of the game you’ll also meet different criminals who serve as fences, so you can sell them whatever you’ve got to build up your savings account. Sometimes they’ll even text you targets that are particularly lucrative.

The structure feels natural and gives you a lot of freedom in how you play. I’m not a big fan of armed robbery, for instance. There are just so many things that can go wrong, and I almost always end up killing some innocent bystander when I try to escape. But I love getaway chases, and so stealing cars became my main form of income. Most importantly, though, this structure gives you a lot of reasons to go out in the world and explore. The missions take you all over the map — which is actually entirely accessible from the very beginning, if you choose to play that way — including not only the bright lights of the Miami-like Vice City, but also tourist beaches, swamps, trailer parks, and a wild variety of other locations, each with its own landscape to explore and characters to meet.

To be clear: Despite being larger, more mature, and more lifelike, this is still very much GTA. This is a game about chaos and crime. This comes across in a few ways. First, there are those smaller missions where you never really know how things will play out. The cashier at the pawn shop you’re robbing might have a shotgun, or you might accidentally smash into a big rig during a high-speed getaway. The world itself is full of unpredictable moments that force you to think on your feet. Several times I stopped my car to talk to an NPC whose vehicle broke down on the side of the road. In one instance the driver just swore at me to leave her alone. In another, I got pulled into an entire storyline involving a delivery driver who needed help to keep her AI chatbot manager off her back. I delivered her packages and ended up dealing with everything from porch pirates to tigers.
The structure feels natural and gives you a lot of freedom in how you play.

There are also the multistep heists, which return from GTA V more intricate and complex. These are the big scores and involve several different missions: You spend time getting the right gear and gathering all of the information you need to actually pull them off. Even some of the sub-missions can be gigantic, including one where you have to go undercover for weeks of in-game time to get everything you need in order. But the payoff is incredible. The heists play out like over-the-top action set-pieces, as if they were pulled out of a Christopher Nolan movie like Tenet or Inception (but without all of the sci-fi twists). Even better, all of the missions in the game feel streamlined with a new checkpoint system that allows you to spend less time replaying sequences after failing, and if you fail too many times, you can just skip that mission altogether. There are still a few too many prolonged shootouts, but the checkpoints mean they’re much less tedious than in past GTA games.

All of this action is crammed into a world that isn’t just huge, but also feels more alive than ever before. Like in Red Dead Redemption 2, you can talk with any NPC, but here you have more options, letting you either greet them or, if you feel like causing trouble, taunt them. Most of the time you’ll get a simple “hey” or someone begging for a few dollars. Other times you’ll get pulled into a fistfight or an unexpected storyline. Once, on my way to buy new clothes, I accidentally bumped into some gang members who followed me inside the store, and I had no choice but to fight them. The owner of the shop called the cops, and so I figured if I was in this much trouble, I might as well empty the register. What started out as a quest to find a cool T-shirt turned into a high-speed escape from the cops.

Another important thing to note: While the game retains the series’ satirical tone in many ways, the humor doesn’t punch down like in past GTAs, at least from what I’ve played. Instead it makes fun of stuff that deserves to be made fun of: men’s rights activists, NFT bros, conspiracy theorists, Bryan Johnson.

But what really makes the world so special are all the small, meaningful details. Changing your clothes is a lot of fun, but it also helps keep the cops off your back when you’re wanted. Eating and drinking helps improve your physical abilities. And, this being GTA, you can use just about every kind of vehicle imaginable. That includes taking the bus, which runs on a predetermined route, making stops along the way. You can rent electric scooters, and just like in real life, they’re a menace clogging up the streets of Vice City. Your cars even need to be gassed up from time to time.

It’s a careful balancing act. These details make the world feel more nuanced and textured, but they’re also minor enough that they don’t feel tedious. This isn’t The Sims where you’re constantly monitoring your characters’ bodily functions. Usually, I only remembered to eat when the fitness app on my phone told me I needed more protein, and I didn’t once have a car break down because I forgot to fill up the tank. These smaller mechanisms are just enough to add a sense of realism without getting in the way of the action. You can also ignore a lot of them; at no point do you need to shower, but you might hear some snide remarks from your partner if you don’t.

Perhaps the best example of this is the in-game smartphone, which is integrated into the lives of both characters in a thoughtful, plausible way. Crime bosses might text you a location to meet up, for instance, and you can add it to your GPS and head over. Or Lucia might text Jason a link to a funny video, which you can then open in a social networking app, and you can even read the comments. Smartphones have become a common user interface in games, but in GTA VI it’s a part of the world; the game doesn’t pause when you pull out your phone, meaning that if you get a text while you’re driving, you can either pull over and read it or try to text and drive.
Despite spending more than 70 hours in the world, I’ve only managed to get through less than 60 percent of the total experience

I also found these details, like the phone calls and texts between the couple, pulled me further into the story of Jason and Lucia and made me feel closer to both of them. When the two are together, you can press one of the shoulder buttons to make them hold hands. As long as you keep pressing it, they stay together. At first I used this strategically, imagining that if a couple holding hands was casing a jewelry store, it would be much less conspicuous. But eventually, as I grew to know the couple, it just became a thing I did without thinking about it. These two are crazy in love; of course they’re going to hold hands all the time. You can even do little things like make a coffee and choose to hand it to your partner instead of drinking it yourself, and all of these acts improve your relationship, which in turn impacts how the characters relate to each other and how some of the narrative elements play out.

You don’t have to do any of that. There are just so many ways to interact with the world that different players will find their own things to fixate on. For me, it was a lot of holding hands and drinking coffee every morning. Someone else might get really into fashion or hunting or customizing cars. I barely touched on any of those elements and still felt like I had a substantial experience.

Jason and Lucia are two very different people, each with their own kinds of stories to explore within the game. The big missions are cinematic heists that usually involve some combination of the two. But there are large, branching narratives that are only playable as one or the other character. Jason, for instance, has an old friend who is trying to start a record label in the back room of a strip club. As with the best GTA stories, the tale steadily escalates until you’re feuding with a famous rapper and facing down a number of life-or-death situations. Lucia, meanwhile, has to deal with her mom’s quest to become a real estate agent that gets her caught up with a violent gang, and her best friend pulling her into a pyramid scheme that seems very much like a cult but turns out to be something even more ridiculous. These storylines are so big and absorbing that I would often forget about the main campaign for long periods of time.

It’s not that there are zero issues with the game. The combat is still clunky, and the weapon wheel is still frustrating; there were multiple times when I accidentally equipped a flashlight instead of a shotgun when in the heat of battle. I also ran into a handful of small bugs, like dead bodies comically flopping around or a coffee mug that was stuck floating in a hotel room. But given how ambitious GTA VI is, and how badly things can go with large open games, the relative lack of technical issues during my playthrough is impressive. Even better: I played the game on a launch-version PS5, and it ran just fine.

Back in 2018, I called Red Dead Redemption 2 “the most convincing open-world game ever made,” and over the last eight years that has remained true. There have been great examples of the form since then — Elden Ring, Tears of the Kingdom, Control Resonant, Cyberpunk 2077 (eventually) — but none that approach the scale and detail of Rockstar’s works. Certainly none that attempted to do it in anything like the contemporary, real-world setting that has made GTA so pervasive. Now that mantle has been passed to GTA VI.

To give you a sense of how big this game is, despite spending more than 70 hours in the world and completing the main story, I’ve only managed to get through less than 60 percent of the total experience. And I just spent 2,500 words explaining how good GTA VI is without even touching on some of the best parts: the incredible selection of music, the hilarious talk radio stations, the pitch-perfect casting, the lifelike graphics. There are full-on TV shows, books, and video games that you can experience inside of the game. The most pretentious indie game of 2026? It exists in GTA VI.

For the last decade the idea of GTA VI has been inseparable from the hype around it. All of the noise caused by leaks, delays, and the protracted development time has turned the game into something larger than life, an experience hailed as the biggest game of all time before it even launched. It really seemed like no project could live up to the level of scrutiny that GTA VI has been and will be subjected to. But now we can forget all of that, because GTA VI is actually here. And the game is so good that the outsize hype is the least interesting thing about it.
Grand Theft Auto VI launches on the PS5 and Xbox on November 19th.

items.title: ‘It’s a risk’: How Rockstar built the most detailed (and romantic) GTA yet
paragraphs: Grand Theft Auto VI isn’t just the biggest GTA game to date; it’s also the most romantic. Though the series is well known for its sordid assortment of criminal leads, GTA VI switches things up by starring a pair of thieves who also happen to fall in love after meeting while stealing a car. It’s still an open-world action game full of chaos and mayhem. But many players will also be attempting to nurture the budding relationship in between heists. The sprawling game is designed to support both audiences.

“It’s a risk,” explains Rob Nelson, producer on GTA VI and co-studio head at developer Rockstar North. “It’s a real change for Grand Theft Auto. You can still play it the old way, you can reject all of this stuff. But for people who do engage, it’s meaningful — you’re earning it, you’re working at it, just like in a normal relationship.”

Despite the couple — named Jason and Lucia — being so central to the GTA VI experience, the development of the game didn’t start with characters or story. It began with a place. Nelson says that “pretty quickly” the team settled on placing the game in Leonida, the GTA universe’s version of Florida and the setting of one of the series’ most iconic games, Vice City on the PS2. In 2015, a small group of developers from Rockstar headed to Florida to get a sense of the place and set the groundwork for what would go on to become GTA VI.

“We just went around to feel it out,” explains Nelson. “Go to the Everglades, go to the Keys, go to the city, as many places as we can, and start thinking about what aspects of the place we want to incorporate. And then the map team starts building our version of that and talking very loosely and very broadly about what types of people we want to include and what types of places.”

The team realized they wanted to tell a story that would pull players through the various locations they were creating. And the best way to do that was to have characters who were relatively small-time criminals. They would start near the bottom of the criminal underworld and work their way up, traversing Leonida’s various locations, culminating in the splashy Vice City.

At the same time, the developers also wanted to do something different with the character-switching mechanic from GTA V, which let players swap between three unique criminals, each with very different stories and motivations. For GTA VI, a couple working together to steal enough money to escape the outlaw life fit both of these ideas perfectly. But it also presented some new challenges.

“Could we make a relationship work?” Nelson remembers thinking. “It’d be very different from three characters living separate lives that come together for narrative purposes and then split. These two are going to need to be together all the time and that’s going to be a challenge. It felt really wrong to have these people that are supposedly together only be together when we’re giving you scripted content.”

While GTA V is the obvious reference point, the new GTA also builds off of Rockstar’s 2018 Western Red Dead Redemption 2. That game was notable in particular for giving players more ways to interact with the world: You could talk to any NPC, sit around a campfire while drinking coffee or playing cards, or grow out your beard for a new look.

GTA VI expands this in ways that are designed to reinforce the relationship aspect of the experience. For instance, not only can you drink coffee, but you can also make a cup and hand it to your partner. The two can spend time together sitting on the couch watching TV, or go out to a club and dance. There’s even a button dedicated exclusively to making Jason and Lucia hold hands when they’re together.
“If it’s additive, and it makes you laugh, we include it.”

Nelson notes that when the team implemented the hand-holding feature, it was a revelatory moment for showing how the story and gameplay could connect. “When we got that mechanic in — and it’s not just a toggle, it’s an active thing that you have to commit to and hold — it was a really profound thing,” he says.

But it’s also a careful balancing act. While RDR2 was a widely praised game, it also received criticism for its slow pace, which was due in large part to all of the small mechanical details. These added animations and button prompts that gave texture to the world but could also lead to a plodding pace. That would be a much bigger problem in a game like GTA, which is built around action. Nelson says that he can be “freakishly obsessive” about these kinds of details, but he and the team had to learn to let go when realism got in the way of the game itself.

“Maybe you don’t have to carry around antifreeze in your trunk so that if your engine starts smoking you can top it up,” he says. “Certain things fall by the wayside in developing the game, where it’s like, we don’t need this. But other things, like eating food, it was important for us. You want to feel like you are this person existing in this world to a degree. That felt like it was additive. I love walking down the street with a beer and a cigarette and switching between the two, feeling like a dude. If it’s additive, and it makes you laugh, we include it.”

This also led the team down some unexpected paths. For instance, GTA VI is the first game in the series with functioning bedsheets. In past titles, and in basically every other video game, characters simply lay on top of a bed to go to sleep. That’s because it’s a lot of effort to both animate a character going under the covers as well as rig the sheets so that characters can interact with them in a way that looks and feels natural. The payoff isn’t worth it. But in the context of GTA VI, where the characters hide out together in everything from dingy motel rooms to fancy hotels, it made sense to actually build it.

“Because you’re sharing a living space, and you come in and see your partner sleeping at 3AM, it’s weird to see them laying on the top of the bed all the time,” Nelson says. “Nobody does that. It’s a lot of work to rig the covers on all of the different beds and have them both be able to get in and out of it and be able to be under the covers together.”

Bedsheets, holding hands, cups of coffee — they’re seemingly small details in a world as large as Grand Theft Auto VI, one that encourages players to run wild. But they’re also indicative of the approach Rockstar took with this latest GTA and how the studio attempted to make every element work in concert, even if it required a lot of extra work, like the bed covers. “That’s an example of something that was a lot of work, but it was worth it.”
