items.title: GTA 6 review: Holy sh*t it’s good
paragraphs: Funny, sad, euphoric… GTA 6 is the most entertaining and emotionally engaging open world I’ve played. Rockstar has taken the sandbox freedom of Grand Theft Auto and the environmental storytelling of Red Dead Redemption 2 and made something that feels lived-in. The characters, humour, and systems are all wonderfully written, and the attention to detail makes Leonida a place I want to stay in long after I’d finished the story. The set pieces rival Hollywood, but I'll remember the small, unplanned moments.
An extraordinarily detailed, living open world
Jason and Lucia are brilliant protagonists
Hilarious, unpredictable emergent gameplay
Superb environmental storytelling and art direction
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
In brief: 5/5. Grand Theft Auto VI (reviewed on PS5, out 19 November) is the most convincing open world I’ve played.

I laughed out loud multiple times within minutes of starting Grand Theft Auto VI. Not a chuckle or a smirk, but proper laughs, grinning ear to ear, as a particularly large resident of Leonida giggled, ran, stumbled, staggered and tripped over a railing into the river below. It was ridiculous and completely unexpected, and I loved it.

We've waited 13 years for GTA VI and from the opening credits, Rockstar has crafted a hyperreal but intensely personal world where every corner of Leonida and Vice City offers a surprise. I've been playing for three weeks, finished the story, seen some endings, and I'm still playing to find out what random secrets Leonida has left to share. Much of it has nothing to do with the fate of Lucia and Jason, GTA VI's modern-day Bonnie and Clyde. (Read our GTA VI coverage for more on the game.)

Driving around, you'll spot Just Stop Oil-style protests blocking traffic, teenagers dropping rocks onto motorway cars, or posters and flyers that lead to mysteries and new characters to call from your iFruit phone's contacts list. These aren't side quests in the traditional sense, with a marker on your map and a list to tick off; they're connections to random people, and the sense that this world exists beyond the screen.

Those teenagers dropping rocks? I detoured to teach them a lesson. Later, I stopped for someone posting for social media while balancing on a bridge, and failed to save him when he fell, and I actually felt bad. I pulled over for some teens daring each other to jump from a bridge into a river, decided to show them how it was done, and while I was swimming, they stole my car.
It's not risk and reward; it's just life in Leonida. It's incredibly fun.

The scale of GTA VI is incredible, but not in the usual sense of a vast map to cross. It's the depth and detail that gets me: the branding, signage, store shelves of snacks and comic books that can be read, snatches of conversations from passersby muttering about their lives or something they heard on the radio, the same thing I heard on the radio. Most buildings can be broken into and explored, and I've spent far too long sneaking into warehouses that have no obvious reason to exist beyond making the world feel authentic and the possibility that something of value could be snaffled away inside.

Shops, bars and clubs are lovingly detailed, and once inside you're free to toy with the world. Buy something, drink something for a stat bonus, steal something, change your clothes, or earwig and people watch. Sometimes you'll need to change outfits, because it throws off the cops chasing you; sometimes just because you feel you should wear beach clothes on the beach, because I'm completely hooked into this world.

The geography is considered too. Vice City is a maze of overpasses and winding spaghetti motorway junctions; the city itself is a muddle of back alleys, malls, and beachfront hotels, while the roads out in the country are simpler and more relaxed; the swamps need care to navigate; the sandy, wooded isles of the north are a stolen boat. Beaches, swamps, forests and distinct neighbourhoods all have their own character, and you feel it: stressed in Vice City, calm and playful up north, the mullet of map design, if you will. Even the residents and police behave differently depending on where you are.

Early on, Jason and Lucia visit a rich, enclaved community filled with jewellery shops, polished pavements and high-fashion stores practically demanding to be robbed. A policeman on a bicycle stops them and warns them that their kind isn't welcome. I pushed my luck, choosing confrontational dialogue options, refused to obey, and he called in backup from other pedal-bike cops who made it clear our kind wasn't welcome. I returned at night and stole everything, and it felt so good.

Giving you an emotional reason to do things is one of GTA VI's biggest successes. You start to understand the people who live here, the divisions between communities and the little injustices that make you want to cause trouble.

There's always something happening, too. An armoured car is robbed, so I follow it to the thieves' hideout and steal everything. A farm sign says 'pilot wanted', so I drop in and end up in a whole side story about meth-strawberries that eventually riffs on a Marvel character I never expected. Leonida's residents are 'Karens on crack', too. Scrape someone's car, and they'll chase you down; look at someone too long, and they'll demand a fight; drive down a motorway, and hyped up teen will lean out of their car to challenge you to a race. Once I planned a bank heist, only to find a random gang shooting the place up, and I got caught in the melee. It's layer upon layer of random, living events, and even on a mission, it's easy to get sidetracked as gunshots ring out.

GTA VI rewards your downtime too; it wants you to simply enjoy the place and the moment because conversations eavesdropped on in a bar are hilarious but also tease secrets about the world, whether residents are complaining about the weather or arguing over culture-war nonsense raised by the State's shock jock, who is furious about that weekend's Manatees football result and the demise of 'mansculinity'. Some can be engaged with and will share random but useful news about Leonida.

There's no Ubisoft-style checklist here. Stunts, hidden collectable cards (which you can sell in-game), fishing challenges and sporting events are there if you want them, but the world grows as you explore, meet people and build up your contacts list. You just exist in Leonida and enjoy exploring, competing and completing things.

The weather is a big part of that experience, because it looks beautiful – golden morning sunlight cuts through thick mist over a wildflower meadow with realism, dramatic storm clouds and dense golden fog engulf a city skyline, obscuring buildings and bridges in an atmospheric haze.

But weather also affects how you engage with the world. Days feel long enough to play in, different things happen at different times, and the weather is dramatic and distinct. That hazy mist can obscure your visibility, while hard rain can limit distance and disrupt sound, something used to dramatic effect in a nighttime kidnapping rescue where large halogen lights pierced the rain and mist, creating drama but affecting line of sight in some spaces.

Likewise, a plane handles differently in wind, rain and cloud, as the controls judder and inputs feel less responsive. Flying through a storm, with lightning sparking and rolling across the horizon, gives you a real sense of place and moment but also puts you slightly on edge.

Jason and Lucia's relationship really surprised me in GTA VI, and it's one area where Rockstar picks up where Red Dead Redemption 2 left off. Both are well-rounded protagonists with motivations and shared dreams that you help build. Lucia is alive and sprightly, Jason is dour and determined, and how their connection develops, or doesn't, becomes a game of its own.

A subtle romance and empathy system is at play. How much time the pair spend together, the conversations you choose, the dates, time at home (yes, you can make love in the shower, on the sofa, in the kitchen and, well, all sorts of places) and even how and when you plan and commit crimes all feed into how their relationship develops, and it can affect how their story ends.

What you do on a job matters too. Kill lots of people, and you get a different criminal rating than if you spare lives, and the duo seem to have a healthier relationship if you play to control a room with threats or shoot to injure rather than murder. I wanted a loving crime couple, so almost without meaning to, I started shooting people in the legs and arms to make them fall or drop their guns instead of headshotting everyone in a room. I wanted my Lucia to like my Jason.

Likewise, when Jason went undercover as 'the poolboy' for a saucy film shoot, I held back on how far I took things. Lucia was getting madder in my ear as Jason applied lotion to an actress, and when given the choice to go all in, as it were, I pulled out, as they say, as it were, because I wanted Lucia to still like Jason. I still don't know how far you can take that mission, but this is Rockstar, so I imagine it's all the way (and that's what she said).

Few games get that emotional connection right. It doesn't come only from good writing and characterisation, but from all the little conversations, actions, reactions and animated moments when they meet up or succeed. You'd have a heart of stone to go out of your way to ruin their romance, because you can. You monster.

Controlling when and how they meet up is part of GTA V's character-switching development. Moving between them is nearly instantaneous: the camera pulls out to a global view, zooms back down, and you can message the other to hook up or tell them to meet you somewhere. And you do get committed: when I occasionally Irish-goodbye'd Jason, I felt the need to call him and check up.

The central narrative picks up what worked in Red Dead Redemption 2, splitting the story into chapters that each introduce a new gang or cast and a grand setup to plan towards. The structure gives you plenty to play with, and the story spans more years as the couple bounces from backwater crimes to epic, militarised heists. These feed into cinematic tentpole moments that draw on everything from the later Fast and Furious movies to Assault on Precinct 13, with even a little nod to Die Hard as Lucia sparks a lighter in an air vent, laughs and paraphrases the classic line, "Come out to the coast, we'll get together, have a few laughs."

It's also where Rockstar's love of a good heist movie really shines. Some of the bigger set pieces have the clockwork precision of an Edgar Wright film, with different characters, objectives and moving parts all working towards one carefully choreographed finale. The editing is part of the fun: the action cuts between Jason and Lucia as they tackle their separate jobs, each sequence dovetailing with the next as the plan unfolds, the clock ticks down, and the stakes rise.

The grand finales of each chapter are proper spectacles that never play out the same way and deliver 'cinema'. You might be flying gunships over a stormy ocean, or swapping between Jason and Lucia as they complete different parts of a larger plan. Jason races to a rooftop to stop mobster reinforcements while Lucia hacks a vault, and you're jumping between the two as the action cuts back and forth, the tempo building with each switch. One moment you're holding off a gang; the next, you're working through the other side of the operation, and it all clicks together like clockwork. It's a wonderfully cinematic way to make character switching part of the action, not just a convenient way to get around the map.

Around these set pieces that take time to build are lower-key missions, some tailored to each character, and this is where Rockstar earns its rewards. The satire of modern America, social media, celebrity culture and consumerism that we love about GTA is here in abundance. A favourite is a storyline in which Lucia becomes embroiled in a bored-housewives vape cult that's like Goop meets Elizabeth Holmes.

Then there are the random encounters that make Leonida feel active, and never run how you think. An elderly woman screaming for help on a back road took me to her farmhouse, where I expected a robbery or a rescue. Instead, a client had 'died' in a bondage orgy gone wrong, and I needed to dispose of the body in a river. Even that didn't end as I expected.

Even 40-plus hours into the main story, Rockstar finds new ways to surprise me. It introduces a vault-hacking mini-game that uses haptics and controller prompts for one bank job, then drops in a drug-dog sidekick for a single mission. Ideas are picked up, enjoyed and dropped before they go stale. GTA VI has so many that it never has to hang around with one for long.

Shooting and weapon handling are superb, and each gun feels distinct. The cover system and enemy AI respond nicely even in busy rooms, and stealth is reliable and effective. While the big set-piece story missions can feel a little restrictive and scripted because they need to reach the cinematic heights Rockstar is aiming for, anything can happen outside them.

A bank heist, for example, needs proper planning. Park a getaway car, choose the right vehicle, pick the rear door lock, hack the cameras, wear a disguise, and don't overstay your welcome. The world is so well designed and systematised that everything feels connected. Next time, go in through the front door, or steal a truck and pull an ATM from the wall. Heists in backwater towns are easier because there are fewer police around. And nothing plays out quite as you expect; every bank is unique, and after two seamless jobs I go for a third and it all goes wrong – an unexpected teller wanders into the office for a coffee, an alarm is tripped, and before I realise it, I'm shooting my way out, bags shouldered, and looking for a new car to steal… the best-laid plans are shot.

The police react to all this more deeply than in previous GTAs. There's no longer just a star rating and a zone to escape, but how you escape matters. Swap cars and clothes, and they'll lose you, because they're looking for your description, not you, me, the player. All the old tricks are still here, from roadblocks and air support to increasingly aggressive police AI, but you have new ways to shake them off beyond just driving fast.

It ties into car ownership too, another Red Dead Redemption 2 influence. You can't carry everything, so it's worth stowing a change of clothes and weapons in your car. Carrying a gun openly gets the police involved, but some Vice City passers-by will also decide to take you out as well.

Driving feels familiar from GTA V, but with enough nuance to feel like an evolution, as cars have different weights and handling, and each one reacts differently through the DualSense triggers: sports cars resist less than family saloons when you pull to accelerate. Boats, bikes, planes and helicopters all work as you'd expect, but even here there are subtle shifts in how responsive each can be – one helicopter I stole was uncontrollable and spun into the swamp.

Character models, facial animation, skin, hair, and clothing all deliver the hyperrealism I expected from a new GTA, though they're still larger-than-life caricatures built to feel relatable rather than photorealistic.

Animation, including the transitions between gameplay and cutscenes, is where GTA VI takes its biggest strides. Lucia and Jason are wonderfully handled, whether it's the little snuggles and embraces or the way they hold up a bank and play off one another, but the breadth of animation across GTA VI is what impresses. Every Leonida resident feels uniquely animated, and it's fun just to people-watch. Early on, a drunk girl follows Jason around a bar and is authentically annoying, and the nightlife feels realistically overwhelming. Bar bands are animated to sell their next song, and even the wildlife has moments: I watched a white-tailed doe and buck nuzzle each other lovingly and naturally through Jason's rifle scope. It was cute enough to make me take a breath, but Jason needs more money, so the shot rang out and the wildlife scattered.

Leonida has a recognisable visual identity, bold and vibrant, with every corner full of quirks, from the deep forests of the north to the out-of-town mall and rows of copy-and-paste suburban houses. Fictional adverts, billboards, shops, signage, and TV build the world, as if you see an ad for a beer or car, and you can buy it (or steal it). Beyond signage, graffiti walls, sculptures, exhibits, and more invite you to linger and just take in the world.

It also feels like a realistic evolution of the 1980s Vice City I knew and loved, a city with a history inside a broader world, with references to Liberty City aplenty, from car number plates to Jason and Lucia's accents. It's somewhere to wallow, whether you're having a cocktail under palm trees swaying in a breeze or tearing up Vice City in a neon-lit supercar while crypto bros trade and wannabe rappers parade.

It's a wonder this all runs on a base PS5. I remember the mess of equally ambitious games like Cyberpunk 2077 at launch, but GTA VI is in a different league. The frame rate is locked at 30fps, and it's fine: stable, with little slowdown or stutter, and controls and handling feel spot on. There's occasional soft pop-in, but few visual compromises or trip-ups. You can feel the work that's gone into making everything run smoothly, and GTA 6 is polished to perfection.

I'm really only scratching the surface. Familiar street races, bank heists, and chilled fishing and hunting trips are joined by crypto rug pulls, golf tournaments, and deep-sea treasure hunts. Or I just drive, hunt a swamp thing, stop to solve a mystery from a local ad, or relax with a game of pool and a Patriot beer. You can take on the State's sports and races, go sailing, or listen to 80s FM hits, the biggest dance tracks, or to the MAGA-inspired Richard Bastion Show – "more volume than logic" – who's mad about everything.

This game has video games inside it that feel more complete than some real games I've played, from the top-down sci-fi shooter Time Jackers: Rewind to a lightgun score-chasing bar game Bang For Your Buck. And in typical Rockstar fashion, they all have a satirical edge, like the indie auteur game Tenebrae Lux, which pokes fun at the po-faced walking sims that were all the rage: it's black-and-white, minimal, and filled with overwritten prose like a Taylor Swift song about metaphors.

GTA VI is a world that exists beyond its main story, where everything feeds into and off each other. It's the best world-building I've experienced in a game in years, partly because its systems all work in a coherent, purposeful and layered way, but also because it's not afraid to be weird, whether that's discovering the dumpster lawyer, becoming a frog, slobbing on the sofa and watching an episode of Whose Dick's Whose, or finding an influencer in the boot of a stolen car who wants to be kidnapped for clout.

There are minor restrictions, mainly when the big cinematic missions take over and funnel you down a more scripted path, but for good reason, and the 30fps cap won't suit everyone (yet it's really not an issue). But in a game that otherwise gives you this much freedom, they're the exception.

13 years? The wait has been worthwhile. I still set off with a plan, get distracted by something ridiculous at the side of the road, and lose another hour to a game I thought I'd finished. I laughed within minutes of starting, and I laugh every time I play. I've also been stressed, revolted, astonished, baffled, heartbroken and euphoric. I've run the full gamut of emotions, and I still do each time I return to Vice City.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

items.title: I want to know if toxic lagoon fire caused my husband's rare deadly cancer
paragraphs: The council said it took "its responsibilities for protecting public health and the environment extremely seriously" and had carried out "extensive investigations over many years" into the Llwyneinion lagoon.
Wrexham council added that concerns about the health of firefighters who attended the fire were raised with their contaminated land officer twice.
The first was in February 2004 by the fire officer in charge at Wrexham fire station and on another occasion by a fire officer, who was told to speak to the health authority.

On the risk of another fire on the site, Wrexham council said that in 2006 advice was sought from the fire service about this, but they were told a number of "specific circumstances" would need to occur for this to happen.
An emergency response plan has been drawn up, and it was revisited in 2017.
North Wales Fire and Rescue Service said it was not in a position to comment on the fire in 1980.

It added: "We recognise the importance of understanding the potential long-term health impacts associated with firefighting. Approaches to occupational health, wellbeing and health monitoring continue to be developed nationally as evidence, research and understanding across the sector evolve."
The Welsh government announced in its draft budget on Tuesday that it would commit £2m to "kick-start a new approach to managing contaminated land".
"We are developing a Wales-wide strategy to progressively restore post-industrial land," the government said in a statement.
"We also continue to press the UK government for funding to address the legacy of Wales's industrial past, including the remediation of contaminated land."

items.title: Harvard GSD students propose alternatives to Trump's arch
paragraphs: Landscape architecture students at Harvard’s Graduate School of Design have designed two proposals for Memorial Circle in Washington, DC, the site of US president Donald Trump‘s proposed triumphal arch.

Both designs feature expansive pools of water that cover the current vehicular roundabout at Memorial Circle, and emphasise connectivity to the city’s historic processional axis and straight sightlines to the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery.

The students, Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner, worked with Washington DC non profit organisation The Cultural Landscape Foundation (TCLF) on the designs. The aim was to engage the public in the design process, as the team views the government did not properly open the arch up for review.

“By recognising Memorial Circle’s implicit expressions of monumentality, this pair of counter proposals asserts design’s capacity to critically engage history, accommodate public life, and advocate on behalf of our shared cultural landscape,” said Dvorak and Geitner.
The project began after Dvork and Geitner attended a seminar at the GSD taught by TCLF founding partner Charles A Birnbaum.
“As graduate students in landscape architecture, we took Birnbaum’s course to ground our emerging practices in critical historical inquiry and public participation,” they said.
“The current administration’s assertion of authority over national memory presented an opportunity to put these convictions into practice.”

The first proposal treats Memorial Circle as “a void along the historic axis between Washington and Arlington”. The designers chose to fill the central roundabout circle, currently covered by grass, with a low-lying pool of water.
A natural stone perimeter surrounds the pool and is inscribed with words of “belonging and unity”.
It’s design is “restrained” according to the team, and primarily meant to be viewed from a vehicle while passing through the traffic circle.
The second proposal does away with the traffic circle entirely and instead inserts a straight thoroughfare to Arlington Memorial Bridge.

Two circular fountains would be located on either side of the road. Additionally, a large pool of water, mirroring the perimeter of the former traffic circle, would fill up the site during commemorative events when the bridge is closed.
It draws upon previous historical proposals for Memorial Circle and seeks to pay homage to the precedent of the site.

“[The fountain] geometries arise from the site’s historic proposals, combining concentric circles, intersecting alignments, and formal planting into a composition that acknowledges history whilst creating its own present identity,” said the designers.
“In this way the landscape becomes a physical record of its own change.”

Trump’s proposed arch was announced late last year with renderings by US studio Harrison Design. It features gilded statues and a neoclassical design and has been dubbed the “Arc de Trump” – a play on the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.
Construction on the arch was set to begin in September with the government barreling ahead, but it was halted in early November by Judge Tanya S Chutkan.
Trump has claimed the arch will serve as a “military complex” with snipers in an attempt to use national security as a pretext for construction.

Many take issue with the arch blocking views to adjacent Arlington Cemetery, including members of the Kennedy family, who filed a lawsuit to block construction, claiming that the arch would cast shadows over the grave of president John F Kennedy.
The US Commission of Fine Arts (CFA), which reviews projects in the capital city, approved the project in May.

The proposals also follow recent efforts by the legislature to change Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, which requires federal agencies to consider the impact of proposed projects on historic properties.

Earlier in November, protesters gathered in Washington DC in opposition of the administration’s proposed rewrite of these protections. They are couched within the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) bill recently introduced to Congress.
Images by Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner courtesy The Cultural Landscape Foundation

items.title: Trump lands in China with key meetings with Xi and Putin on the agenda
paragraphs: President Donald Trump greets as China's President Xi Jinping welcomes him after Trump steps off Air Force One at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport in Shenzhen in southern China's Guangdong Province, Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Mark Schiefelbein/AP hide caption

SHENZHEN, China — President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday, seeking to reinforce the U.S. status as the world's leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public.

The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the United States worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.
"It's fine," Trump pronounced on Tuesday from the Philippine capital of Manila, suggesting it was all just a consequence of being a nation that is "big and powerful."

But then the outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase and the National Security Agency's communications network began to overshadow Trump's visit. They raised the specter that artificial intelligence can disrupt daily life, as new cyber vulnerabilities identified require software to be constantly upgraded to fix flaws or other security holes, known as patching, which is supposed to improve how the technology runs.

So at the start of the second day of Trump's trip, Secretary of State Marco Rubio stepped in to reassure Americans on Trump's behalf. He told reporters there was "zero" evidence that the outages are connected or tied to rival nations, cyber hackers or criminals.
"Sometimes when you are going in to fix your system because you've identified a vulnerability, it creates a short-term disruption," said Rubio, who is also Trump's national security adviser.

Xi paid Trump a special honor by greeting him on the tarmac after Air Force One arrived in Shenzhen, China, reciprocating a gesture made by the U.S. president during Xi's state visit to Washington in September.

The two leaders greeted each other at the foot of the airplane's stairs in a handshake that became a hug as group of dancers waved flowers and flags. When Putin arrived earlier on Wednesday, Xi did not greet him at the airport despite their longstanding friendship.

Trump has signaled that he wants to take an improvised approach during his time in Shenzhen, the skyscraper-filled tech hub that is hosting world leaders for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. It's a bet that his unscripted brand of diplomacy based on personal relationships can create some kind of legacy to reshape world affairs during his final two years in the White House.

On Thursday, at a first-ever trilateral, Trump said he plans to talk with Xi and Putin about limiting nuclear weapons and bringing an end to the war in Ukraine, which began in 2022 with Russia's invasion. Analysts are not expecting substantive breakthroughs, despite the unprecedented nature of the meeting.

Before the trip, Trump's aides had told reporters that the war in Ukraine would not be on the agenda. But Trump said on Tuesday that the deaths of tens of thousands of Russian troops every month had created an opening to resolve the conflict.
"I think it's very close to getting it done," Trump said. "We're going to have a good meeting on that."

Trump also teased the possibility of a private meeting with Putin and a separate sit-down with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Rubio clarified on Wednesday that Trump was "serious" about meeting with Kim as a way of resolving tensions with North Korea. But he suggested no meeting was currently scheduled between Trump and Kim for Thursday.

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., left, walks beside U.S. President Donald Trump during a welcome ceremony marking Trump's state visit to the Philippines at Malacanang Palace in Manila, Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Aaron Favila/AP hide caption
Before he landed in Shenzhen, Trump had lunch in Manila with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the Malacañang Presidential Palace.
Marcos noted that he had sent fried chicken from the Philippine chain Jollibee to the U.S. delegation for a late-night snack Tuesday and complimented Trump for "working very hard."
Trump praised the U.S. bond with the Philippines and the interior decoration of the presidential palace.
"Our people share common history, common values, common interests, common architectural tastes," Trump said. "I love what you've done here."

He said after their meeting that the two nations had reached a trade deal on Wednesday, though he had also said last year that an agreement had been reached. The U.S. trade deficit in goods with the Philippines has risen under Trump, climbing from $4.9 billion in 2024 to $12.8 billion during the first 9 months of this year, according to the Census Bureau.
There were no details about the new agreement, although the White House said it will involve Manila buying more energy and farm products.
Trump also had a short reunion with Imelda Marcos, the former first lady and mother of the Philippines' current president.

Famed for her lavish shoe collection, Imelda Marcos knew Trump decades ago through the New York City party scene. During the 1986 "People Power" uprising, her husband, Ferdinand Marcos, was ousted as the Philippines' strongman leader.
Trump called her "always the most beautiful" and the 97-year-old matriarch appeared to hand him a gift, according to a video posted by the White House.

Russian President Vladimir Putin speaks at the APEC CEO summit held ahead of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, southern China's Guangdong province on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Dmitry Azarov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin hide caption

The prospect of Trump meeting with two of America's largest geopolitical rivals has been a source of unease as the U.S. president has been less welcoming of historic allies such as Canada and NATO partners in Europe.

His tariffs that were intended to curb China's trade surplus have done little to stop the progress of the world's dominant manufacturer, which for the second straight year will have exported $1 trillion more in goods than what it imported.
Even without the digital outages in the U.S., questions about how to handle AI loom over the summit.
The technology is viewed as key to unlocking faster economic growth, but its rapid development has meant it poses national security risks and could evolve in ways that put AI beyond human control.

Trump's close tech industry ally Jensen Huang was recently removed as the CEO of Nvidia after he admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an agent of the Chinese government. Beijing has denied that she was a spy, yet the affair raised concerns about how China has been able to access Nvidia computer chips to develop its own AI models that are competing with the U.S.

When asked this week why the U.S. had not been more aggressive in cutting off China's access to advanced computer chips, Trump said there were differences of opinion inside his administration and that "We have a very good relationship with China, and you don't want to insult them."

Trump has said he does not plan to bring up Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as its own. Taiwan is the leading manufacturer of advanced computer chips, including those designed by U.S. companies.
Still, Trump expects that Xi will push him on Taiwan's sovereignty.
"I'm sure he'll raise it," Trump said. "I won't have to raise it."

items.title: SSE threatens to close Yorkshire gas storage site unless ministers intervene
paragraphs: The energy company SSE has warned it will close its Atwick natural gas storage facility in northern England next summer, if the government does not intervene to offer support amid weak market conditions.

The site, located near Hornsea on the East Yorkshire coast, consists of eight caverns with the capacity to store about 309m cubic metres of gas, estimated at about 1.5 days’ worth of Great Britain’s gas usage.
SSE said in an update to investors: “It is increasingly clear that existing market arrangements do not support their continued operation.”
It added that gas storage facilities such as Atwick have a “strategic importance” to the energy system.

Energy companies rely on stockpiling gas in their storage facilities during the summer, when demand is lower and prices are usually lower, before withdrawing the stored gas and selling it during winter when demand for energy for heating and power peaks.
However, the gas price increase triggered by the Iran conflict and the effective closure of the strait of Hormuz have made it uneconomical to stockpile gas during the summer.
As a result, countries across Europe have entered the cooler months of the year with gas stores at their lowest level in more than a decade.

SSE said: “Despite current commodity prices, favourable spreads are not emerging to support the ongoing commercial operation of Atwick.” It came as the company announced its results for the six months to the end of September.
The closure of a gas storage facility such as Atwick could leave the UK even more exposed to price shocks on global markets.
Britain already stores less gas than some of its European neighbours and is instead more reliant on liquefied natural gas imports.

SSE’s announcement comes months after British Gas’s owner, Centrica, warned it would close its Rough site – the UK’s largest gas storage facility – unless it can agree a long-term financial support deal with the government.
The trade union Unite has called on ministers and Centrica to work together to secure the future of Rough, which the company has scheduled for closure in April 2027.
SSE said it continued to engage with the government “on the need for policy intervention to support a resilient gas system”.
The Atwick facility has been in operation since 1979 and has been owned by SSE since September 2002.

The jump in wholesale gas prices has fed through into household bills. On Wednesday the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight forecast the typical household gas and electricity bill will jump by 26% in January to the equivalent of £2,166 a year.
The government has been contacted for comment.

items.title: Energy bills forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as UK inflation rises again
paragraphs: Gas and electricity bills are forecast to jump by £443 a year from January as energy costs continue to push up the UK's inflation rate.

The annual price cap on gas and elecrtricity is predicted to rise by 26% in the new year, according to researchers at consultancy Cornwall Insight. Energy regulator Ofgem will announce the new cap next Wednesday, 25 November.

A sharp jump means inflation is at risk of continuing to rise - official data revealed prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5% in September mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices.
Inflation is at its highest rate in a year as energy prices have accelerated largely due to the US-Israel war with Iran.
In response to prices surging, the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years earlier this month, in a bid to slow inflation to its target of 2%.
Interest rates increased from 3.75% to 4%, and the Bank signalled a further rise could be likely unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.
Higher interest rates lift the cost of borrowing for some mortgages, loans and credit cards, but can also lead to a better return on savings.
Emma Reynolds, chief secretary to the Treasury, said the government was providing help for households with energy costs.
VAT has been cut on electricity bills to zero until next July and the government will also hand £100 to 20 million homes in January.

But with annual household energy bills forecast to reach £2,166, Cornwall Insight's retail markets principal, Craig Lowrey, said that "ultimately this support can only chip away at the edges of a bill that continues to be pushed up by events in the Middle East".
Sophie, who manages a cafe at the Old Boat Corner community centre in Brighton, told the BBC she watches her smart meter at home "like a hawk".
"I'm very conscious of the cost of energy, and it is having an impact on how we function in the home as a family," she said.
"I try to cook using the oven a lot less than I used to. We haven't got the heating on yet in our household. We're just like 'wear more layers'. We've got electric blankets on the sofa."
Shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, said four successive rises in the inflation rate was down to the UK's "soaring energy costs" and Labour's decision to "hike taxes and employment costs".
Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS, said fuel prices were "once again a major contributor" to the increase in the inflation rate in October.
Rising energy prices can lead to more expensive food and staples for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs.
Earlier this month, the Bank of England said there had been "limited evidence" of this, with some firms absorbing cost increases and accepting lower profit margins.
But Fitzner said on Wednesday: "Annual costs of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continue to climb, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices, respectively."
Petrol prices rose by 5.2p per litre between September and October, the ONS said, with the average price last month hitting 174.7p per litre - the highest since August 2022.
Diesel prices, meanwhile, reached the highest price since records began 30 years ago, averaging 199.5p per litre in October.
But the ONS said price inflation in restaurants and cafes had slowed last month, and that prices had fallen on average for hotels.
And food price inflation rose by 0.9%, the slowest pace in five years.
Core inflation, which strips out energy and food costs, and services inflation were little changed on last month. The figure is closely watched by the Bank of England when setting interest rates.
It could mean the Bank opts to hold off on a further rate rise in December, though policymakers believe inflation could peak at 4.9% in the middle of next year and not return to 2% until 2028.
In an "adverse scenario", where the US-Iran war could escalate further and send oil prices higher, inflation could reach 6.2% in 2027, it has suggested.

A spokesperson for the Bank said it decided to raise rates two weeks ago to "limit how much higher energy costs affect other prices, and will continue to set interest rates to make sure inflation returns to the 2% target and stays there".
Additional reporting by Raphael Sheridan, economics producer

items.title: Van Eyck: The Portraits review – a jewel box of phenomenal death-defeating paintings
paragraphs: The stubble is tiny yet silver-sharp on the chin of an unknown old man whom Jan van Eyck painted in oils 600 years ago: so long after both are dead you can still see this bloke needs a shave. The hairs on top of his head are just as miraculously caught, varying individually in paleness and lankness. You feast your eyes on the sagging skin of his throat with its overhangs and shady gulleys like a rock formation. He is a wonder, a freak of nature and yet a perfectly ordinary person. So are we all banal and marvellous, mundane and impossible, suggests Van Eyck.

The National Gallery has created a jewel box of a show bringing together all Van Eyck’s portraits as we define them – a painting of a person for its own sake. Yet portraitist was a long way from being his only job. Van Eyck painted stupendous religious works, including the Ghent Altarpiece that he collaborated on with his brother Hubert. These too have portraits in them, of real people in uncanny proximity to supernatural beings. You could argue this show cheats by cutting out that medieval context of prayer and faith. It’s also a great way for the gallery to show off that it owns three of his greatest portraits. Yet the result makes you see the utterly strange way he collects his slightly miniaturised people like flies in amber.

This artist who worked in Flanders at the end of the middle ages paints like an alien who has hidden his flying saucer in a barn outside Bruges and gone into town to observe the humans. Every detail of earthly life seems new to him. A woman with a big, blunt face looks at us from under the gold-ribboned horns of her fashionable hennin headdress. Van Eyck records the shine, moisture and green-greyness of her eyes but she remains a mystery to him. She is his wife.

If it seems fanciful to see Van Eyck as an alien, stories about him in the Renaissance were nearly as extreme. Vasari believed he was some kind of alchemist who chanced not on gold but the new medium of oil painting. It’s a powerful fable for there is something occult about a painter who can create gold by a trick of the brush. In Van Eyck’s portrait of Jan de Leeuw, a Bruges goldsmith, your eyes are hypnotised by his tiny ring like a real nugget of gold magically inserted into the illusory space of the painting.

The modern artist Willem de Kooning said oil painting was invented to depict human flesh – he was probably thinking of Titian’s lush nudes. Van Eyck reveals the mystery of flesh just by painting a face. No one before looked at the world the way he does. He didn’t invent oil painting but he was the first fully to exploit its multiplicity of slowly built-up layers to create a mirror-like image of reality. Van Eyck is surely looking at himself in a mirror, gazing with piercing, even merciless eyes in his portrait of a man with his head wrapped in crimson cloth. We see the laughter lines in his gold-tinted skin, the pink flush in his cheeks, the beginnings of age or ill health, for Van Eyck would die at around 50. I think it’s timid not to call it a self-portrait.

He depicts smooth youth too, in his portrait of a young man glowing in a brilliant twilight, perfect for ever, behind a parapet with the inscription “Léal Souvenir”, which means something like “loyal remembrance”. This portrait is surely an aid to mourning, a souvenir of loss.

That’s fundamental to what Van Eyck does. His portraits are phenomenal acts of preservation. Behind the clinical exactness of each wrinkle, each chin hair, is a desperate attempt to freeze time, defeat death, make loyal memories of people who will soon be gone, even if they are monstrous.

The Burgundian courtier Baudoin de Lannoy looks a total bastard. He gazes to the side sulkily under his huge, felt-rimmed hat. His eyes are hooded orbs, his long face pummelled by jousts and battles. Yet he is preserved for ever, the shape of his ear meticulously recorded as if in a criminal profile. Uglier still is the Italian merchant in the Arnolfini Portrait, his thin, pasty face half in shadow. The shady side of his face has a droopy, rheumy eye. Has he got a palsy? His sickly face couldn’t contrast more with the pearly beauty of his wife. They seem an ill-matched couple: Death and the Maiden.

Yet a portrait of the same man alone, done around two years later, shows him with bright eyes. Is he being flattered here or insulted in the Arnolfini Portrait? Van Eyck is not a camera, passively recording his world. His paintings are full of imagination, even whimsy. His only surviving drawing, which is in this show, is a study of the stubbly old man. Comparing the drawing with the painting, you see that the sketch is more respectful: in the finished painting he elaborates wildly on swags of skin, the vortex of the ear.

The weird geology of ears, chins and wrinkles anticipates the impulsiveness and chaos of Hieronymus Bosch. Van Eyck’s portraits are brooding creations of north European melancholy. Entering his world is perfect as winter deepens.
Van Eyck: The Portraits is at the National Gallery, London, 21 November to 11 April

items.title: How the East Potomac golf course became a D.C. landmark — and what could happen to it
paragraphs: Dick Walsh won a championship tournament at East Potomac Park in 1923. Library of Congress hide caption

Runners and cyclists still have access to D.C.'s East Potomac Park, despite the Trump administration's plans to close it over the weekend. But its golf course is conspicuously missing the flags that typically mark the holes — and at least some of the people who typically play them.

Federal Judge Ana Reyes issued a restraining order late Saturday to keep the beloved park open for two weeks, just hours before the National Park Service planned to cut off public access to most of it indefinitely.

But Sunday marked the last day of the government's lease with the National Links Trust, which had operated the golf course since 2020. And Reyes did not order the government to keep operating the golf course — though she has since signaled she may consider it.

"Whether and how Defendants do so is solely within their discretion, but Defendants cannot use the absence of golf operations as a reason to exclude the public from the Course," Reyes wrote in her 30-page order.

Reyes criticized the government's "pretextual" justification and "arbitrary" timeline for closing the park, which she said would "irreparably harm" the people who enjoy it on a daily basis — including the local preservationists and golfers who first sued to protect the course in February.
Protesters gathered at East Potomac Park on Sunday to rally against its planned closure. Tom Brenner/AP hide caption
In comments on social media and to the press, President Trump slammed her decision and said his administration will appeal. The White House referred NPR to those comments.
"What she's done is she stopped it for 15 days," Trump told reporters when asked about the case on Monday. "You can't stop that."
The National Park Service and Interior Department did not respond to NPR's questions about the future of the course.

Trump has his sights set on redeveloping the golf course — which he has repeatedly decried as decrepit and dangerous — into a championship-level venue. Administration officials are due to present that vision to the federal Commission of Fine Arts on Thursday.

According to the government's 64-page submission, architect Tom Fazio's design would replace East Potomac's three courses of varying difficulty levels with one 18-hole layout stretching across almost the entire peninsula.

The plan is broadly unpopular in D.C., as it would eliminate the perimeter road beloved by runners and cyclists, and the grassy areas where people picnic and birdwatch. Critics worry the new course would be less accessible for beginners and less affordable for everyone. Prices currently range from $17 to $48 per round, and the Trump administration has not said what a round at the new course would cost, only that locals would be able to play at a discount.

The proposed redesign, which the Trump administration has submitted to federal arts commissions for review, shows one 18-hole course stretching across East Potomac Park. It would replace the park's three existing courses for different skill levels and eliminate the road around the perimeter. Department of the Interior hide caption

Locals agree that East Potomac could use some improvements, including to its long-eroded seawall. But that's very different from overhauling the course entirely. Reyes pressed government lawyers at a Friday hearing on why the National Park Service chose the latter.

Officials pointed to Trump's social media directives, but also argued that the park needs to be closed for other reasons: to repair the seawall (for which it acknowledged Friday there is no plan yet) and because of the lack of a golf course operator (a situation Reyes described as "entirely self-inflicted"). And it says there are nearby recreational areas people can use instead — though critics say there is no substitute. Reyes seemed to agree.
"Plaintiffs' harms are tied to 'East Potomac's beauty, historic layout, and historic designs,'" Reyes wrote. "While there are other parks in Washington, D.C., there is no other East Potomac Park."
East Potomac Park, as seen from above in 1935, is home not only to a golf course but also to grassy picnic areas and a perimeter road beloved by runners and cyclists. Library of Congress hide caption

East Potomac is a man-made peninsula, originally dredged from the Potomac River to facilitate shipping channels. Congress designated the land a public park in 1897, declaring it should be "forever held and used as a park for the recreation and pleasure of the people." It houses many forms of recreation, including a tennis complex, a perimeter road and a 220-acre golf course.

The golf course at East Potomac is one of seven that the federal government built in D.C. between 1917 and 1948, according to a 2017 National Park Service historical report. It calls that "a testament to the rise in popularity of the sport of golf and the demand for public golf courses for those who could not [afford] private memberships to exclusive golf clubs in the early decades of the 20th century."
That number has since dwindled to three. East Potomac is the busiest, especially after a renewed interest in golf during the COVID-19 pandemic: It hosted some 125,000 rounds of golf in 2025 alone.

"In a city where politicians are constantly focused on what separates us, East Potomac is one of the few remaining spaces where no matter who you are, what you do, or the state of your game, everyone is welcome and everyone is treated the same," plaintiff Dave Roberts said in a statement when the lawsuit was first filed.

Its first 18 holes were designed by Walter Travis, one of the top amateur golfers in the U.S., who shaped dozens of courses during the "golden age of golf" (which ended around the onset of the Great Depression).

He modeled East Potomac after Scottish "links-style" courses, which are known for their coastal terrain and relative lack of trees — in this case offering clear views of the Potomac River and the Washington Monument. And, in a unique twist, Travis designed the course to be reversible, for the durability of the grounds and to the delight of those who played them.

"Travis captured a design style that characterized the era's greatest courses, including East Potomac: difficult for aggressive elite players, yet playable for unskilled beginners," plaintiffs wrote in their February complaint.

The first portion of the course opened to the public in July 1920. It cost 25 cents to play a round, including locker room privileges. The course was a huge hit, drawing 16,345 golfers in its first year. That number nearly quadrupled by 1921, according to the National Park Service.
Golfers play in a tournament at East Potomac in June 1923. Library of Congress hide caption

The links grew to meet demand over the next decade, ultimately expanding into three courses (red, white and blue) plus one of the first miniature golf courses in the U.S., which features tiny replicas of the White House and U.S. Capitol and is now the country's oldest continually operating mini-golf course.

But despite its broad appeal, East Potomac initially allowed Black players access only during limited hours one day per week. A separate course, Langston, opened to serve Black residents in 1939 — on the site of a former city dump — but suffered from neglect and downright hazardous conditions.
One day in June 1941, three Black golfers showed up at East Potomac and demanded to play.

According to historical accounts, they had a "fair-skinned" friend purchase their tickets but were turned away. They returned with some powerful government allies, and park police ruled that the men should be allowed to play since they had tickets. The trio completed 18 holes, accompanied by police and amidst the "boos and chorus of insults" from white onlookers.
The next day, the interior secretary issued an order opening the course to all players, regardless of race.

Harassment and other forms of segregation persisted at the city's municipal courses for over a decade, but the golfers' 1941 protest is seen as a turning point in the fight for equal access to public spaces. The National Park Service says it "opened the door for the full integration of all national park facilities in 1945."
Judge Reyes has nodded to that part of the park's history throughout the case, including while grilling government lawyers at a mid-October hearing.

"We're not just talking about some putt-putt thing that went up by the beach you take your kids to," she said, adding that the course holds a rich history and "deep amount of meaning" to locals. "There was bravery in the people who first desegregated this golf course."

The course has only closed — temporarily — a few times in its history, including for a portion of World War II and for a few days after Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination, in 1968, when National Guard troops responding to riots set up camp at East Potomac.
There have been changes at East Potomac over the decades, like the addition of a two-tiered driving range in the 1990s.

But, as the National Park Service said in its 2017 report, the city's courses continue their original intent "to allow golfers of all ages and skill levels to play at an [affordable] cost compared to private and even semi-private clubs in the area and remain extremely popular."

Plaintiffs note in their lawsuit that a weekend round at East Potomac's blue course costs $48, compared to $89 for a Sunday morning round at the Laurel Hill Golf Club, a municipal golf course in nearby Fairfax County, Va.

Critics worry a championship-style course would be even less affordable — especially one that Trump described over the weekend this way: "All over the World it will be acclaimed as being the Best Golf Course anywhere."

Trump said locals will get a 50% discount. But the administration has not said how much it will cost to play. The administration's proposal only points to "benchmark" championship courses in California, Texas and New York, where locals pay up to $90 per weekend round, even with a discount. The government admitted Friday that those were merely illustrations.
There's also the question of how beginner-friendly the redesigned course would be.
Golfers look at clubs being given away after the National Links Trust stopped operating East Potomac's golf course on Monday. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP hide caption

Reyes pointed out last week that under the administration's proposal, even from the shortest tee at every hole, the course adds up to 6,013 yards. She asked the government how that compares to recommended course length averages for different types of players, including seniors and young players, and did not get an answer.

The administration said repeatedly that its plan is not yet final, as it still needs to undergo various federal reviews that require input from experts and the public. Lawyers told Reyes that there is no contract between the government and Fazio, the architect — despite Trump's repeated social media posts saying work would begin on Nov. 15.
Even so, the government said it had to close the park that day in part because there was no one left to run the course.

The nonprofit National Links Trust had entered into a 50-year lease to operate the city's municipal golf courses in 2020. But the government terminated its East Potomac lease last December, accusing it of failing to make capital improvements. The trust continued to manage the course on an interim basis — and still manages the city's other courses — but announced last month that its role would end at East Potomac on Nov. 15.
Reyes said that timing was no coincidence.

"[The National Park Service] claims that it would be unable to safely manage the course itself. In other words, the Government's hands are tied," she wrote in her order. "But the Government tied the knot itself."

Reyes has been openly hesitant to take the administration at its word at this point in the increasingly inflammatory case. She ordered an inquiry into potential misconduct by government lawyers and officials after they cut down hundreds of trees on short notice in October and repeatedly contradicted the president's social media announcements in court.

At Friday's hearing, Reyes questioned why the National Park Service couldn't renew its lease with the operator, especially since it has already entrusted it to manage two other municipal golf courses for another 50 years. She mulled whether the government could theoretically step in to run the golf course, at least until it finds another party to do so.

Reyes appears to be weighing whether she has the legal authority to compel the Trump administration to do that. On Monday, she ordered both parties to submit briefings discussing "whether the Court may require the Government to operate East Potomac Golf Course in order to maintain the status quo."

items.title: OpenAI announces new AI safety program; researchers worry it won't be enough
paragraphs: The OpenAI logo is displayed on a smartphone screen placed on a reflective surface onto which the company's logo is projected in Creteil, France, on Nov. 6, 2026. Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images hide caption
AI safety researchers say OpenAI's new third party evaluator program falls far short of what the company promised, raising concerns about its effectiveness.

The company announced Monday that staff from four AI safety and research organizations will become "embedded assessors" to "give people a clearer view of how labs are evaluating and managing [potential] risks."

"Getting an outside opinion on the safety work and the robustness of these systems is going to be increasingly important and valuable," CEO Sam Altman said at Semafor's Silicon Valley and the World conference on Monday.
However, many AI safety researchers say the new program is a far cry from Altman's vow in September that independent evaluators would have "employee-like access" to internal company systems.

Altman's promise came after details of the Hugging Face attack by OpenAI's autonomous systems shook the AI field. Worries of the technology's catastrophic risk captured public attention, and rival Anthropic said it would set up such a program.

"We are giving deep access to some of the most sensitive tools and models our researchers use...that are the most important for assessing key, relevant and timely safety claims," said Lama Ahmad, OpenAI's frontier assurances lead, on X.
Prior to these new embedded evaluation programs, AI companies have brought in outside researchers to assess the capabilities of AI models and identify safety loopholes the companies have missed.

The work of outside evaluators have already helped shed light on the companies' work, and have raised public awareness of safety risks that the technology poses. One recent report about Anthropic using AI to significantly speed up model development has prompted concerns in the field about how close the top companies are to using AI to autonomously build even more powerful models, a stage known as recursive self-improvement. Some in the field worry that if this happens, the velocity of development could lead to catastrophic consequences for humanity and are calling for new regulation against the practice.
Researchers say the actual announcements of how these programs will work suggests something more limited than what Altman promised.
"The assessors have very narrow scopes to their access, and only two of them seem to really be allowed to talk to employees," said Sydney Von Arx, founder of AI safety research group Nightingale.

One of the announced assessors, Apollo Research, outlined its limited access to OpenAI employees. If employees that haven't been whitelisted, or pre-approved, reach out to the embedded assessors, then the assessors will have to loop OpenAI in before having substantive conversations with the employees.
It's important for outside researchers to be able to interview employees, Von Arx said. "They help you find your blind spots. They tell you what you're missing."

Another glaring omission: "Nobody has access to internal Slack," Von Arx said, referring to the corporate messaging tool, which would allow assessors to see what employees are talking about with one another. "Imagine being an 'employee' and only being allowed to talk about company information with whitelisted coworkers and having no Slack."

In a statement to NPR, OpenAI said there's currently no standards for embedded evaluations. "We expect to deepen these relationships over time and share what we learn to help establish best practices for effective embedded assessments across the industry," OpenAI spokesperson Gaby Raila said. The company also said assessors can ask to talk to employees that haven't already been whitelisted, and that there is a process in place to get statements from OpenAI about things they've learned informally.

The third-party organizations will focus on various aspects of AI safety, according to OpenAI. Some of the work is related to preventing models from trying to engage in undesirable behavior, and other parts are related to catching bad behavior when it happens. The assessors will have access to some internal models, training processes and some OpenAI employees. The assessors will be able to publish their findings after OpenAI redacts confidential information, the company said.

OpenAI's commitment to embedded evaluations was questioned when three employees who worked on safety were fired. They subsequently said they were worried OpenAI is walking back from its promise of having embedded evaluators.
One of the fired employees, Tomek Korbak, was OpenAI's technical point of contact for two outside evaluators that investigated the Hugging Face attack.

"Embedded auditing will only fulfill its aims if the auditors really get employee-level access as opposed to being hired to do a specific job," he posted on X in response to OpenAI's announcement. "Sadly, OpenAI makes it clear now that [Sam Altman's] September tweet about 'employee-like access' was just an awkward overpromise that the company wants to quietly walk back."

items.title: Iran-backed militias tortured him, but Iraqi environmentalist refuses to quit
paragraphs: Environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi stands on a boat and looks out over the marshes where he grew up in southern Iraq. Despite having been kidnapped, tortured and accused by an Iran-backed militia of being an Israeli agent, Asadi is back in the marshes. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption

CENTRAL MARSHES, southern Iraq — For all he's been through, environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi still approaches each sighting of wildlife in Iraq's marshes as if it's the very first time — even though he has seen them thousands of times before.
"Do you see?" he asks excitedly, pointing out a white egret perched on the back of a water buffalo as his long, narrow boat glides by. "It's a buffalo! With a bird on its back!"
Kingfishers with bright flashes of blue on their wings perch on reeds rising up from the shallow water. A wild boar and her piglets dart in front of the boat and disappear into the tangled grass.

Despite having been kidnapped, tortured and accused by an Iran-backed militia of being an Israeli agent, Asadi is back in the marshes, monitoring water levels and talking to fishermen and buffalo herders to find out what difference a season of rain has made in the biggest wetlands in the Middle East.

Five devastating years of drought dried out some of the marshlands. In places where water remained, it was brackish, stunting the reeds and grass. Water buffalo were dying from lack of food and contaminated water.

Birds sit in the reeds around the marshes, which was named a UNESCO world heritage site in 2016 for its biodiversity and legacy as the site of one of the world's oldest civilizations. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
Residents who make their living from breeding the animals and selling milk and cream headed with their remaining herds in search of water or to the outskirts of southern Iraqi cities.

They have now begun to return, repopulating some of the tiny floating islands where, aside from some modern technology, marsh residents live a way of life little changed since Sumerian times, more than 4,000 years ago.

Asadi is a leading environmental figure in Iraq. In the 1990s, in retribution for a Shiite uprising in southern Iraq, Saddam Hussein drained the marshes and set parts of them on fire to flush out resistance fighters.

After Saddam was toppled in the U.S.-led invasion in 2003, Asadi and Iraqi-American environmentalist Azzam Alwash helped residents tear down packed earth embankments holding back water from the Tigris and Euphrates rivers and the water flooded back in.
The two engineers founded the environmental organization Nature Iraq in 2004.

Asadi has been a high-profile figure, working with embassies and government ministries to garner support for the marshes and helping successfully lobby for inclusion as a UNESCO world heritage site in 2016. The inscription recognized the marshlands' biodiversity and their legacy as the site of one of the world's oldest civilizations.

A widow fishes across from Chibayish — a town on the edge of the marshes. She has caught just a few small fish. Pollution and increased salinity have decreased fish native to the marshes. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
Gregarious, welcoming and with a zeal for showcasing his homeland, Asadi frequently took Western journalists through the marshes, often hosting them at the Nature Iraq offices.
Kidnapped, tortured and accused of working for Israel

In February 2023, Asadi was kidnapped by an Iran-backed Iraqi militia, which accused him and the journalists he met of being Israeli spies who had fomented anti-government protests that had rocked Iran a few months earlier.

He was returning from Baghdad to his southern hometown of Chibayish after a meeting with the Iraqi president to discuss help for destitute families in the marshes when gunmen in pickup trucks and SUVs cut off his car on the road south.
They blindfolded him and threw him onto the floor of a vehicle, and with their feet on top of him drove him to what he believed to be farmland. There he was beaten and told to confess to being a spy.

"They showed me a map of the world," he says. "They were showing it on a screen and there were networks on it, connecting all the countries of the world — in Europe, Africa, Asia, America — to Tel Aviv. They said 'You are not just a spy, you lead a spy network from all the capitals of the world to Israel.'"

They accused him of ferrying journalists, whom they also accused of being spies, across the marshes into Iran. Nature Iraq, like almost all non-governmental organizations, often takes journalists and others on tours in Iraq to raise environmental awareness.
Asadi, who is 69 now, was born in the marshes — literally in a boat when his mother went into labor two months early while she was collecting reeds and grass.

Asadi, 69, was born in a boat in the marsh when his mother went into labor while she was collecting reeds and grasses. He says the landscape has changed after the drought — entire lakes drying up and plants that normally grow in desert taking root where there would normally be marshes. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
"When I opened my eyes the first time, I opened my eyes to the blue sky, to the water, to the reeds and also birds," he says. "My mom returned home with the grasses, reeds and a baby."

At the age of 6 he rowed his own small boat to school. In the rainy season he says, the students would collect reeds to put on the classroom floors and when the school flooded there would be fish swimming under their desks.
In 1978, he was jailed for nine months for refusing to sign allegiance to Saddam Hussein's Baath party.
Asadi says when he was kidnapped three years ago and refused to admit to being a spy after being beaten, his captors decided he should be tortured.
They held him for two weeks. Asadi says they placed a plastic bag over his head until he thought he would suffocate and plunged his head underwater over and over.
"When the oxygen ran out I felt like I was going to die," he says.
They ran electric shocks through his body.

"They started from my feet, to my head, my genitals, my chest, my nose," he says in his office in Chibayish, on the edge of the central marshes. "They suspended him from the ceiling "like a sheep being slaughtered."

"They took my left arm behind my neck, and my right arm next to it, and beat them with metal chains. You feel like you're being pulled apart," he says. "I would scream, I would be on the verge of fainting, then they would stop and say, "So will you admit it?""
Then they would throw him back into his cell to await the next torture session.
Asadi has memorized many hundreds of Arab poets' writings, which he recited when he was imprisoned. He still recites poems while sailing in the marshes today. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
He says the waiting was also a form of torture.
"You think about your family, you think about your children and you think of your fate in the coming days and your fate in the coming sessions."
Asadi is also a poet. He wrote his first poem when he was 13 and has memorized many hundreds of other Arab poets' writings.

"I found a way to recite poetry to myself, so I didn't have to think about anything but poetry," he says. "When I hear the sound of the cell door opening — it means they are coming to take me, they are going to torture me."
Even now, in the boat three years later, he recites poems to himself — over several minutes — start to finish.

The one he told himself hundreds of times in captivity is called In Those Days, by Saadi Youssef, an Iraqi poet from the southern port city of Basra jailed in Iraq decades ago before he went into exile in Algeria and the U.K.

"I left the court with the guards' beatings and the judge's ridicule," reads part of the poem in translation. "I have a wife whom I love and a book made of date palms." Asadi recites it in Arabic like a mantra. It comforted him, he says, to imagine that he himself was the prisoner in Youssef's poem decades ago.

Water buffalo are the backbone of the marsh economy – mostly because of their milk. Families living on tiny islands in the marshes let them out in the morning to graze on grass and reeds and bring them back in the evenings. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption

After two weeks, his masked captors, dressed in military uniforms and using phrases that Asadi said were uniquely Iranian, told him he could either sign a confession that he ran spy networks and smuggled journalists into Iran, or he could write a will.
They placed a pen and a piece of paper in front of him and gave him an hour. If he didn't confess, they said, "We are going to kill you today."

"So I wrote my will," Asadi says. "I wrote that I love Iraq very much. That I have not done anything wrong, not to Iraq, not to anyone else. And I said that I wish for our country to be independent and strong and at the same time I am against all hatred and division."
"And I wished for my children to follow in my footsteps and in my path," he says he wrote.
"Yes, though that path led to my death, we only have one life so let us live that life honorably."
Instead of killing him, his captors ended up throwing him onto the floor of a vehicle and leaving him by the side of a road in Baghdad near where his family had been told to wait for him.

Asadi, injured and weak, insisted on returning home to the marshlands the very next day. There, hundreds of marsh residents walked for miles to welcome him back, many waving celebratory posters and Iraqi flags.

Asadi says he knows the militia that kidnapped him and he believes the government did as well while he was being held. His cousin, who was driving, had memorized the license plate number of the kidnappers.
"Within two hours they found who owns the car and the name and who he works for," says Alwash, the Nature Iraq co-founder.

The Iraqi government had pledged to secure his release. But in certain areas, some of the Iran-backed militias that flourished in the security vacuum and the subsequent civil war after the U.S. invasion have grown more powerful than Iraqi security forces. And in some parts of Iraq, tribes are even more powerful still.

Environmentalist Azzam Alwash, an Iraqi-American engineer, the co-founder of Nature Iraq, in Amman, Jordan. Alwash has not returned to Iraq since he was warned three years ago of kidnapping threats against him as well by Iran-backed militias. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
In the end it was Asadi's powerful Bani Asad tribe that won his release after mobilizing hundreds of armed tribal fighters to drive home their demand that he be freed.

"Four hundred members of the Asadi clan — all with guns. They surround the guy's house and say 'Ok, if he dies, you're dead'," says Alwash. "Jassim was known — I mean everybody was like, 'What the hell? Why mess around with Jassim?'"

As part of the deal for his release, Asadi says he did not pursue the case in court. He says it never occurred to him he was in danger of being kidnapped because Nature Iraq is purely environmental and not affiliated with any political party.

He was offered asylum in Europe after he was freed. He refused, saying it was what his captors wanted — for him to leave the country and stop his work. Instead he asked for asylum for two of his children, who are now in Sweden.
"He basically told people, 'Take my children away so I can work for the marshes without putting them in danger,'" says Alwash. A third child lives in the United States.
Boatman Razzak Jabar, also known as Abu Haider, and Asadi measure the depth of the water in the marsh. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
Alwash, speaking to NPR in Amman, was told by intelligence services of three different countries after Asadi was seized that he was also at risk of being kidnapped and has not returned to Iraq since.
"Iran's operating theory is that we are a Mossad operation," Alwash says of Nature Iraq. "They cannot understand why Western governments would give money to the environment."

He says Iran's suspicions about the organization go back to 2016, when Nature Iraq began a project with Iranian conservationists working on the endangered and elusive Persian Leopard in the mountains between Iran and Iraq. Two years later Iran arrested nine Iranian conservationists related to the project, accusing them of espionage.
The Iranian-Canadian co-founder of the Persian Wildlife Heritage Foundation died in detention while the rest spent years in prison.

This year, with the return of the water and grasses for water buffalo to eat, more calves were born. Caring for the animals is a family endeavor – many of the children, particularly girls, are not sent to school. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption

Nature Iraq has raised a generation of environmentalists working mainly from southern Iraq and Iraq's Kurdistan region. In the marshlands, the group has built floating islands for water buffalo breeders and reed guest houses intended for tourists. They have lobbied the Iraqi and regional governments to implement water policies that would revive the marshes — primarily Turkey whose huge dams have reduced the water flow downstream.

Because there is no water treatment plant, the organization has constructed a pond to naturally clean marsh water contaminated by sewage pumped from towns into the marshes. The collection pond is now full of reeds that naturally remove toxins from the water before it is pumped back out.

They are a small fraction of the cost of water treatment plants but they are still waiting for the Iraqi government to make a decision on constructing two more ponds needed near Chibayish, Asadi says.
At its peak, the environmental organization had 94 people on staff, operating in Iraq and the Iraqi Kurdistan region.
Boats line a canal that brings people from the marshes into the town of Chibayish. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption

"Anyone who works on the environment in Iraq has gone through Nature Iraq," Alwash says. In 2018, after secret allegations that the environmental organization was misusing public funds, Iraqi prosecutors froze the group's bank accounts. They dropped the investigation four years later due to lack of evidence. Only four staff members who could afford to work without being paid, remained.
Asadi's arrest and Iran's imprisonment of Iranian environmentalists who worked with Nature Iraq have had a chilling effect on environmental activism.
"After the kidnapping people were like — 'Why are you working with Jassim? It's dangerous,'" says volunteer Muntadher Abedali, 21.

"Nature Iraq has been teaching me how to protect the marshes, the biology, the biodiversity and even the culture," he says. "I will stay with Jassim forever, no matter what. Why should I feel afraid? We are the next generation to protect nature."
