items.title: Elton John backs Australian artists in fight against AI in surprise Aria awards appearance
paragraphs: Elton John has made a surprise appearance at the 2026 Aria awards to draw attention to Not AI’s To Take, a major campaign backed by the creative and media industries calling on the Australian government to protect copyright law in the face of lobbying from AI companies.

Delivering a pre-recorded message at Australian music’s biggest night on Wednesday, the British singer backed the new campaign, which is calling on the Albanese government to ensure Australian artists are reimbursed and consulted by AI companies interested in using their works for AI training.

“I have long admired the talent and creativity of Australian artists,” John said. “So I want to send an important message to the Australian government. You have a duty to protect Australian artists and their work. Don’t let AI use any Australian artist’s work without full permission. Please, protect the next generation of Australian artists. Thank you.”
John hosted the very first Aria awards ceremony in 1987.

Australian musicians Jack River, Dobby, Josh Pyke and KLP also addressed the room at Sydney’s Hordern Pavilion on behalf of Not AI’s To Take, joining the likes of Jimmy Barnes, Paul Kelly and Peter Garrett who were among the artists who launched the campaign this week.

“It is not just lyrics and songs from Yothu Yindi, Missy Higgins, Gurrumul and Jimmy Barnes – you’ll be handing over Elton John, Beyoncé and the Beatles’ work too,” Dobby said. “Do not let Australia be the weak link that lets the world down.”

Not AI’s To Take is being supported by dozens of groups representing the recording, writing, publishing, film, television and media industries, including news outlets such as News Corp, Foxtel, Seven Media and Guardian Australia. The campaign warns that changes demanded by AI giants could put the $70bn creative industry and its 600,000 workers at risk.
“When Peter Garrett, The Guardian and Newscorp are all singing from the same song sheet, the Parliament should take notice,” said Greens senator Sarah Hanson Young in a statement.
The Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) is also backing the campaign, emblazoning the slogan on a billboard at the Hordern Pavilion on Wednesday.

“I can’t just go and film a movie at the movies. I can’t do whatever I want with other people’s IP,” musician Ben Lee told Guardian Australia on the Aria red carpet. “Corporations should be subject to the same laws. So if AI companies want to train on Australian music, it’s simple: pay us.”

Rapper Miss Kannina told Guardian Australia: “The Australian government doesn’t care about anybody but the billionaires, and they don’t care about artists especially. Any kind of opportunity the Australian government can get to make money, they fucking will.

“If you’re using datacentres and AI and shit like that, you’re not really an artist,” she added. “I think the Australian government would do a lot better putting a lot more money and time into communities and lower socioeconomic communities to do music programs and to really lift up the Australian music industry, because honestly, this thing is hanging by a fucking thread.”

Multiple music figures used their Aria speeches to address the threat of AI. Bluey composer Joff Bush, who won the award for best children’s album, paid tribute to the “real life human beings” who contributed to the show’s soundtrack, while Tim Minchin delivered a rousing speech in defence of “shitty, fucked-up, striving, stumbling, needy, petty, hopeful, heartfelt, fucking humanness”.

“Art is the way we reach out to one another, and it is defined and made beautiful by the glorious messiness of its human creators. This will only remain true if we assert it as true and act accordingly,” he said.
“Which is to say, AI can suck my balls,” he added to cheers.
Danny Rogers, the co-founder of Laneway festival, used his win for best music festival to call for urgent action.

“Original music and live music simply don’t exist without incredibly talented, dedicated and creative human beings,” Rogers said, adding: “The misuse of AI poses a real threat to our industry and things could change much faster than anyone realises. We simply cannot take human creativity for granted. We need to protect the people who make music we all love.”

While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has declared it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, and that artists “need to be compensated”, some AI companies have argued it is too difficult to make individual licensing deals under existing copyright law. AI companies have said they need legal certainty on the copyright issue before investing and training models in Australia, with Anthropic putting forward an “opt-out” model to scrape creative works unless a rightsholder objected.

A spokesperson for the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, told Guardian Ausrtralia on Tuesday that the government was “committed to supporting” creatives, and pledged any copyright changes would “deliver meaningful control and fair compensation”.
The government is expected to unveil a long-awaited legislative package on AI in late 2026 or early 2027, with proposals around datacentres, online safety, productivity and copyright.

items.title: Artists and creators are leaving Etsy in droves over its new AI policy
paragraphs: You might be suffering whiplash if you've been watching things at Etsy lately. Just a couple of weeks ago, things looked tentatively hopeful for the marketplace as Etsy promised to crackdown on AI slop. Now creators are fleeing the platform in droves because of its own AI policy.

Creators have largely welcomed Etsy's decision to ban listings by bots and to insist that product photos resemble the actual product being sold – surely a rule that all marketplaces should implement. But new wording in its terms of use has caused alarm over how content could be used for AI training. As a result, the best website builders could be about to see an influx of custom from artists and crafters.

For years, Etsy has been one of the best places to sell art and design online, particularly handmade craft items, from jewelry and gifts made with Cricut machines to illustration and poster design. But like many platforms, it's faced the problem of quality products being drowned out by AI slop and copied art posted by bots.

Shortly after updating its content rules to try to get on top of that, Etsy's also updated its Terms of Use. The new text adds a clause that has echoes of the policies introduced by certain social media platforms.

Section 5 already included a perpetual licence allowing Etsy to reproduce, modify, distribute and create derivative works from user content. The revised policy now adds a specific authorisation that reads: "This also includes the right for us and our third party partners and vendors to use Your Content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies, including to improve the Services and/or help keep them safe, subject to any applicable opt-out rights described in our Privacy Policy".

The new terms come into effect on 16 December, and they've sparked an exodus from the platform. Many creatives have taken to social media to announce the closure of their Etsy stores, using flyers and goodbye letters created in their signature art styles.

Some speak of wrestling over a decision that they fear could harm their business in the short term. Others who have yet to take the leap say they feel trapped because they depend on Etsy as their main source of income and the update has come at the most important time of the year for sales.

Like with Cara for social media, alternative specifically anti-AI marketplaces like Marmalade Handmade, but they remain small compared to Etsy. Some sellers say they can't leave the platform yet but are taking the step of writing to customers to ask them to shop with them directly instead of using the platform.

In an update on the Etsy Community site this week, VP of Customer Operations James Ossman stressed that sellers retain ownership of their creative work on Etsy that the company was focusing on using AI to support sellers and improve the Etsy experience.

He writes: "We do not use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity. Again, this is not changing. Our goal at Etsy has always been to connect you and your unique items with buyers."

He provided some examples of how the platform is training AI, including to identify potentially fraudulent accounts and related listings, to understand inventory, to help buyers find items and tailored recommendations and to build tools to help sellers run their businesses more efficiently.

He said Etsy uses security tools to detect and limit unauthorised scraping, while its terms prohibit unauthorised use of marketplace content for AI training. However, he doesn't specify whether authorised partners can use seller content to train models for applications unrelated to Etsy, and the platform has not provider a general opt-out mechanism for sellers who don't want their content used for AI training.

It may be that sellers have nothing to fear, in which case Etsy should really have tried to find a better way to communicate the update. It's aware of the sensitivity around AI, and it's natural for sellers to be frightened by the language in the new terms at a time when AI is being used to clone artists' work in a multitude of fields, from illustration to video game development.
Are you concerned about Etsy's AI policy? Let us know in the comments.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: Harry Styles, Billie Eilish and Sam Fender to be youngest set of Glastonbury headliners for 30 years
paragraphs: Electro pioneers Kraftwerk will make their Glastonbury debut with a headline set at West Holts - the festival's third-largest stage.

The event will also welcome experimental Canadian band Angine de Poitrine, who have drawn attention for their prog-rock sound and polka-dotted stage costumes; rap legends De La Soul and Mike D; and pop provocateur FKA Twigs.

"We are so happy to be coming back after our fallow year and, as we head into winter after that peaceful period, we wanted to give you an early musical taster of what's to come at Glastonbury 2027 with this spread of incredible artists," said organiser Emily Eavis.
"We can't wait to see you down here on Worthy Farm in June for some much-needed good times!"
The gates will open at Worthy Farm in Somerset to 200,000 fans on Wednesday 23 June, with music on the main stages kicking off on Friday 25 June.
Tickets prices are at an all-time high of £408, including a £5 booking fee per ticket.
Sam Fender will headline the first night, in what will be his second appearance at the festival.
He last played in 2022, immediately before Billie Eilish, and fought back tears as thousands of fans chanted along to hits like Seventeen Going Under and Hypersonic Missiles.
"Me and the boys have never been here before," he said. "We've never been here as punters, never played here before and we're doing that all in one day, which is the most crazy experience."

He will return as one of the UK's biggest rock stars, having won the Mercury Prize for his third album, People Watching, in 2025. Earlier this year, his duet with Olivia Dean - Rein Me In - became the UK's longest-running number one single of all time.
Fender is expected to release a new album ahead of his Glastonbury slot, which will land in the middle of his catchily-titled Proper Massive Stadium Tour.
Harry Styles will take the Pyramid Stage crown on the Saturday.
It comes amid acclaim for his euphoric and athletic Together Together tour, which largely focuses on the understated dance anthems of his fourth album Kiss All The Time. Disco Occasionally.
The pop star has previously been spotted partying at the festival's late-night dance arenas, despite attempting to go incognito in tracksuits and sunglasses.
In 2022, he was rumoured to be making a guest appearance during Eilish's set after his music was played during an early-morning soundcheck - but the duet never materialised.
Instead, Eilish gave a universally well-received performance, described as "imperious [and] hugely engaging" by the Guardian,, external and "proof that the future is here" by the NME, external.
At the time, she was 20 years old - making her the youngest-ever solo act to headline Glastonbury.
Aged between 24 and 32, Styles, Fender and Eilish represent the festival's youngest set of Pyramid Stage headliners since 1997.
Cher, meanwhile, will be the oldest ever act to play the legend slot - strutting through the gates of Worthy Farm at the age of 81.

The diva's appearance will come eight years after her last UK tour, and 63 years into a career that began with her ex-husband Sonny Bono, and recording sessions with Phil Spector's legendary Wrecking Crew band.
She emerged as a solo artist in the 1970s, scoring three US number ones, before switching into disco mode with Take Me Home.
In the 1980s, she became an award-winning actress and scored chart hits with FM rock staples like Turn Back Time and Just Like Jesse James.
Then in 1998, she revitalised her career with club anthem Believe, which helped to popularise the use of autotune in dance music.
Inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2024, she is about to release the second volume of her memoir.
She has previously talked about retiring from live performance - but it seems the lure of Glastonbury was too tempting to turn down.
Cher will follow previous bookings in the crowd-pleasing legends slot including Sir Rod Stewart, Shania Twain, Diana Ross and Kylie Minogue.
More details about the 2027 line-up will be revealed in the New Year. Eavis has previously dismissed rumours that Madonna and Oasis will feature on the bill.

items.title: ‘I didn’t notice his body being purple’: Byron Bay doula left newborn to inflate a jumping castle, court hears
paragraphs: Baby DH was born in an inflatable pool, in a candle-lit room in his parents’ home near Byron Bay, with no one medically trained present. There are two very different versions of what happened next.

In the parents’ version, the doula reassured them Baby DH was OK, then left to inflate a jumping castle while their newborn turned purple, became floppy, and struggled to breathe. In the doula’s version, everything seemed OK but she suggested they seek more help if they wanted to.
The New South Wales coroner’s court heard the two competing narratives on Wednesday as part of an ongoing inquest into the deaths of four babies born in free births or home births.
The babies died in NSW’s northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024.
“The evidence will be that from his first minutes of life, [Baby DH] showed signs that something was seriously wrong,” the Lismore courtroom heard.
“His parents saw those signs. They raised them again and again with their doula, who they had engaged to watch for exactly that. Their doula, in this case, was a woman named Amy Lou Smith.
“Each time the parents raised their concerns, they were reassured by Amy Lou. An ambulance was not called until moments before [Baby DH] stopped breathing.”

His father described the baby as floppy after birth. “His colour, his whole body was purple with his hands and feet darker still,” the court heard, and Smith told them some purple in the hands and feet was normal.
“I didn’t notice his body being purple,” Smith told the court.

Told the baby’s colour wasn’t improving, Smith said “as long as his abdomen isn’t purple”, according to evidence from the parents. The mother was shocked. His whole body had been purple all along. His temperature was low, 34.5C. Smith suggested trying to get it up to 37C.
“I believed if they had real concerns, that they would call an ambulance and not be texting a non medically trained doula,” Smith told the court.
Smith, the inquest heard, described his laboured breathing as “cute little noises”. “I didn’t say that,” Smith told the court.
The court heard Smith told the couple Baby DH would have been put on oxygen if he was in hospital. But Smith later told the court she didn’t know what the hospital would have done.

He had strange lumps on his body, and wasn’t feeding. Smith suggested they get the lumps checked out, and warned that babies sometimes take a while to latch on to the breast, according to the parents’ evidence.
The court heard Smith left to set up a jumping castle for her son’s birthday. She sent the couple a picture of the castle later, as they were trying to contact a doctor, the court heard.
Smith told the court the castle was already set up, and the couple was happy for her to leave.
“Everything felt like it was OK,” she said.

Eventually, the parents spoke to the GP they had tried to contact earlier. The GP told them to call triple zero. They did, and did CPR until the paramedics got there. But Baby DH was declared dead at the hospital.
After the father had made the emergency call, Smith also told them to call an ambulance, and sent them instructions on infant CPR.
Throughout the hearing, Smith denied that any of her advice or comments constituted clinical advice.

Neonatologist Dr Paul Evans, the court heard, had found Baby DH had a complex heart defect, one that would have shown up on an X-ray. The baby could have been treated, and a birth plan with proximity to a major hospital and specialist cardiac care prepared, the court heard.
The child’s death was not inevitable, Evans found.

While pregnant, Baby DH’s mother decided to rely on a doula. She first approached a woman the court heard was likely to be Sita Tara Kali, a self-described birth keeper who was also involved in the care of another baby previously mentioned during the inquest. But Kali didn’t feel she could help, so they turned to Smith.
The court heard the couple paid for an online “sovereign birth course” for Smith and was reassured that she had enough experience. They agreed on an emergency plan.
Smith, who became a birth doula in 2020, was quizzed on her experience in court.
She has a degree in fine art and has worked as a social worker and a youth worker.

She told the court she is not medically trained in any way but did an online “full-spectrum doula course”. She learned CPR but was not familiar with how to apply it to a newborn – she denied she had given the parents the impression she was.
She had no training about a newborn’s colour, breathing, or feeding, but she did go to a retreat where she learned about referring a woman to more support if needed.

She had been present at 15 births over four years, nine alongside a midwife, and conceded she didn’t know what a low-risk birth would look like. She had read a couple of books about birthing, but they were more “spiritual”, the court heard.
She agreed that she now believes the best model of care for a home birth is for a clinically trained midwife to work alongside a doula.

items.title: £10m ‘once-in-a-generation’ study to explore effects of children’s social media ban
paragraphs: Countries around the world are considering social media bans for children, but whether this would work in practice has been hotly debated. Now researchers are seeking answers through a major scientific study led by Wellcome, which will be the first of its kind.

Ten research projects will explore topics ranging from children’s mental health to their sleep and physical activity, comparing factors before and after the social media ban for children under 16 is introduced in the UK in spring 2027.

Backed by £9.3m of funding from Wellcome and working with more than 300,000 young people across Britain, researchers hope to provide crucial answers for those working on online safety and digital policy.

“We all know there has been a quite heated debate around the social media ban here in the UK [and] also around the world, but there is very limited scientific evidence about how social media and its restrictions [are] actually affecting the mental health of young people,” said Dr Camilla Iannone, research lead at Wellcome.
Iannone said restrictions will offer a once-in-a-generation opportunity to study at scale how social media affects young people’s mental health.

“We really don’t think that this is a simple binary question of whether social media media is good or bad, or whether restrictions work or don’t work,” she said. “Instead, the teams will study whether changing young people’s digital environment leads to meaningful changes in their mental health and wellbeing.”
Australia brought in a social media ban for under-16s last year, and other countries are also taking action,including Canada, Greece, and Denmark.

In the UK, a social media ban for under-16s is expected in the spring, barring children from platforms such as Instagram, YouTube, TikTok, Snapchat, Facebook and X. There will also be restrictions around live-streaming and contact from strangers on gaming platforms.
Opinions have been split, with some raising concerns about the impact on young people who rely on social media for friendships, white others point out children could find ways around bans.

One project in the study is called Smart Schools Plus and is co-led by Prof Victoria Goodyear of the University of Birmingham. The research will span 16 schools and 800 pupils in England, focusing not only on mental health and wellbeing, but also on physical activity, sleep, social networks, disruptive school behaviour, attainment, and attendance. As part of the work, the team will use surveys, apps, interviews, digital diaries and research-grade activity trackers.

“We’re going to look at whether sleep, physical activity, social networks, and these other educational outcomes influence the mental health outcomes,” Goodyear said. “So it’s answering, why are there any changes or why are there not any changes?”
The team will explore whether risky content – such as material relating to self-harm, suicide and eating disorders – has moved from one online platform to another as a result of the ban.
Another project, co-led by Dr Gemma Knowles of King’s College London, will explore whether the ban’s impacts differ for young people of different genders, social class, and sexual orientations.
Meanwhile, Dr Alex Kwong from the University of Edinburgh said his team will work with families across England, Wales and Scotland.

“We’re interested in understanding how these social media restrictions impact children and families together,” he said. “So, understanding if that will then lead to potential conflict and how families then navigate the battle.”

The team will also look at whether young people find workarounds for the restrictions. “If children and adolescents still use social media after the ban, that’s the difference between understanding policy on paper and policy in practice,” Kwong said.

items.title: Bikie ‘not surprised’ if he used fake $20,000 souvlaki invoice to pocket thousands on Big Build site, inquiry hears
paragraphs: A Bandidos gang member says it is possible he used a fake $20,000 invoice for souvlaki to pocket thousands of dollars while employed on a Big Build site.
The former CFMEU member and bikie Joel Leavitt faced a second day of examination by the royal commission into alleged corruption across Victoria’s construction sector on Wednesday.
In 2023, while employed as site health and safety representatives, Leavitt and another man, Charles Farrugia, exchanged messages which were shown to the commission.
“Just make up a quote that hits 20K and we will get the other nine off the subbies,” Leavitt wrote. “Which will mean five each.”

The commission viewed a genuine receipt for roughly $9,000 for souvlaki catering, and another allegedly fake invoice for $20,000 which was sent by Leavitt to the site superintendent, Tim Alford, from the firm Acciona.

The commissioner, Chris Kourakis AC, said the evidence strongly suggested the two CFMEU health and safety representatives had organised a meal for workers to get a few souvlaki and had pocketed $5,000 each.
“I’ll accept that,” Leavitt said. “I’m not surprised that I could have.”
The commission also viewed messages between Leavitt and Alford in which the bikie appeared to direct who could and who couldn’t be hired to work on the site.
In one message, Alford appeared to address the arrangement, saying: “I don’t care bringing your mates on and putting them in spotting roles and finding homes. But they all need to do there jobs.”
The counsel assisting the commission Chris Carr SC asked Leavitt if he, on behalf of the CFMEU, was dictating who could work on the site, to which he replied he couldn’t recall.
“I had my own demons at the time, so I may have dropped the ball on a few things,” Leavitt said. “That’s my answer to that question, counsellor.”
Earlier on Wednesday, questioning returned to a $165,000 invoice paid to Leavitt’s now defunct company, JVL Consulting, by the union-aligned subcontractor BK Labour Hire in July 2025.
When shown a copy of the invoice Leavitt was unable to recall anything about it, or even give a clear answer as to what services his former company had provided.
Later on Wednesday, the BK Labour Hire director Bernard Kearney admitted he paid the invoice despite Leavitt not having done any work for the firm.
“I just decided to pay it and move on,” he said.
Carr said there were likely only a couple of reasons why BK Labour would have paid Leavitt, including a fear of violence or to suppress some information he had on them.
“Was it one or both of those two?” Carr asked.
BK Labour also received a succession of invoices from the senior CFMEU organiser Joe Myles totalling $256,000 over about a year.
Carr had earlier asked why Leavitt appeared to become uncomfortable when asked about the invoice.
Leavitt blamed his poor memory on having ADHD, as well as PTSD from being shot in May 2023.
“Around that time I actually got told by gang squad that there was a contract on my life,” he said. “So it brought back some uncomfortable memories.
“That’s why I blocked out a lot of that time.”
Kourakis warned Leavitt it was an offence to fail to answer questions put to him by the commission, something he said could ultimately be tested in a courtroom.
“I’ve been shot … I’ve had drug issues … I am answering these to the best of my recollection,” Leavitt replied.
“How do you think you would act if you’d ever been shot?”

After the commission briefly adjourned for Leavitt to speak to his lawyers, the bikie returned to the stand and said JVL Consulting had provided safety advice to companies. “Maybe helping them out with their procedures and policies and stuff like that,” he said.
The commission viewed a copy of Leavitt’s bank statement at the time which fluctuated between $0 and minus $20, before the $165,000 landed in his account.
“Everyone likes money – I’m sure all youse are on good money for this,” said Leavitt, addressing the bar table.
Kourakis informed Leavitt that the commission had evidence he did not do any work for BK Labour.
He said an inference that could be made was that Leavitt was “standing over” BK Labour for the payment because he needed money.
“If that’s the way you want to look at it, commissioner,” Leavitt replied.

Carr asked if Leavitt knew something about BK Labour that the company would have wanted to keep quiet. “Is the conclusion the commission should draw is that you just stood over them with some sort of explicit or implied threat of violence?” he asked.
Leavitt replied: “I’d like to talk to my counsel before I answer that.”

items.title: Is the 3pm football blackout outdated or still relevant in 2026?
paragraphs: The 3pm blackout has existed in English football since the 1960s
After 60 years, is time finally running out on the 3pm blackout in football?
With pretty much every available television slot now exhausted, next year the Premier League and the EFL are set to hold serious discussions about its future.
There are concerns, especially within non-league football, that removing the blackout could have detrimental effects on attendances and finances.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham agrees, urging caution and suggesting the health of the football pyramid should come first.
But many Premier League fans feel they are short-changed, locked out of many of their team's fixtures just because they live in this country.
Go anywhere else in the world, and every single match is available live.
With streaming so prevalent, to some the blackout feels archaic.
Yet it is a complex situation, and many feel the depth of English football's pyramid is like nowhere else.
BBC Sport looks at the history of the blackout, why it is unique to British football and the arguments for and against keeping it.
It is the start of the 1964-65 season and the BBC launches a programme called Match of the Day.
Highlights of one match would be broadcast on BBC Two, a channel which at the time was only available in London.
Yet some clubs were concerned. Would fans still turn up to games?
Burnley chairman Bob Lord was the first owner to refuse to allow the cameras into Turf Moor. At the end of the season, several other clubs tried to block the renewal of the deal.
A compromise was reached and the BBC agreed not to reveal the televised Saturday match until all games had ended.
Shortly afterwards came the blackout for live matches.
Fast forward 20 years to 1987. With dwindling attendances across the European domestic leagues, partly influenced by crowd trouble, Uefa took up England's idea.
Article 48 was added to the Uefa Statutes.
Each country could designate a two-and-a-half-hour "transmission-free period", as long as at least 50% of matches in the top two leagues were taking place.
This was "designed to ensure that spectators are not deterred from attending local football matches of any kind and/or participating in matches at amateur and/or youth level".
Today, the situation has gone full circle. The only leagues that apply Article 48 are England, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
The reason for this is simpler than you might imagine.
No other major country qualifies for the blackout - because no other major country has a kick-off time that runs from the top flight and through the divisions.
It is a tradition that is unique to football in the United Kingdom.
Let's take Germany, often held up as an example of a country with excellent attendances despite not having a blackout.

This misses a key point. The Bundesliga has its own kick-off slot, 3:30pm on a Saturday, and no other division plays at the same time. The 2. Bundesliga, for instance, has a standard Saturday kick-off time of 1:30pm.
Could you imagine English football replicating this?
In Spain, it is rare for either of the top two divisions to have games that kick off simultaneously. Each match has its own slot, and is broadcast live.
In Italy, Serie A plays on a Sunday afternoon, and Serie B on a Saturday.
In France, Ligue 1 has Saturday night as its main time slot, Ligue 2 plays largely on a Friday night, and Ligue 3 on a Saturday lunchtime.
So there is no blackout, because the football calendar works in a completely different way.
Football fans give their thoughts on the Saturday 3pm TV blackout
The next television rights cycle presents a unique opportunity.
The deals for the Premier League, EFL and Scottish Premiership are all up for renewal in 2029-30.
There is the chance for all the top stakeholders to come together and agree to end the blackout.
Last year, Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said there were no plans to remove the blackout.
But this summer there was a clear shift in emphasis, with Masters admitting there would be talks with the EFL ahead of the renewal of TV rights.
Scottish football has gone first, with broadcasters invited to bid to show all matches live - and is open to those shown on a Saturday afternoon.
It will be another year before we discover what the Premier League and the EFL - which seriously considered ending the blackout three years ago - are prepared to offer to broadcasters.
So, why would the leagues need to offer up the Saturday 3pm slot to broadcasters? After all, the latest domestic Premier League deal was worth a record £6.7bn - an increase of 4%.
However, to achieve that figure, the Premier League had to make an additional 70 games available. In real terms, it means each live Premier League game is worth less than it was before.
Now every single game not shown at 3pm on a Saturday - and there are only 110 left - is on TV.
Could the Premier League need to offer more matches for the rights to keep their overall value?
If so there are two options: try to find more TV slots, or show games at 3pm on a Saturday.
Could the Women's Super League benefit too? It looked into playing a 3pm on a Saturday but could not find a way around the blackout.
Most of the competition's games are shown live already, with a greater concern being stadium availability and consistency of kick-off times.
There is a danger that the issue of the 3pm blackout is viewed only through the lens of Premier League and EFL television rights.
Tom Greatrex, the chair of the Football Supporters' Association, says there are attendances in non-league football that some top flights in Europe "would look at jealously".
"We have one of the strongest football pyramids in the world, with excellent matchday attendances deep into the non-league game," Greatrex said.
"The prime minister is right to point out the value of the blackout to clubs further down the pyramid, and to urge caution over the impact rushed change could have on the overall health of the game."
BBC Sport understands that senior executives at the National League, which has a long-term global streaming deal with DAZN, are steadfastly against the blackout ending.
It has serious reservations, shared by the vast majority of its 72 clubs, that attendances would be impacted.
Included in this is transient attendance from season ticket holders of league clubs, many of whom go to non-league football when their team is away from home, boosting receipts considerably.
The fear is this could be lost if all league games are streamed at 3pm.
Nick Boom, the chair of Northern Premier League side FC United of Manchester, worries that the issue is only viewed through the lens of top-flight football.
"Football doesn't begin and end with the Premier League," Boom told BBC Sport.
"Every Saturday, thousands of people turn out to support their local clubs.
"For many of those clubs, the income from people coming through the turnstiles, buying a pint or something to eat is what keeps them alive.
"The 3pm blackout isn't about nostalgia. It's about protecting something that matters."
Boom added that clubs in non-league football are huge community assets, and losing them would have an impact "well beyond 90 minutes on a Saturday".
Some clubs are more open-minded about what ending the blackout could mean for non-league football.
Others have changed the way they operate to get around it.
North West Counties League Premier Division side FC Isle of Man have stopped playing at 3:00pm on a Saturday so they can stream all their games live.
Brian Shotton, a director at eighth-tier Ashington FC, told BBC Sport that he would not be automatically against removing the blackout.
"I would still have concerns, because every person through the gate makes a difference," Shotton said.
"I don't think we should just assume it would damage non-league football, but equally you need to know what it could mean for clubs like ours."
Ashington, who have attendances of about 400, see gates rise by up to 25% when Newcastle are not at home - but they already feel the impact of illegal streaming of the Magpies' games.
For the official broadcasters like Sky Sports, these supporters are seen as lost revenue.
There is an argument that the blackout drives piracy. Just how many of those particular fans would pay for a legal subscription is open to debate.
Added to that, there are now many weekends when when fewer than 50% of matches in the top two divisions are played at 3pm on a Saturday anyway.
For instance, on 28 November there are just two in the Premier League, and seven in the Championship.
Other non-league clubs, like Dorking Wanders and Hashtag United, have spoken of the opportunities ending the blackout could bring, such as more income streams and fewer inconvenient kick-off times.
But this, for now, seems to be a minority view. The concerns for the health of the entire pyramid, on attendances and finances, are real.
Once the blackout is gone, it is unlikely to come back.

items.title: BBC drama Shetland to return for 12th series
paragraphs: The BBC detective drama Shetland is to return for a 12th series, with filming starting next year.
The new six-part series will see the return of Ashley Jensen, playing DI Ruth Calder, and longstanding cast members Steven Robertson as DS Sandy Wilson and Lewis Howden as PC Billy McCabe.
But DI Tosh McIntosh will be a notable absence because one of the original stars, Alison O'Donnell, leaves the drama at the end of the current series following a 13-year stint.
She has promised a "memorable" departure from the show, with the first episode leaving fans in suspense as she was left trapped in a locked water tank.
Further casting details for the next series will be announced in due course.
The show, filmed both in Shetland and at locations in mainland Scotland, averaged seven million viewers across 2025.
Anita Vettesse will take over as lead writer on the new series, which will be produced by Angus Sharpe and distributed internationally by ITV Studios.
The TV series, adapted from the novels by Ann Cleeves, was first broadcast on BBC One in March 2013.
DI Jimmy Perez, played by Douglas Henshall, was the central character for the first seven series, with Ashley Jensen then joining as DI Calder in 2023.

items.title: Conservationists searching for large river eels
paragraphs: Conservationists have spent summer and autumn searching for critically endangered eels to tag as they begin their downstream migration.
The Tees Rivers Trust have found 12 large eels by fyke netting, a method of catching eels with a cylindrical net, around the River Tees catchment.
The team managed to electronically tag 10 of them and the largest was 60cm (23ins) in length and weighted 435g (0.9lbs).
Project manager Ellie Ward said the eels caught this year were not as large as usual and were "harder to catch".
The team has been searching for "silver" eels which have finished maturing and are preparing to head back out to the Sargasso Sea near Bermuda.
Ward said: "European eels start to migrate downstream during autumn and winter, when river discharges increase.
"We suspect that low flows in summer that have continued into autumn have contributed to low catch rates so far this year."

items.title: What's gone wrong at Britain's worst bathing site?
paragraphs: The official sign on the banks of the River Tone at French Weir Park in Taunton advises people not to swim.
But that hasn't stopped Jo, Jenny, Sue and a second Jo from enjoying a regular dip together.

"People think, oh you're swimming down by the supermarket, that can't be very nice, but it's gorgeous," Jenny Hillier says, as the women huddle round with their coats and hot drinks after a bracing October plunge.
People have been swimming at the spot on the River Tone in the centre of Taunton for more than a hundred years.
But it is only since 2024 that French Weir Park has been designated an official bathing site, which means from May to September the water gets tested by the Environment Agency (EA).
Those tests regularly confirm what the women's senses have been telling them for a while - the water quality is poor.

"There are times when we've come down and we haven't got in, either because of the look or the smell," says Jo Macdonald. "We don't take risks. We don't put our faces in. We don't swim with cuts or anything."
"This summer I got quite poorly," Jenny says, explaining that she'd had diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle cramps.
"I'd swum and then within six hours I was unwell. I was poorly for probably about seven to 10 days and it was not nice. I think it was the river that day."
"There are germs everywhere, all over the place. You can catch Covid in Tesco," she says.

"The counts from just outside the treatment works in my experience were high for treated effluent", Dr Rob Morley from Index Microbiology told us at his laboratory near Bristol as he peered down at small dots of E. coli bacteria on a transparent plastic plate.
What was of particular interest to Morley were the results of the test on water samples we'd taken above and below the point where the treated wastewater enters the River Tone.
It showed 199 CFU of E. coli above, which is fine for swimming and 7,701 CFU just below, more than eight times the regulators limit.
"You can see where it's seeding the river with pollution," Morley says.
"If we were to look further down the river, we would expect the levels to get lower with the dilution effect. But that does quite clearly show the impact that treated effluent can have on the river."

We shared our findings with Dr Andrew Thompson, a fellow at the Institute of Chemical Engineers. He was involved in a 2024 report that warned high concentrations of bacteria and viruses were common, external, particularly in the summer when river levels are lower and could cause serious diseases if ingested.

Thompson told the BBC the levels of E. coli we found in the River Tone were not illegal, or even particularly unusual, because there are currently no laws or regulations about how much bacteria water companies are allowed to discharge in what the industry calls treated effluent.
We also wanted to know whether analysing the E. coli samples from the bathing site could give us clues to where it came from.

With assistance from researchers at the University of Bristol, Morley arranged for e-DNA analysis to be carried out to identify whether the E. coli bacteria were more likely to be from a human or animal gut.
The answer, as is often the case with water quality, is complex. There were lots of different types of E.coli in the samples.

"Some were from humans, some were from animals and some were just generic from the environment," Morley says. "It definitely suggests that some of the E. coli is definitely coming from human origins, therefore potentially from that treatment works."
As with all of our testing, more needs to be done to reach firm conclusions.

Both the EA and Wessex Water are investigating what's causing the water quality in Taunton to be so poor. But sources at the EA told the BBC that constant flows of treated effluent is high up the list of likely culprits.
In response to our testing Wessex Water told the BBC its treatment works at Bradford on Tone was working normally and was meeting all its permit conditions set by the EA.
So could steady flows of treated effluent loaded with bacteria be behind many of the problems at bathing sites across the UK?
"All the sewage treatment works in the UK and in England have permits to protect the ecology and the wildlife within the river," says Jim Flory, a regional manager for the EA in the south-west.
"They've not set permits for bathing water regulations, which are all about protecting people who may want to be swimming, canoeing or using the water."

That has led to a system where a popular bathing site gets officially designated – the testing regime discovers it has high levels of faecal bacteria – and then a lengthy process begins to try to work out where the sources are and whether it's affordable to fix them.

items.title: George thought his funeral was paid for – but now his wife will get nothing when he dies
paragraphs: George Davies says he feels resentful towards the insurance companies
For 17 years, George Davies made payments to an insurance company to cover the cost of his funeral.
The 82-year-old, who has stage 4 cancer, thought he had prepared and provided for his wife Marion.
George took the policy out through his local credit union, but it was cancelled after the company backing the product pulled out of the UK.
Credit unions say the closure of the plan has left thousands of people like George in limbo, with many unable to arrange an affordable alternative because they are elderly or unwell.
A coalition of 17 credit unions across Scotland and the north of England is calling for those affected to receive fair compensation.
George, from Bellshill in North Lanarkshire, is currently undergoing palliative care after being diagnosed with oesophageal cancer in 2023.
He says he can't sleep at night because of worrying about how his wife of 50 years will cope when he's gone.
"I needed something to leave to Marion so that she didn't have to worry about funeral expenses," he says.
"The only consolation is that when I die, I stop worrying about it. I just worry about it all the time."
George had been paying into a policy called the Family Protection Plan (FPP), which he took out through Mosshill Credit Union.
He initially thought it was "excellent", promising a cash lump sum on death to policy holders and up to five named family members.
But as his health deteriorates, George says he feels resentful towards the insurance companies involved.
"How can these people do these things?" he asks. "I'm going to need this money sooner than later."
George said he had not wanted his wife Marion to worry about funeral expenses
The FFP was a renewable life insurance product which did not build up a cash value over time and could be cancelled with 30 days' notice.
It closed in November 2025, leaving about 5,000 people across the UK without cover.
The Family Protection Plan was first offered in 1999 and closed to new business in 2009, with cover continuing for those already on the scheme.
Although the money could be used for any purpose, BBC Scotland News understands that it was initially advertised to help cover the cost of funerals.
An early leaflet, provided to us by the credit unions, says the FPP could be used for "any of the costs associated with the funeral" – including the wake and travel expenses for relatives.
It was sold exclusively through credit unions to their members.
Credit unions are not-for-profit financial institutions where members pool their savings to lend to one another. They are often community-based and offer an alternative to traditional banking.
FPP was offered by insurance broker CMutual, which was formerly known as CUNA Mutual Group.
The underwriters on the policy changed over the years, with Maiden Life covering the plan between 2022 and 2025.
Maiden Life announced it would leave the UK market in 2024 and gave notice of termination.
CMutual was unable to find another suitable insurer and the plan closed in November 2025.
The coalition of credit unions group says it represents about 1,500 people who have been affected by the closure. Some have paid premiums for up to 25 years.
Julie Reddin is the chief executive of Mosshill credit union and co-chairs the coalition, which is campaigning for members to receive a fair pay out.
She says it is a "scandal" that so many people have lost out on what they regarded as funeral cover.
"We would just like the people that have made money out of the policies to actually stand up and be accountable and not step back and say no that wasn't us," she says.
"It may not have been illegal what they did, but it was immoral."
Julie Reddin says legislation needs to be changed
Credit unions in the coalition have agreed to help with the cost of funerals for affected members as a goodwill gesture as they feel a level of responsibility.
At the time the FPP closed, Julie's branch had 139 members with the policy. She says many are now nearing the end of their life – like George.
"We've had 11 people pass away since the policy closed at a cost of £58,000 to our credit union," she says.
Julie estimates it would cost Mosshill Credit Union £1.3m to cover all policies.
"If we had to pay that out straight away, the credit union would go into liquidation. We just don't have that type of money to pay out," she said.
Julie says the Financial Conduct Authority should have stepped in sooner and wants financial redress for the most vulnerable customers to be split between credit unions, CMutual and Maiden Life.
"Legislation needs to be changed - this should never be able to happen again," she added.
Credit union trade body Altogether Money receives payment from CMutual for offering products through credit unions.
A spokesperson for Altogether Money said the family protection plan had been an optional product that credit unions could choose to offer.

"The decision as to whether or not to offer such products to credit union members has always been one for individual credit union boards to determine and they are responsible for their regulatory compliance and due diligence in relation to these products," it said.

"Some have taken decisions to provide financial ex-gratia payments as a goodwill gesture but in doing so are only concerned to support their members as co-operative, member-owned organisations and do not admit any liability.
"Each credit union should consider its own financial, legal and regulatory position in offering such support and we are providing advice and guidance to credit unions that wish to do so."
The Financial Conduct Authority investigated the cancellation of the plan, and acknowledged the closure had caused "real worry" to those affected.
"We have looked carefully at the circumstances. Based on this evidence, we have decided against taking further action in relation to historical conduct at this time," said a spokesperson.
"This was a renewable life insurance product, meaning that the insurer was not required to provide it indefinitely – and we don't have the power to make them continue.
"We know this is disappointing. We have strongly encouraged the firms involved to help impacted consumers and will support them to achieve this."

The coalition of credit unions will hold a meeting on Wednesday with the UK Treasury, which previously said it was holding talks with the industry and encouraging those involved to "explore all options" to support those affected.
In a statement issued in 2025, Maiden Life said the interests of CMutual's clients and policyholders had been "foremost in our plans" during its dealings with the insurance broker.
"As part of closing our life business we ensured we gave CMutual considerable notice to enable them to inform and provide their customers with alternative arrangements," it said.
A spokesperson for CMutual said the FPP had been "much valued" by credit unions and their members.

It said more than 70% of those holding a policy had claimed at least once, and over 25% had claimed more than once. The FPP enabled the policyholder to claim after the death of other people named on the policy.
CMutual also said the FCA had concluded that many people aged 80 and under were likely to be able to secure other insurance cover.
"Credit unions across the United Kingdom have a tremendous record of supporting and safeguarding their members, and we remain instrumental in helping them achieve this," it said.

"For those members and insureds most affected by the withdrawal of FPP, including those aged over 80 years for whom alternative cover may not be widely available, we remain supportive of both individual credit union initiatives already implemented and sector wide discussions to support such members."

items.title: Police boss vows to expel racists and misogynists
paragraphs: A police chief has admitted his force includes racists, misogynists and people who abused their power but said he was working to identify and remove them.
Devon and Cornwall Police Chief Constable James Vaughan said he was doing everything in his power to remove "bad officers". "There is zero tolerance here, there is no room to hide," he said.
It follows accusations the force failed to investigate serving and former officers for domestic abuse and sexual violence and its payment of compensation to women who claimed they were victims.
Since the BBC reported the claims from the nine women, a former female officer has also alleged she was sexually assaulted by a colleague on a work trip.
If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.
Kay (not her real name) said she had a poor response from colleagues when she told them of the serious sex assault and was given no support.
"All I remember is going out of my body as he continued to violate me," she said.
"I managed to get out of that room and get back to my room somehow. I remember waking up a number of hours later just feeling disorientated [and] confused.
"I couldn't even recall what had happened so I couldn't really tell anyone."
When she got her memory back, she said she told a senior female officer and other colleagues but was given no support.

"They carried on laughing and joking with him when in my presence, which really messed with my head, but reinforced my belief that I just had to get over it so I just had to push it down and pretend it hadn't happened," she said.
Chief Constable Vaughan said he was "utterly ashamed of the actions of a small minority of staff".
"The force has accepted and agreed the cases have not properly been managed and we haven't achieved justice where potentially we could have achieved justice," he said.
"I have accepted what they have said, I have apologised and I have compensated."
Vaughan said police perpetrated abuse was a major issue in policing generally and it was an issue in the force.

"In the 18 months I have been here, I have personally chaired 14 panels. In 12 of those panels, I personally dismissed officers for their behaviour that fell below the standards that we set," he said.
The force said it had introduced several measures to better support victims of police perpetrated abuse. They include:
Enhanced internal intelligence monitoring to identify concerning behaviour at the earliest opportunity
Cultural change programmes to address misogyny
Inappropriate conduct and bystander training alongside improved reporting mechanisms

The force said it had increased awareness of its internal domestic abuse peer support network and, along with other forces nationally, brought in more diligent pre-promotion vetting and intelligence checks.
Vaughan urged any victim of police perpetrated crime to report it and promised any report would be properly and proportionately investigated.
"I ask you to place some trust in me and my senior officers in gripping this and dealing with this as we go forward," he said.

Follow BBC Cornwall on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Follow BBC Devon on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to spotlight@bbc.co.uk, external.

items.title: How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
paragraphs: Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.
That partnership has now ended following Huang's resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which is alleged to have been with a Chinese spy.
The company has been rocked by the scandal, with hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value and questions swirling about the extent of the impact of Huang's departure.
While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.
The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.
Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.
It is now one the most valuable firms, worth $3.8 trillion (£2.9 trillion), and on Tuesday said its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.

But there's now an air of uncertainty over Nvidia's future direction. Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on the company, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at investment firm AJ Bell, says because Huang was also a key figure in "flying the flag" to drum up enthusiasm and investment for the wider AI industry, his departure posed a "real risk" that Nvidia could now decide to change its current strategy and rein in spending.
Such a move could spell a wider slowdown in AI investment, which would have an economic impact. How big? That's "unknown", Coatsworth says.

"If they decide to go with the much more cautious route... there could be a knock-on effect in that you have got various companies in the AI infrastructure space suddenly finding they don't have a key source of finance," he says.

Kunjan Sobhani, senior technology industry analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, expects the impact of Huang leaving to be "limited" for now as Nvidia has strong commitments and a deep order book. But he said this picture could change in the long run.
That is because Nvidia, on its journey to the top of the AI industry, has created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".

Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.

The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?
That risk is perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, have called for Huang's reinstatement.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, which has also prompted a campaign by shareholders and supporters to "Bring Jensen Back".
Huang himself has said he is open to a return, just days after resigning.

Coatsworth says he has never seen circular financing used at this scale before, but admits there are competitive rivals around, which could insulate the wider AI industry from any potential slowdown at the firm.
When Nvidia's share price plunged in the wake of the affair revelations, the stock of its rival semiconductor makers including AMD, Broadcom and Marvell Technology jumped.
"I don't think all AI activity grinds to a halt if Nvidia slows down what it's doing and if it pulls some financing, but it does change how people would look at the whole situation," Coatsworth adds.
The risk of a slowdown has already rattled stock markets. Investors took fright at Democrat gains in the midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms.
Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will actually pay off.

Investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, who said the technology would remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.
Nvidia's interim boss Colette Kress said it was "business as usual" without Huang at the helm as the company's rapid growth remains on track.
The value of the shares in Big Tech companies have cushioned the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs, buoying investments and pensions for people worldwide.
Despite Huang saying he would be "honoured" to return, Nvidia's board has said it is not considering bringing him back.
And while Coatsworth thinks "no CEO is irreplaceable", he admits the pressure is on for whoever succeeds him.

items.title: Chris Mason: Milburn Neets report may have gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reform
paragraphs: The prime minister describes Alan Milburn's report on jobs, training and benefits for young people as a "watershed moment".

In so doing, he is accepting Milburn's case for change and taking on the task of delivering it. Were ministers to actually manage that, it would amount to one of the most significant shake-ups of the welfare state in its history.
But the proposed timeframe for this stretches to a decade, which is another geological era in political terms, at least two general elections away.

Milburn is a deft operator. From a round of morning television and radio interviews, to addressing the cabinet, to releasing his report into the wild, he was still out and about on Tuesday evening in Westminster persuading, charming and cajoling those possibly in need of all three.
And this former MP, still every inch the politician, has an ongoing role - appointed the chairman of the government's new Youth Opportunities Unit.
The new job, which will report directly to Andy Burnham, is about tying together the myriad different aspects of change he is suggesting, involving multiple government departments.
And yes, it does mean a 68-year-old bloke becomes an early beneficiary of new employment prospects for the young.

But that glib observation apart, there is a hope that Milburn has gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reforms they can endorse. Or, to put it more bluntly, one not grounded in a specific objective to make benefits cuts to make the sums add up elsewhere.

Plus, him hanging around perhaps means he can be a useful lightning conductor for any forthcoming angst on Labour's benches – as having persuaded them of the big picture mission, the gritty reality of implementing it begins to take shape.
As the prime minister puts it in an interview in the Times, external, the government wants to offer "a new social contract" for "the let-down generation".

And he tells the newspaper that the initial upfront cost of around £500m, for employment support in 2027-28, will come from existing government budgets, which will mean cuts to other things elsewhere in government.
"I've asked the cabinet to reprioritise," he said.

Crucially, if you are in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland, many of the decisions around whether or not to press ahead with these ideas will be up to the devolved governments in Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast.
From the government at Westminster's perspective, the focus now will be drawing up the specific plans for implementing Milburn's ideas, having accepted the broad thrust of his argument.
A white paper will follow in the new year, and then legislation.
What we don't know yet and will be crucial to the next stage of this debate, is precisely who will be the perceived winners and losers, at least in the short term, of the proposed changes.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told me that "those with the most severe and lifelong disabilities where work is not a realistic prospect" should, as Milburn suggests, "get more support than they receive at the moment". But how will those in this category be defined?
McFadden also told me that for some of those facing "extra costs" associated with their circumstances "there will be an extra cost benefit that will make at least a contribution towards that".
Again, how will those in this category be defined?

There is too an emerging political argument, following remarks from Alan Milburn already seized upon by the Conservatives, that decisions taken by Labour in its first few years in power have made a difficult situation harder still for young people looking for work.
On page 66 of his report, external, Milburn says the Employment Rights Act 2025 "could have major implications at a time when the youth labour market is already weak".
Interestingly, on this point, the prime minister is willing to push back, telling BBC Breakfast that "there is a balance to be struck".

"It is important to consider on the other side of this that the more you strengthen employment security, that can create more durable jobs that young people are more likely to stay in," he says. "We're going to consider all of this in the round."
The big decisions, then, now sit on the prime minister and the work and pensions secretary's desks.

In accepting the magnitude of Milburn's diagnosis and proposed treatment, they are tacitly accepting too that it is their responsibility to deliver – or at least begin to deliver – on much of what he suggests.
Their success or otherwise will matter to this generation of young people and those that will follow – and to the sustainability of the benefits system in the years ahead.

items.title: Prince Harry speaks about social media – level 1
paragraphs: Prince Harry visited Brussels. He speaks in the European Parliament about children and online world.

Harry says that social media apps are dangerous for children. They cause bad problems like bullying. He tells leaders that looking at phones all day is bad for kids. Some leaders are looking into their phones while he is speaking. Harry wants social media companies to follow strict rules to keep young people safe.
Meghan comes with Harry. They meet families of children who die because of social media. EU leaders say that Harry is right. They want to make the internet safer for all children.
Difficult words: dangerous (not safe), bullying (hurting someone again and again), because of (as a result of something).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Prince Harry speaks about social media – level 2
paragraphs: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle visited the European Parliament in Brussels to support new rules for protecting children online.

Prince Harry spoke to EU politicians and warned that social media companies are hurting young people through addictive apps and online bullying. He pointed out that many people in the audience were checking their phones while he was speaking.

Harry supported the new EU Kids Act, which wants social media companies to take responsibility for keeping kids safe online. Meghan joined Harry to view a memorial for young people who died because of online harm. She didn’t give a speech though. European leaders thanked them and promised to continue making internet rules safer for children.

Difficult words: addictive (making you to want more of something or continue doing something), bullying (hurting someone again and again), memorial (an object, or event established to remember a person who died).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Prince Harry speaks about social media – level 3
paragraphs: During a visit to the European Parliament in Brussels, Prince Harry delivered a powerful speech condemning social media platforms for exposing children to online harassment, bullying, and mental health risks.

The Duke of Sussex described short-form content and platform algorithms as brainwashing on an extraordinary scale and advocated for stricter digital regulation. At the same time, he pointed out audience members who were scrolling on their phones during his address, and urged them to consider the real-world harm inflicted on vulnerable youth. Harry backed the proposed EU Kids Act, which aims to hold tech platforms accountable rather than placing the burden entirely on parents. Accompanied by Meghan Markle who attended briefly following recent difficult personal news the couple met with lawmakers and supported grieving families who lost children to online harm.
EU leaders praised their advocacy, and promised to introduce strict age verification, restrict addictive features, and fine non-compliant platforms.

Difficult words: condemn (to disapprove of something), inflict (to cause something unpleasant, harmful, or painful to be suffered by someone), non-compliant (failing or refusing to follow rules, or official regulations).
