items.title: Carolina Zimbalist pours bioplastic over silk for Emma Watson's LACMA Gala dress
paragraphs: Artist Carolina Zimbalist has co-created a biomaterial dress with actress Emma Watson, who wore it at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art’s 15th annual Art+Film Gala.

Zimbalist, a graduate of the Parsons School of Design, employed a homemade bioplastic she frequently uses in her artistic works in order to create the one-of-a-kind garment, which comprises a longline bodice and floor-length skirt rendered in shades of red.
The petroleum-free poured-and-dried material, containing vegetable glycerin alongside naturally derived proteins such as pea powder, is layered over silk – a natural biopolymer itself.
“The formulation draws on naturally derived proteins and other ingredients, with the exact composition varying depending on what I’m making,” Zimbalist told Dezeen.
“Very often I favour the usage of byproducts.”
The material’s technical makeup lends itself to a distinctive aesthetic once poured and dried.
“My biomaterial creates sculptural forms and flexible surfaces that move with the body,” said Zimbalist.
“The visual qualities are meant to draw greater interest in sustainable materials while remaining fundamentally artistic.”
Zimbalist has variously referred to her recipe as a bioplastic, a biomaterial or a biopolymer, but now favours the latter to avoid negative associations with the term “plastic”.
“For years, I described my formulas as bioplastics, but about three seasons ago, I switched to ‘biomaterials’; when people hear ‘bioplastic’, they tend to focus on the plastic,” Zimbalist continued.

“‘Biomaterial’ opens up a different conversation about what the material is and what it can become. All three terms apply, but they bring different associations – although biopolymer is the most technically accurate.”
Zimbalist hopes that by experimenting with these natural materials, they can become a mainstream and accessible means of constructing garments beyond one-off pieces.

“The environmental benefits are something I’m developing along with the growing wave of biomaterial artists now assembling – I like to think we are presenting sustainable fashion in a way that inspires more interest beyond the fringes.”
Zimbalist is no stranger to clothing celebrities: 2024 saw musician Chapelle Roan wear a hand-painted, garden-inspired dress that the artist made partially using seaweed.
As well as garments, the artist also creates ethereal and sculptural homeware, including lighting and vases.
Biomaterials are sweeping the fashion world, opening up opportunities for aesthetic and sustainable progress in a sector not historically known for its eco-friendliness.
Designers are increasingly finding ways to derive materials, fabrics and ornamentation from pioneering sources, including mycelium, tree cellulose and soil.

items.title: After a week with the iPhone Duo, I never want to go back
paragraphs: I remember my first Apple product. It was the fourth generation iPod – the last model to feature a monochrome screen. For a few years I'd backed the wrong horse, thinking Sony's minidisk players were the future of portable music. But as soon as I held the iPod, I was smitten. It felt like it had fallen out of the future, and like it was designed just as much to be looked at as it was to be used. And for the first time in decades, I'm feeling the same way about a new Apple product.

After a week with the iPhone Duo, I'm, well, smitten again. After years (and years) of incremental upgrades, we finally have something that feels genuinely new and exciting. And if you can swallow the huge asking price, I think this might be the ultimate smartphone for creatives.

I'll be exploring how the iPhone Duo fares for specific creative tasks over the coming weeks, but today I want to talk specifically about the design. This thing feels truly luxurious. With its gleaming metallic finish and satisfyingly compact proportions when closed, it reminds me somewhat of a vintage cigarette holder. There's something almost Art Deco about it. Foldables have always felt awkward, but Apple has somehow made it elegant.

Speaking of size, I've seen plenty of online commentators complain that the Duo is too small (Apple is even rumoured to be working on a larger version). But for me, it's perfect. As someone who prefers phones that don't require three hands to hold, I've always been one of the few defenders of the iPhone mini. For me, its diminutive dimensions are precisely the point. After years of phones getting progressively more enormous, there's something wonderfully refreshing about a device that actually wants to fit in your pocket.

But of course, the real headline here is the larger internal display. This has been the subject of debate too, thanks to the matte nano-texture layer. This does take some getting used to (and in my experience, seems a little harder to clean), but there are massive benefits too – namely, vastly reduced glare. And perhaps even more importantly, it makes the dreaded 'crease' less visible.

There are some delightful software touches that make the Duo a joy to use. The open/close animation, which blurs content as the screen is folded or unfolded, is subtle way of explaining that content is moving from one screen to another. And my personal favourite touch is the new StandBy mode, which works when the phone is propped in 'tent' mode, turning it into a desk calendar and clock.

As a creative, the possibilities of the Duo are immediately appealing. Having more room to view images, browse design inspiration or work with visual content without reaching for a separate tablet feels like a meaningful improvement, rather than another feature invented to fill a keynote. I'll be exploring the creative potential in more detail soon. But for now, after just a few days with the device, it's clear that Apple's sense of fun is well and truly back. This is a bold yet playful product design that feels, for the first time in forever, like it has fallen out of the future.

Daniel John is Design Editor at Creative Bloq. He reports on the worlds of design, branding and lifestyle tech, and has covered several industry events including Milan Design Week, OFFF Barcelona and Adobe Max in Los Angeles. He has interviewed leaders and designers at brands including Apple, Microsoft and Adobe. Daniel's debut book of short stories and poems was published in 2018, and his comedy newsletter is a Substack Bestseller.

items.title: 'Human' is Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year
paragraphs: "Human" is the Cambridge Dictionary's Word of the Year — defined as "having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines".
"The growth of AI means it is now necessary to explicitly say 'human' for things that once could only be done by humans," said chief editor Colin McIntosh.

Examples of current usage included actors Scarlett Johansson challenging "an assault on human creativity" and Matthew McConaughey protecting himself against unauthorised digital reproduction of his voice or image.
"The measure of AI's success should be how much it improves human lives," said Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates on learning about the dictionary's choice.
McIntosh said dictionary editors had to be on top of how words could change over time "to reflect what people say and what they write".
His research revealed a four-fold use of the word human since 1900.
"'Man' used to be used in this sense a lot more, but now it is not acceptable to use 'man' to mean men and women," he added.
"Human didn't come into use in Middle English until the 14th Century, from a French word. Shakespeare used it, but after that it was very restricted in use."
There had also been an increased use of compound words such as human-made and human-driven, to distinguish the works, qualities and skills of people from AI.
"Fears about what humans may lose when we outsource our thinking have made us reconsider the extent to which we rely on AI, from top mathematicians to teachers of young children," said McIntosh.

items.title: Watch: Marco Rubio says recent tech outages are 'completely unrelated' to one another
paragraphs: Microsoft, major US banks, Apple and Air Traffic authorities have been hit over recent days by tech glitches.

items.title: ‘Human’ wins Cambridge dictionary’s word of the year
paragraphs: In a world where the line between people and machines is more blurred than ever, Cambridge dictionary has sided with natural intelligence for its word of the year: human.

Breakthroughs in artificial intelligence – led by the arrival of ChatGPT three years ago – have made the question of what it means to be human as vexed as ever, but the dictionary has drawn a firm line with its choice of the word of 2026, defining “human” as “having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines”.

AI advances have spurred questions about whether computers can achieve consciousness, with the evolutionary biologist Richard Dawkins among those who answered in the affirmative, saying he was “left with the overwhelming feeling that they are human”. Sceptics, on the other hand, argue that there is a vast difference between how a human brain evolves and how an AI system is built.

Cambridge dictionary said the meaning and use of “human” had become more important in the age of the chatbot. Colin McIntosh, an editor of the dictionary, said AI was “changing the way we talk about being human” and had led to the word of the year being deployed to distinguish our work from that of advanced computer systems.

“Fears about what humans may lose when we outsource our thinking has made us reconsider the extent to which we rely on AI: from top mathematicians to teachers of young children,” he said. “A recent increase in compounds such as ‘human-made’ highlight how the word has come to distinguish works or qualities of people, as distinct from AI.”

Prof Rachel Adams, an expert on AI governance and human rights at the University of Cambridge, said: “AI brings us back to questions that we’ve asked for millennia: who are we, what does it mean to be human? The answer to these questions has never been fixed or stable, but the act of asking it is something we have in common.”

Other tech-related words were on the shortlist: “agent”, the term for an AI system that can operate – sometimes alarmingly – without human control, and “analogues”, relating to non-digital activities. A non-tech contender was “wholesome”, a word to describe something which is likely to improve your life either physically, morally, or emotionally.
Earlier this month, “mogging” – meaning to outperform or outshine someone or something – was named the Collins word of the year.

Tech-adjacent words also stood out among the new additions to the Cambridge dictionary. “Looksmaxxing”, describing the act of making oneself as physically attractive as possible, which has been associated with the online manosphere, and “aura farming”, another term often encountered on social media, which refers to “the activity of doing things with the intention of showing a personality that people admire and think is attractive and interesting”.

The former UK prime minister Keir Starmer made the news late last year when some social media users wondered “why he was aura farming” with his TikToks; Andy Burnham also appears to be attempting to master the art after becoming prime minister.

items.title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
paragraphs: The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.

The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.

Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.

The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.

Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.

In confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.

If Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).

According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.

In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, said she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.

“The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik said. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”
Under the plan, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.
The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.

The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.
One of the EU conditions for Egypt to gain the first €1bn loan was to increase the number of Takaful and Karama beneficiary households by 100,000 to 4.7 million.
In a leaked report to lawmakers in the EU council of ministers and the European parliament, the commission described that requirement as “broadly fulfilled”.

The data in that report, however, reveals a net fall of 62,281 households during this period, owing to what the EU officials describe as “a multi-annual recertification process”. Some beneficiaries were added to the list but a larger number were removed because they were deemed ineligible.

In order to achieve a later instalment of €1.5bn, Egypt was required to “further expand” the programmes, adding 60,000 households to the Takaful and Karama beneficiaries list. A second leaked report to EU lawmakers shows that the commission concluded the target was “fulfilled” because 442,118 families were added to the list.

On this occasion, the commission did not report on numbers removed. Figures from Egypt’s ministry of social solidarity, however, show a net reduction of 23,453 beneficiaries to the programmes in the 11 months until June 2026, the period leading up to the release of that payment. The EU announced the release of the €1.5bn payment in July 2026.
The data has since been deleted from the Egyptian ministry website but the Guardian has seen screenshots and archived webpages.
During a period from 2024 to 26 when the EU required Egypt to add 160,000 households to the rolls of the Karama and Takaful programmes, there was a net decline of 85,734 households.

Timothy Kaldas, the deputy director of the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, said the commission had generally “done a poor job of leveraging the funds of European taxpayers to support genuine stabilisation” on the other side of the Mediterranean. “The strategic interest of Europe is seeing a more economically stable Egypt with a population that is less precarious,” he said.

Sandra Gómez López, a Spanish socialist MEP who recently visited Cairo to assess human rights in Egypt, said the data presented by the Guardian raised important questions. “The commission must explain transparently why it considers these commitments to have been fulfilled and demonstrate that European funding is genuinely contributing to improving social protection for the Egyptian population,” she said.
She stressed that the EU should not withdraw support, “but neither can we allow the country’s strategic importance to lead us to lower our standards when it comes to human rights”.

For critics, the questions about the EU’s willingness to hold Egypt accountable on very precise socioeconomic targets do not bode well for the broader but less defined goals for democracy and human rights.

Strik said: “The fact that Egypt and the commission even seem to ignore the crystal-clear socioeconomic conditions doesn’t increase my expectation that they adhere to the vague precondition on democracy and the rule of law.”
Claudio Francavilla, an associate EU director at Human Rights Watch, said: “Without benchmarks, the EU has turned a human rights conditionality into a blank cheque for Egypt’s authoritarianism.”

In a statement to the Guardian, the European Commission said the policy target on Takaful and Karama referred to new beneficiary families “and not to its net increase”. The spokesperson said there was “no contradiction” between this statement and that in a confidential document that said Egypt was required to “further expand cash transfer programmes”.

Asked about the release of the remaining €1.5bn in promised loans, the commission said it “will be made once all conditions have been met”, referring to 24 economic policy conditions, keeping an IMF programme on track and “taking concrete and credible steps towards respecting effective democratic mechanisms, including a multiparty parliamentary system, and the rule of law, and guaranteeing respect for human rights”.
It added: “Compliance with the conditionality is examined thoroughly” by EU officials and diplomats based on “information provided by the Egyptian authorities and other relevant sources”.
Egypt’s mission to the EU in Brussels did not respond to a request for comment.

items.title: Australian wages grow at fastest pace since 2023 – but prices are climbing even more quickly
paragraphs: Wages grew at their fastest pace since late 2023 over the three months to September, buoyed up by this year’s boost to minimum pay rates for millions of lower paid workers – but still not fast enough to keep up with the rising cost of living.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics’ wage price index climbed by 1.1% in the most recent quarter, lifting the annual increase to 3.5% – a pace that economists said would keep the Reserve Bank on edge about the need for further interest rate hikes.
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said the pickup in wages growth was thanks to the government’s support for the minimum pay rise.
“We’re helping to deliver higher wages for workers because we know this is one of the best ways to help with the cost of living,” he said.
While wage rates are climbing about 1 percentage point faster per year on average than before the pandemic, prices are climbing even more quickly – a reality that Chalmers recognised.

“Real wages are declining not because wages have been too low but because inflation is still too high, which is why helping in the fight against inflation and getting the budget in better nick are such high priorities for the government.”
The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said the latest figures confirmed that “Australians are working harder for less”.
“Australians are poorer under Labor. That is the reality of the economy that has been built by a Labor government that simply does not get it,” he said at a press conference.
Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

The Fair Work Commission in early June implemented a 6% pay rise to about 100,000 of the country’s lowest paid employees to help compensate for cost of living pressures made worse by surging fuel prices.
The annual review also gave a 4.75% pay rise to 2.7 million workers on award wages.
Rachael McCririck, head of prices statistics at the ABS, said these decisions “were a key driver of much of the growth in private sector wages this quarter”.
Analysts said wages were growing faster than the Reserve Bank had been expecting, and that this added to the case, if only at the margin, for a potential sixth interest rate hike.

Cherelle Murphy, EY’s chief economist, said she did not expect a move after the RBA’s final board meeting for the year on 7-8 December, even though the wage growth figure was “uncomfortably high for the central bank”.
“[It’s] unlikely to prompt any immediate reaction, given the economy is now slowing in response to the five interest rate hikes delivered between February and November this year,” Murphy said.
“We expect the central bank will be in wait-and-see mode,” she said.
The ABS figures showed pay rates are rising fastest in the public sector, up by an annual 3.9%, while private sector wages increased by 3.4%.

“The main driver of public sector wage growth was pay rises for state government frontline workers covered by enterprise agreements. This included groups like nurses, midwives and police officers,” McCririck said.

Jeff Borland, an economics professor at the University of Melbourne, said while the wage price index was useful to assess inflationary pressures in the labour market, it was less useful as a way to assess workers’ actual incomes.

“The WPI is the labour cost to an employer of having a particular job done. If you want to know what is happening to the average worker, then the weekly income from the [ABS’s] characteristics of employment survey is a better measure,” Borland said.
By this broader measure of worker pay, the story is not as dire as that told by the after-inflation change in the WPI, he said.
Real average hourly labour income received per employed person was artificially boosted through the pandemic but has since come back to be just 3.4% higher this decade.
This extends the overall weak trend through the 2010s, Borland said.
In contrast, the wage price index is down 4.4% since the start of 2020.
“None of the real wage measures are telling you things are going gangbusters,” Borland said.
“But there’s a difference in the degree to which they tell you how badly things are going.”

items.title: Waymo temporarily pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways
paragraphs: Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways, the company has said.
The decision comes after California banned Waymo's driverless taxis from state freeways following a series of recent traffic incidents.

California's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) cited an "imminent hazard to public safety" for the ban, noting an incident this month in which several driverless Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on US Route 101.

Waymo said it was working with state officials "diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations", adding that no injuries or collisions were reported following the incident on US Route 101 south of San Francisco.

California's DMV said Waymo's driverless taxis presented a risk "due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present".

In another incident earlier this month, footage widely seen on social media appeared to show a Waymo car trying to overtake patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing the pace of traffic on a San Francisco highway.

The California ban, which came into effect on 11 November, would remain in place until Waymo "demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions".
A Waymo spokesperson said: "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance."
Data on Waymo's website suggests that its cars, compared to human drivers, are involved in 95% fewer crashes resulting in serious injury.
Waymo currently operates driverless taxis in 15 US cities, but only offered freeway rides in a handful of those locations, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Miami.
The company's driverless taxis can continue to operate on regular city streets.
In May, Waymo recalled thousands of its self-driving cars in the US over a software issue that could allow vehicles to drive into flooded roads.
In the same month, multiple Waymo cars were spotted driving around a cul-de-sac in Atlanta, Georgia, in the early hours of the morning.

items.title: Jeff Bezos says he was 'heavily involved' in casting Robert Pattinson as new 007
paragraphs: "There was something special about Rob", Bezos said at Semafor Silicon Valley & The World Event on Tuesday.
Pattinson was unveiled as the franchise's seventh James Bond on Monday, taking over from actor Daniel Craig. He will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.
In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."
The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.
The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.
Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.
But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.
"We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on Friday," Bezos said.
There were five finalists who went through "real, old-fashioned screen tests", acting out three different scenes in full costume, with real sets and other actors, he said.

"By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance," Bezos added. "It was immediately undebated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director … we all gravitated toward Rob."
The pick comes amid widespread Hollywood cuts and consolidation, with studios struggling to get people into cinemas.
Hollywood insiders have said Pattinson was viewed as a safe pick to bring audiences in, rather than taking a risk on a new actor who could grow with the franchise.

"Maybe he's boring. Maybe Hollywood would be passing up a chance to anoint a badly needed new star. But with so much at stake for everyone involved, that all makes him the obvious pick," Hollywood journalist Matthew Belloni, who predicted the pick, wrote in his newsletter.
The BBC's Regan Morris contributed to this report.

items.title: Sleeve checks and no smartglasses: South Korea races to protect all-important university exams against AI
paragraphs: The integrity of South Korea’s career-defining university entrance exam has been thrown into doubt after the top scorer in a recent professional exam admitted using a concealed camera and AI to cheat.

On Thursday, more than half a million people, mostly school students, are due to sit the exam, known as the suneung, at 1,312 centres across the country. The exam runs for a gruelling eight hours over a single day and determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.

The country goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended.

The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre. Extra trains run from 6am, police drive latecomers to their exam halls, and tourist attractions open late to ease traffic. Offices are asked to open at 10am.

But in recent days, exam organisers have faced a renewed threat to the validity of the entire exercise, after the top scorer in this year’s tax accountancy exam- who got just one question wrong out of 160– admitted on Sunday he had cheated by using AI.
Prime minister Han Seong-sook told a cabinet meeting in Seoul on Tuesday that AI-assisted cheating was a “social evil” that the government would “root out”.
“We will block outright the carrying of smart devices during the exam,” she said. The education ministry and other agencies should approach it “as if staking their jobs on it”, she added.

Han said smart devices must be turned off and handed in, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.
The government will also send emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sound at full volume and cannot be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.

More invigilators will be deployed, and the government said it was preparing to switch off school wifi inside exam centres and public wifi nearby, and that personal hotspots, which cannot be blocked, would be traced through connection records.
The weekend’s cheating revelation captured national headlines in South Korea, stoking concern about the security of the suneung.

In a video posted to his lawyer’s YouTube channel, the exam cheat said he had photographed the questions with a concealed microcamera, sent them to an AI system and read the answers from a smartphone. “I cheated in the tax accountant exam,” he said. “My top placing is not the result of legitimate effort.”
His lawyer handed police a camera, a laptop and a phone. No charges have been brought, and the prime minister has ordered procedures to begin that would void his result and bar him for five years.

The education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, told parliament on Monday that while authorities could screen out the smart glasses already on sale at Thursday’s exam, newer variants could not be dealt with perfectly.

Choi has ruled out postponing the exam, which has been delayed several times before, including in 2017, after an earthquake struck the south-eastern city of Pohang, and in 2020 due to the Covid pandemic.

Smart glasses have been banned in exams since the end of June. In October, several candidates were caught with them while sitting university-run admissions exams. At the suneung, wearing a pair counts as using one even when switched off.

The education ministry looked at using radio-frequency equipment to detect the glasses in exam halls, but concluded conditions varied too much between venues for deployment this year. Checks will instead rely on visual inspection, with at least one dedicated official placed in each exam centre.

Teachers’ unions have criticised the government response as belated. A survey last month of 2,716 secondary school teachers by the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union showed that 82.3% said they could not tell whether a candidate was wearing smart glasses under the current procedure, with only 3.5% saying they could.

To avoid facing scrutiny on exam day, some candidates are reportedly switching to contact lenses. An optician in Suwon, south of Seoul, said students who had never worn contacts were coming in to ask how to put them in.
Han said on X on Monday that the checks would be handled carefully “so that candidates acting in good faith do not suffer unnecessary anxiety or inconvenience”.
In his video confession, the accountancy test cheat addressed suneung candidates directly. “The suneung is coming up soon,” he said.
“To anyone thinking of cheating as I did: I am going to tell the investigators everything, so please don’t think, ‘I won’t get caught.’”

items.title: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as firm reports bumper results
paragraphs: Nvidia's quarterly sales doubled to top $100bn for the first time as the company insisted it has no plans to reinstate ousted co-founder Jensen Huang.
In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it is "business as usual" and told investors: "We've got this."
The company's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier, reaching $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading.
Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.
"The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said during a call on Tuesday with financial analysts.

The company's profits also doubled from a year ago. For the quarter, which covered the three months to 25 October, profit hit $65bn. Its revenue from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn in the same period.
Going forward, the company said its rapid growth is poised to continue, and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.
Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.

"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."
Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry.
"It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."
She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects".

"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."
The interim CEO also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China.
The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.
They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US.
Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped.

items.title: One Nation says it would cut Australia’s refugee intake by 90% under ‘tough stance’
paragraphs: One Nation has vowed to cut Australia’s refugee intake by 90% and scrap the permanent parent visa program under its latest hardline plan to slash migration.

Pauline Hanson announced the policy on Tuesday, labelling it a “tough” approach to migration. It was quickly criticised by political opponents and advocacy groups who labelled the announcement a “predictable and cheap” attack on refugees.

The rightwing party said if it held power it would cut the refugee program from 20,000 places a year to 2,000 and claimed that Australia would still remain above the OECD average for places per capita.
“The cost [to] … the taxpayer is enormous,” Hanson told reporters. “The cost is, on average, about $500,000 a year in a lifetime of expenditure per person in the country.

“We’ve got to take a tough stance on this. My concern is for these people out there … that are doing it tough. You don’t bring more people into the country if they cannot fund their own bed or hospital beds.”

Hanson claimed that her plan would save the budget more than $140bn over 10 years. Migrants from countries on the Albanese government’s “do not travel” list, including Iran, Lebanon, Syria and Somalia, would still be banned from entering the country.

One Nation says analysis based on Treasury modelling, adjusted for inflation, found the lifetime cost of a humanitarian entrant was $523,000. Treasury modelling done in December 2021 found the cost was $400,000, with 90% of it borne by the federal government.
Labor has committed to retaining the refugee intake at 20,000 a year while the Coalition has promised to halve it to 10,000.

The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, accused One Nation of trying to divide the country. She said Australia had the right balance and questioned Hanson’s claim that Australia would remain above the OECD average under the minor party’s plan.

“I don’t accept those figures and I find when Ms Hanson speaks, you always have to check what is actually being said. There are countries which take more refugees, there are countries which take fewer. We think this [20,000 a year] is the right balance,” Wong said.

“We have unprecedented people movement around the world. We have displacement of more human beings than at any time since world war two. We make a very small contribution to that by our refugee intake.”
The OECD reports that Canada and Australia have the most generous refugee settlement programs per capita but it only uses data of refugees resettled through the UNHCR process.

The intakes of other OECD countries, including Germany and the US, are made up largely of asylum seekers who cross their borders and claim protection, meaning their intake levels appear much lower under the OECD figures Hanson has used.
Wong said it was “more of the same” from One Nation.
“I know that they think dividing Australians is the best response to the politics of the time,” the Labor frontbencher said. “I take a different view.”
The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, stood by his policy of halving the refugee intake to 10,000 but said “some of the greatest Australians came here as refugees to this country”.

“Some of those who have built the most successful businesses – an extraordinary group of people. But we need to make sure the people who come here as refugees do share our values, and they’re the right people,” Taylor said.
The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, said he didn’t take One Nation’s policy announcements seriously because they changed frequently.
“I just take it as another statement. It’ll be replaced by another one in a few days’ time, and I don’t see any of the substantial policy work,” he told News24.
“Their answer just seems to be to announce a number, then to walk away from it the next week because they need another number.”

The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, accused One Nation and the two major parties of being “engaged in a race to the bottom to turn back refugees, lock them up in offshore detention, and blame them for the cost of living crisis”.
“Pauline Hanson’s attack on refugees is just the latest shameful chapter in a decades-long campaign against people seeking safe shelter,” Shoebridge said.
Meanwhile, the Asylum Seeker Resource Centre called it a “predictable and cheap attack” on refugees, and said Victorians would reject One Nation at the upcoming state election.
The ASRC’s deputy chief executive, Jana Favero, said the public wanted leaders to bring communities together, not divide them.

“People are sick of politicians finger-pointing and blaming our newest arrivals for problems,” Favero said. “Reducing the humanitarian intake will not make Victorians richer or safer. People want solutions, not scapegoats.”
Other nations including the US and Canada have tightened their migration programs, with Canada reducing its parent visa program.
Hanson said One Nation was not barring migrant parents from moving to Australia but they would have to be sponsored or they could visit their families on temporary visas.
“We’re not saying parents can’t come out … [but] they will actually be sponsored by the families not the taxpayers.”

items.title: Largest British study to check social media ban's effect on youth mental health
paragraphs: The work, funded by health charity The Wellcome Trust, will help inform future online safety policies in the UK and internationally, with some early results available before the ban happens.
Researchers will use wearable technology, smartphones, digital diaries and surveys to collect data to see how young people respond to the ban, both physically and mentally.
And they will check whether young people find ways to circumvent restrictions.
Dr Camilla Iannone, research lead at Wellcome, said it was a once-in-a-generation opportunity to study at scale how social media and its restrictions affected youth mental health.
"We really don't think that this is a simple binary question of whether social media is good or bad, or whether restrictions work or don't work.
"Instead, the teams will study whether changing young people's digital environment leads to meaningful changes in their mental health and wellbeing."
Participants are being recruited to reflect a diverse range of young people, including different genders and sexual orientations.
People with existing mental health conditions, such as anxiety and depression, will also be included, as well as young people who are neurodivergent.

Groups have been set up at Cardiff University, the University of Oxford, the University of Birmingham, King's College London, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Manchester, the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, and University College London.

items.title: Government risks missing climate targets if EV rules weakened, adviser warns
paragraphs: The UK is likely to miss legally binding climate targets if the government reduces electric vehicle (EV) targets, independent adviser the Climate Change Committee (CCC) has warned.

In a letter to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander, the CCC argues that weakening the targets would result in "economic and energy security costs" and leave households "more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices".
The CCC says that switching to an electric vehicle can save a typical household around £800 a year, with fewer people benefiting if the targets were watered down.
The warning comes after weeks of speculation that the government plans to announce changes to the EV targets. Government sources insist no decision has been made.

Under the current rules, a "zero emission vehicle" (ZEV) mandate requires 80% of new cars sold in the UK to be zero emission by 2030 and all new cars to meet that standard by 2035. Companies that fail to meet their ZEV mandate face a potential fine of £12,000 per car, although there are exemptions.
Industry groups have long complained the current rules impose too heavy a burden, calling instead for a "sustainable transition".
Latest data from trade body the Society of Motor Manufacturing and Traders (SMMT) shows that EVs, as well as plug-in hybrids, are driving growth in new car sales.
In the year so far, 26.6% of all new car registrations have been fully electric, the SMMT says, which is below the headline target of 33% for 2026.

But the industry as a whole appears on course to comply with this year's mandate once flexibilities are accounted for, according to analysis by New AutoMotive, a transport research organisation which supports the transition to electric cars
SMMT Chief Executive Mike Hawes accused the CCC of ignoring the costs of the targets it was defending.
"The industry cannot subsidise the transition indefinitely, which is why it is unified in seeking change," he said.
The CCC analysis also argued that weakening the targets would lead to a hole in the government's carbon savings that need to be made in order to meet its legally binding climate targets.

The CCC said the ZEV mandate "underpins the largest share of emissions reduction to 2037" in the government's net-zero plan. The climate targets set for 2033-2037 will be missed "without alternative action at the same scale", the CCC argued.
CCC analysis shows surface transport - which includes cars, vans and trucks - remains the country's highest carbon-emitting sector and one of the slowest to decarbonise.
Lord Deben, former CCC chairman, said going against CCC advice would "not be sensible" as it would "cost people money".
He said climate targets were "not random targets" and "if you don't reach them then you put yourselves in really serious danger of having climate change, which we can't handle".

A government spokesperson said: "We remain committed to the phase out of all new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and to all new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, as well as to our legally binding net zero targets. Our consultation on the Mandate will not change this and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition."

items.title: The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left
paragraphs: "Opening the door to uncontrolled immigration," is how Reform UK described it. "Dragging us into the European Union via the back door," was the charge levelled by the Conservatives.
You could be forgiven for expecting drastic change come Friday's EU-UK summit in Brussels judging by some of the criticism levelled by opponents of the Labour government.
Instead, what's on the table is a limited youth work and mobility scheme (the source of Reform's ire), agreement on cross-channel carbon emissions pricing and a deal to ease food trade.

There's also talk of reducing tuition fees for EU students at British universities (something EU member states, like Germany, really want) in exchange for the UK being admitted to an EU manufacturing scheme (which is important to the Burnham government).
Even in these limited areas, I'm told, not all details will be ironed out by the time of Thursday's meeting.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham admitted last week this is all a "step" towards a closer working relationship with Europe.
It's certainly not a leap, and definitely not a matter of rejoining the bloc at this stage.
Other "steps" under immediate discussion are the UK rejoining the EU's electricity market, and the UK trying again to join an EU-backed defence loan scheme.

"Small steps… to make both sides stronger," is how the EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas describes this process. She also warns: "We have in Europe a lot of trauma from Britain leaving [the EU], so things will not be easy."
At this week's summit, the UK and EU are expected to discuss a limited youth mobility scheme, cross-channel carbon emissions pricing, and a deal to ease food trade

Bigger, potentially more politically explosive EU-UK questions look likely to follow after Friday's summit. It's thought Burnham may propose rejoining the EU's customs union and/or the single market. There are suggestions he could eventually table a new referendum on rejoining the EU. None of this before the next general election, though.

On this side of the Channel, the debate is very much focused on what Britain might want. Burnham's plan is bold, belated or completely barmy - depending on your political perspective. But there's been little discussion about the EU point of view, and less still on how the EU has changed since Britain left it.

Just how different is the EU in 2026 from the bloc Britain turned its back on a decade ago? And with the UK still mired in arguments over its relationship with Europe, does the EU even want GB back in the fold or would Brussels now rather avoid more drama?
Since 2016, a series of international shocks have fundamentally changed the EU.

The Covid crisis collapsed international supply chains. Europe became aware just how dependent it was on China for medical supplies, for example. Then, Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine showed the EU how utterly reliant many members were on energy supplies from Moscow. Big EU beasts like Germany and Italy were particularly affected.

The Ukraine war, the continent's biggest active conflict since World War Two, has persuaded the EU that Europe's domestic defence industry and industrial policy needs a boost and far better coordination.

Donald Trump's two stints as US president convinced the EU that it can never again fully rely on the US to be Europe's best friend abroad, either in trade or security terms. And China's attempt to 'dump' cheap cars and steel in Europe, hurting the Continent's businesses, has made the EU more protectionist-minded.
Brussels's main takeaways: Europe should become more self-reliant. And where imports are needed - with fossil fuels, for example - it must diversify which countries it buys from.

The French used to be a lone voice amongst big EU countries, pushing for more protectionism. Other member states prioritised finding the lowest possible prices, as was once the case with Russian gas, for example. Now there's a growing acceptance that economic efficiency must at times be sacrificed to achieve security of supply.

Some think the UK won't want to align itself with an increasingly protectionist, borrow-happy bloc. While an EU member, the free-trade-minded UK was credited with pushing Brussels to be more "British" and make its single market more competitive.
Britain's 2016 EU referendum prompted years of political drama
Others point out that Britain has also changed since 2016.

"The British are less 'British' than they once were," Charles Grant, director of the Centre for European Reform, told me. When the EU introduced steel tariffs to protect itself against Chinese dumping, the UK followed suit with its own, similar tariffs. Now, the EU is placing high tariffs on Chinese imports of electric vehicles - and once again the UK is considering a similar move. "Everyone is a bit more French now," says Grant.

Another big EU change, according to European policy expert Georgina Wright, is that EU citizens have become more comfortable with the idea of centralised European power: a pooling of sovereignty in times of emergency.

The Covid crisis prompted the EU to embrace 'common borrowing', where Brussels raises debt on behalf of member states, who then share the benefits and the risks. It was a historic move, particularly for Germany which was once allergic to the idea. Now there's discussion about a new round of common borrowing focused on defence, in answer to Russian aggression and a US proposing to withdraw defence capabilities from Europe.
Some in the EU tell me that none of this would be possible had the more sovereign-minded UK remained a member state.
But there are political winds of change blowing through the bloc.

Nationalist, more Eurosceptic parties are polling strongly in big EU members states ahead of upcoming elections. The EU that Burnham wants Britain to align with might look very different by the end of next year.

In France, one of the EU's two most influential countries, the hard-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading opinion polls ahead of the spring presidential election. Nation-first parties in Italy, Spain and Poland, as in France, say they want to transform the bloc from the inside.
Britain's centre-left government - as well as some UK voters - might be put off by an EU with Le Pen as a dominant force.

Conversely, there's an argument that an EU led by Eurosceptics might actually become more appealing to Britain. While those parties have their differences, they generally want to take powers back from Brussels, making the EU a looser club of stronger nation states - less of a political project, and more of a transactional club of common economic interests.

One change we can pretty much bet on is this: if Le Pen becomes French president, Brussels will become embroiled in internal existential tussles over the EU's future. These fault lines will pit the left against the right; pro-Europeans against Eurosceptics; Ukraine backers against those (like Le Pen) who want to stop financial aid; fans of a bigger EU budget against parties wanting to slash national contributions.
With all that going on, negotiations with the UK would very likely slip further down the priority list. British diplomats might find their calls unanswered.

If Burnham really wants to get closer to the EU, the time to act is now, says Wright. She identifies a window of opportunity before France's election for the UK to get "creative" in its re-set proposals.
Marine Le Pen leads the polls in France for next year's presidential election

Brussels is certainly under pressure to be more flexible in its relations with trusted allies outside the bloc, because of the threatening geopolitical climate. The EU embrace of Canada is a clear example.
"The prime minister should get out and about on the continent more, be more visible and talk more positively about what can be done together," says Wright.

Wright insists people in the UK are open to the idea. She quotes a survey by the National Centre for Social Research, published this month, which suggests 42% of Britons prioritise closer links with Europe over the US, while only 9% of Britons prioritise links with the US.
Then there's the question of how much Brussels actually wants Britain back in the European bloc.

Some in the UK believe they could take advantage of current geopolitical uncertainty. With the Russian threat looming, they think Brussels wants to have the UK close because of the UK's military and nuclear capabilities. In exchange, the UK could push for an ambitious deal with the EU, says Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey.

But Dr Ilke Toygür, a politics professor at Madrid's IE University, points out that European countries already work closely with the UK in defence, through Nato and the British and French-led support for Ukraine - so UK military leverage may not matter so much in EU terms.

Having the UK back in the European Union would certainly give the bloc more economic heft. In fact, some in the UK argue Britain is far better outside the bloc. Member states' economies are struggling, they say: look at stagnant Germany and Italy, and spluttering France. The UK, on the other hand, has grown at its fastest rate in two years thanks to AI investment. The UK enjoys freedom to regulate the AI industry outside the EU that it wouldn't have as an EU member state.
But EU diplomats I speak to believe the UK needs Brussels more than the other way round.
Germany and some European countries are investing in defence - and Britain now wants to join an EU-backed defence loan scheme

"The UK alone is a middling power in a field of giants," an EU diplomat from a big European country told me. He asked to remain anonymous in order to speak freely. "With China on the one side and the US on the other, the UK will be trampled underfoot if it stands alone. It must know that."
If the UK were ever to rejoin the EU, he says, it wouldn't necessarily have to join the euro currency or the open-border Schengen scheme.

But Michael Barnier, the former EU lead Brexit negotiator, tells me that as long as Britain remains outside the bloc it can't just cherry-pick all the benefits . It's the same argument the UK faced during cross-channel talks 10 years ago. The EU views the single market as the jewel in the bloc's crown, says Barnier, and Brussels does not want to devalue it by making major exceptions for the UK that other non-EU countries would then demand too. But he adds that the UK remains a much-appreciated ally and trading partner.

It would help Burnham, says the academic Toygür, if the UK had a more positive story to tell. She says Brussels is used to hearing Britain saying "we want to get closer to the EU because it's better for UK economic interests". Instead they should emphasise benefits to the EU, she says.
"We face a competition of great powers (China, US, Russia) and we are stronger together.
"The UK needs to commit resources: innovation and financial capacities to a continental-level project. It doesn't have to call that project 'the EU' but this is the only story moving forward."
What you hear from EU diplomats is that member states are more than OK with the existing post-Brexit trade deal. There is not a huge appetite to unravel it and start again.
The "little steps" of change, beneficial to both sides, like easing exports and imports, are what the EU is comfortable with right now.
Still, economist Heather Grabbe, from the Brussels-based economic think-tank Bruegel, predicts an "inevitable drift together" between the two sides.
British universities have historically been popular with Europeans - and now Brussels wants the UK to lower tuition fees for EU students

"We face the same challenges: aging populations, wildfires and storms, the impact of climate change, with our continent warming at twice the global rate. Russia is attacking us all with its hybrid warfare, we have the same outlook in world affairs: we're not pro-Trump, we're not pro-Putin. Working together makes sense," she says.

EU countries express a lot of warmth when asked about the UK inching closer. But behind closed doors, there is clear reticence. "Commitment" is a word you hear over and again; they're not sure that Britain really means it. They hear the Conservative Party deputy leader, Alex Burghart, for example, who vowed that, if elected, his party would "rip up" Labour's upcoming UK-EU agreements.
"The UK first needs a national conversation. And a binding decision. They need to know what they want and stick to it," say EU figures I speak to.
This is exactly what the EU insisted on 10 years ago, after the UK voted for Brexit without a clear political plan for what future relations with the bloc should look like.
As a journalist who's covered the UK's divorce from the EU right from the outset, I'm getting a rather strong sense of déjà vu.

BBC InDepth is the home on the website and app for the best analysis, with fresh perspectives that challenge assumptions and deep reporting on the biggest issues of the day. Emma Barnett and John Simpson bring their pick of the most thought-provoking deep reads and analysis, every Saturday. Sign up for the newsletter here

items.title: Brexit work travel rules need urgent improvement, say UK business leaders
paragraphs: Business chiefs have called on the UK government and the European Commission to urgently ease Brexit restrictions on business travel for cross-Channel work trips.

A group representing industry bosses said it wants commitments from Andy Burnham and European political leaders that the restrictions will be one of the priorities in 2027 for furthering ties between the two sides, after a summit in Brussels this week.

The Confederation of British Industry (CBI), which represents some of Britain’s largest companies, welcomed the prime minister’s recent calls for a reset with Europe, designed to reverse some of the damage to Britain’s economy caused by Brexit.

But it said Brexit restrictions, which include making employees obtain work permits for travel, are deterring cross-border investors and hampering trade at the very time both sides are trying to build resilience against China.

Sean McGuire, the CBI’s director of Europe and international, said discussions should have been a priority in the talks this week, after a UK-EU summit in 2025 held by Keir Starmer also referenced improving business mobility.
“Very little has been achieved. In fact, practically nothing has been achieved. The emphasis was put on youth mobility,” said McGuire.

EU diplomats have said in the past that the UK pushed hard for improving business mobility but was met with resistance from the bloc, where member states see British services – a big export particularly in the financial sector – as a threat.
McGuire said that energy, defence and car industry bosses say they are being hampered by the inability to travel freely in Europe to service or run multinational operations.
He said the issue should be of interest to all sides as they build on multiple existing laws to protect European supply chains.

“Now that we’ve got youth mobility potentially in the Friday deal, we should move seriously to address the kind of business mobility, which would apply to both the goods sector and the services sector,” he said.
British citizens travelling to the EU post-Brexit are restricted to 90 days at a time out of a maximum of 180 days a year, limiting companies’ ability to promote employees and travel.
“If you are a CEO of a multinational you can very quickly clock up 90 days,” McGuire said.

Separately, work permits have to be obtained for each country that a worker travels to. That can affect the servicing of equipment, particularly in engineering, where products that cost millions such as lifts, escalators and factory machines come with service and maintenance contracts.
“There is a big difference between irregular migration, which needs to be tackled, and business mobility, which is bringing investment into the UK and vice versa,” he said.
While an agreement is close on youth mobility, Burnham faces the same roadblock when it comes to opportunities for under-30s, who will be offered a three-year visa scheme to work, travel or study.
“It is a trick because the UK is negotiating with Brussels but work permits are a national competency,” said one EU diplomat.

But McGuire said there is a quick fix for business mobility, involving changes to the annex of the EU-UK trade and cooperation agreement, which allows the two sides to expand visa-free business travel across more industries without reworking the main treaty.

The CBI said it is also “disappointed” that no progress has been made on mutual recognition of qualifications allowing British or EU professionals to practise in each other’s territories as they did before Brexit.
Sources said there was a view in Brussels that mutual recognition of qualifications was more beneficial to the UK than to the EU, causing energy around the talks to drain away.

items.title: Ofqual urges ‘life-altering’ penalties for students who use tech to cheat
paragraphs: Students in England could suffer “life-altering” penalties if they are caught relying on AI or smart glasses to cheat, England’s qualifications regulator has said.

The head of Ofqual, Ian Bauckham, said students could be disqualified from GCSEs, A-levels and other qualifications if they tried to use AI in assessed coursework, and called for retailers to be barred from marketing wearable technology for exam cheating.

“If you are caught committing malpractice with an important, high-stakes qualification … in extreme cases you can lose the entire qualification which, as I am sure you can imagine, can be life-altering for somebody’s future,” Bauckham told the Press Association.

As coursework submission deadlines near, Ofqual is launching a publicity campaign to make it clear to students that using AI for assessments such as extended essays and failing to declare it will not be tolerated.

Bauckham is also writing to examination boards in England to tell them that exam hall invigilators and supervisors should be trained to spot the “emerging risk” posed by wearable devices during next summer’s exam season.
He said he was increasingly concerned about the potential use of wearable devices during exams, especially those able to access AI.

In a speech to an education conference in Birmingham on Wednesday, Bauckham will say: “It is completely unacceptable for any retailer, online or otherwise, to market items explicitly for the purpose of exam cheating. This has to be challenged.”
Ofqual recorded 2,225 cases of smart device and mobile phone cheating during GCSE, AS and A-levels in the summer 2025 exam season.
Bauckham also suggested that the use of extended essays was under threat because of students’ increased access to AI.
“We will need a radical rethink of the conditions under which it is done and the design of that coursework to make sure it is secure for the future and remains fit for purpose,” he said.
“Unsupervised extended essays, with no other forms of assessment associated with them … the time for that is likely to be quite short now.”
Academic subjects for GCSE and A-levels in England have had little or no coursework for the past decade, but A-level history and English are among those that still allow extended essays.

Bauckham said: “Where we do have extended writing being completed in unsupervised, uncontrolled conditions that is counting for coursework, counting for qualifications, I want … routes to malpractice, routes to cheating, to be closed down.”
Ofqual recorded 100 cases of plagiarism involving AI misuse in GCSE, AS and A-level entries last summer, an increase from 85 in 2024.
Bauckham said Ofqual was considering ways to guard against AI and plagiarism, including greater interrogation of the sources students use.

“It could mean linking the coursework in some formal way to the examination, whether that’s a written or a spoken examination, to make sure that we have a guarantee that students have genuinely done the work and genuinely understand it,” he said.

items.title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave
paragraphs: "Photonic chips are on the verge of a breakthrough," says Ton van Mol of the Dutch research institute TNO.
If van Mol is right – and TNO, the European Union and the Dutch government are backing the idea with millions of euros - then the technology could be a gamechanger.
The chips which run today's society, from your phone and TV, to the vast data centres meeting our insatiable desire for AI, are mostly electrical.

They process data by shunting electrons around tiny circuits – a single microchip produced today can contain billions of transistors, and sizes are measured in nanometres (one nanometre is a billionth of a metre).
Because they use light instead of electricity, photonic chips are faster, use less energy and generate less heat than traditional computer chips.
Van Mol hopes for an acceleration in photonics similar to the one seen in electrical chips since the 1970s.
"With optical chips, you are now where electronic chips were maybe 40 [or] 50 years ago."
American, Taiwanese and Chinese firms dominate the computer chip industry, but Europe sees the emergence of photonic chips as a fresh opportunity to lead, on what could be, a key future technology.

Which is why the European Union has committed €400m ($450m; £330m) to a project called PIX Europe, external, with the stated goal of making the continent "a global leader in emerging technology for Photonic Integrated Chips".
"Europe said 'we need to have our own manufacturing in-house'," says van Mol, who is leading a key part of the programme.

"We cannot depend like in the past that everything is manufactured in the US or China - that's not wise, so the [European] Chips Act was called into life, and one of the parts of the act is to build pilot lines to really bring the technology, which is now in labs, to the next stage - manufacturing."
Electronic and photonic chips are produced on wafers made up of hundreds of individual chips. Factories with machines that can handle bigger wafers can churn out chips more efficiently.
"[Photonic chip] manufacturing worldwide is [currently] done on wafers which are four inches (10cm) in size, and the next step is to scale-up production to a six-inch wafer," says van Mol.
His team are already building a 10,000 sq m factory to produce six-inch indium phosphide wafers on the High Tech Campus in the Dutch city of Eindhoven.
It's due to fully open in 2030 and will be a major step forward, not just for photonics in Europe, but around the world, according to van Mol.
"That's the development TNO is going to do, in a pilot line which is really serious.
"In 2030, we hope that we have a stable, reproducible, high-yield process, and then the intention is that the pilot line [opens] to industrial parties who can make commercial production out of it."
Europe does have one crucial player in the current computer chip industry - ASML.
The Netherlands-based tech giant is the only company in the world able to build the machines needed to make the most sophisticated semiconductors.
Which is why ASML products will sit at the heart of the pilot line in Eindhoven - it's no coincidence that van Mol's project is based around the corner from ASML's headquarters.
"The way you produce these [photonic] chips is very similar to the way you produce electrical or electronic chip," says van Mol.
"You use the same type of equipment, you also need a high-end clean room, you also use wafers, so the production method is very similar to the traditional semiconductor technology."
ASML itself is keen to explore the opportunities that the emerging technology of photonics could offer.

"Europe has a strong position in photonics research. The next challenge is translating those innovations into industrial-scale manufacturing," says Stanislas Baron, who is the head of ASML's EU/US Customer Team.

ASML's unique success has helped build an influential and lucrative network of companies and institutions devoted to semiconductor technology in and around Eindhoven, and it's a model for what Europe is trying to achieve with photonic chips.

The Eindhoven project has the backing of former ASML chief executive Peter Wennink, author of an influential report for the Dutch government called The Roadmap to Future Prosperity, external, which noted that the market for photonics was expected to grow 10 to 20 times in the next 10 years.
In a news release backing the new pilot line, Wennink described it as "a launchpad for Europe's future digital economy".
"By investing in scalable production capacity, we are creating an ecosystem that can help shape the global technological direction," he said.
Of course, Europe is not alone in looking to the potential of photonics to earn a global economic advantage.

In June this year, US photonics company Coherent, external announced what it called "the world's first and largest volume-production six-inch indium phosphide manufacturing platform" at its plant in Sherman, in Texas.
The expansion is backed by chip manufacturing giant Nvidia, as well as $50 million public funds under the US Chips Act.

It's an illustration of how quickly the market is moving, and how central photonic chips could be to the continuing race to retain an influential stake in AI and technological development more generally.

Europe's bid to establish itself as a global leader in photonic chips – exemplified by the Eindhoven project – is the kind of strategy that makes sense in a globalised economy, says Joris Teer, policy analyst at the European Institute for Security Studies in Brussels.
If the continent can take a lead in photonic chips, then future developments in AI and data will partly be dependent on Europe.
"Europe knows that its high energy and labour costs, skilled workforce shortages, and lack of private and public capital make an across-the-board reindustrialisation strategy impossible", Teer says.
"To retain influence, ensuring dependence on European parties rather than European autonomy is key."
Once up and running, the Eindhoven project will provide a pilot production line which can be used multiple companies.
It will be open to businesses across Europe and beyond, who can design and build chips without having to develop their own expensive production facilities.
"What we want to establish here is what we call a foundry model; there's no intention to have our own product," Ton van Mol says.
Instead, they will produce to order for outside customers.
It's the same idea which, at huge scale, has brought Taiwanese-based giant TSMC a position of global dominance in the manufacture of microchips.
Photonic chips are already in use, in highly specialised areas in data centres and in Lidar (light detection and ranging) sensor technology, for instance.

For van Mol of TNO, helping the industry to scale up, by easing production challenges and increasing capacity, is the key step to moving them into the tech we use in our daily lives, like phones and laptops, and to drive innovation in areas like medical scanners and 6G communications.

"The demand is there", says van Mol, "and the end goal is to have, in Europe, manufacturing of these chips, which is strategically very important because these chips [could] become the backbone of all data and telecom."

items.title: Satya Nadella says he’s AGI-pilled now
paragraphs: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says he’s AGI-pilled, at least when it comes to how AI might make startling changes to the structure of the economy and how politics might change because of it. “I am AGI-pilled in the sense that at an economy level, what is the political economy’s organization around AGI?” he asked at a roundtable discussion following his Microsoft Ignite keynote at the Chase Center in San Francisco.

But Nadella doesn’t think frontier models like Claude are conscious. “I don’t think so,” he said, adding that he follows Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman’s view that companies should not give rights to models and treat them like they might have a moral status, which companies like Anthropic do as a matter of principle. Suleyman has told me he thinks Anthropic’s team has “wireheaded” themselves, and that this approach is dangerous.

Nadella wasn’t quite as firm about it. “It’s a good debate,” he said. “I’m not sort of dogmatic about it. What I’m saying is the most important social technical issue we have to deal with is how do you ensure that an economy can diffuse this technology broadly?”

I asked Nadella how he was thinking about AI after hearing his response to another reporter’s questions about Anthropic releasing more products in its office suite. Nadella talked at length about the potential collapse of the economy and the end of democracy if one AI model were allowed to achieve monopoly status.
“If the Marxist sort of view is that there’s only one firm, then it’s over, right? For all of us.”

“Most people think about this as a competition between tech firms, which of course it will be,” he said. “But remember, the model has no limits. It’ll be a healthcare company. It can be a financial services company. It can be anything if it wants to be. It can take over the government. Thinking of this as some narrow competition between tech firms, of who is going to get to the next trillion dollars of market cap, is one of the strangest, narrowest ways to think about it.”

Nadella went on to say that the very nature of companies stood to be disrupted in the future. “If intelligence has network effects, what is the future of a firm?” he asked. “If the model sees anything and learns it, and essentially all of human capital collapses into token capital, what is the role of a firm and the human capital in a firm? That’s the debate.”

“I think the political economy is going to get more and more interesting in that context. No one — at least in a democracy — can even win an election if this just goes that way, if there’s only capital and there’s no labor. I mean, I don’t know, that’s not an economy.”
“If the Marxist sort of view is that there’s only one firm, then it’s over, right? For all of us. Not just for me. You are also going to somehow be some affiliate of Anthropic.”
Needless to say, this is not how tech CEOs usually talk about the launch of competing spreadsheet software.

Of course, Nadella was also promoting Microsoft’s various AI tools at Ignite, which promise to let enterprise clients pick the most cost-effective models for various tasks, run their own models, and control their own data in different ways. The idea here is that the market will demand many different kinds of models and sovereign data in order to keep control from centralizing, a theme Nadella kept coming back to as we spoke.
“I think that if you believe that the world, the economy needs more than one firm or two firms, then by definition there need to be as many models as firms of some sort,” he said.
