items.title: Some EU countries ‘could accept unlimited young Britons’ under youth mobility scheme
paragraphs: EU countries including Germany could accept an unlimited number of young Britons under a youth mobility scheme, according to sources.

Fresh details on how a scheme might work have emerged with EU leaders and the UK expected to settle on a quota of about 100,000 a year being allowed to work, travel or study in each others territories from 2028.

The UK has insisted on a quota of EU citizens entering the UK under the scheme to guard against mass migration, but some countries have said they will not follow suit on the other side of the Channel and would be open to taking unlimited numbers.

The quota is expected to be worked out on a country-by-country basis with smaller countries such as Malta and Luxembourg seeking a system that will not be based on a per-capita quota per EU member state.
The youth mobility scheme for under-30s is expected to be sealed in principle as the EU-UK summit in Brussels on Friday.

In what looks like a win for Andy Burnham, however, several diplomats have said the tricky question of EU students paying the same fees as their UK counterparts if studying at a UK university under the scheme would be postponed for six months.

This is to allow linkage with the Made in Europe legislation that will not reach its final stages until possibly April next year in a vote in the European parliament. The legislation is designed to give priority to EU supply chains in the car and other industries.
By linking the two issues the UK can get assurances that the final detail of the deal on mobility cannot be signed off unless it has been included in the Made in Europe legislation.

It is also understand that the majority of the 12-page draft joint statement has been agreed, with negotiations expected to continue to the wire and perhaps even during the summit between Burnham, the European Council leader, António Costa, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, which starts at 10am on Friday.

The details came as Burnham has said there is “no rush” to decide on the UK’s longer term relationship with the EU, as he came under pressure from his own party to press the brakes on the pace of the rethink.
The prime minister said he would “take stock” of the wider relationship after Friday’s summit in Brussels at which he also hopes to secure agreements on food and farming and emissions trading.

In an interview with Sky News, Burnham admitted that he would now not set out the full options for a closer EU relationship until December – but denied he was “stepping back” from his previous commitments to pursue ties.

The prime minister had been expected to give a speech or deliver a statement setting out options for a closer relationship early next week, probably Monday, and to argue that it would be in the UK’s long-term interest.

While he may still address MPs, he is now likely to focus on the details of the deal secured at the summit, delaying his bigger plans to around the same time as his 10-year plan for the country, No 10 sources said, adding that the two were linked.

No 10 insiders told the Guardian that Burnham wants to “frame the conversation, not go straight to the endgame” before testing public opinion, with even some Remain-minded MPs acknowledging there is more work to be done.

These will include discussions with European counterparts to establish what the EU is willing to negotiate and whether it might be possible to get a better bespoke deal, or what the terms of rejoining the single market or customs union might be.

Since Burnham announced in September that he would look again at the UK’s membership of EU, he has reiterated that the existing deal is not good enough, and that he would set out plans for a longer-term relationship this autumn.

In addition to the customs union or single market, these could include trading relationships along the lines that Norway, Switzerland or Canada have with the EU, reversing Brexit in its entirety, or no change at all.

But after revealing his personal preference would be to fully rejoin the bloc, Burnham has encountered some resistance, including from within the cabinet, with some MPs with Leave-voting seats anxious about reopening the debate.

Senior government figures say that Burnham wants a mandate to start negotiations with the EU in Labour’s next election manifesto, but that any subsequent referendum would be confirmatory after MPs had endorsed a deal.

In his interview, Burnham said: “All I’m going to do is look at what options might be available. And so that people can see the pros and cons, we’ll set those out in due course. There’s no rush to do that. The British public will be in charge of whatever comes next.
“We’ll see how [Friday’s summit] goes. And then we will consider whether there are options to further the relationship with the EU. I’ll set that out later this year alongside the 10-year plan.”
The prime minister denied that he was “jumping the gun” or “making any assumptions” about where the UK would end up – but pointed to polling which shows the public wants closer ties with the bloc.
Some Labour MPs, however, are concerned about the impact of freedom of movement in particular, as the debate around immigration in the UK has grown with the rise of Reform UK.
“I won’t get ahead of public opinion. I will listen to what the public feel is the right long term solution,” Burnham added.
While much of the deal expected to be agreed in Brussels on Friday is over the line, there are still tensions over the level of the cap on the youth mobility scheme cap, as well as over tuition fees.

Officials are also expected to discuss the agenda for the next round of the reset, which could include another attempt for the UK to join the EU’s €50bn (£40bn) safe defence fund, collaboration on law enforcement and borders, and mutual recognition of qualifications.

items.title: “We're not saying they're perfect” says architect fighting to save Melbourne's public housing blocks
paragraphs: Architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its plan to demolish all of Melbourne’s public housing towers. In this interview, he sets out why he believes retrofit is the smarter approach.

Announced by the Labor-run state government in 2023, Homes Victoria’s High-Rise Redevelopment Program (HRRP) will see all 44 of Melbourne’s public housing towers and many other lower-rise blocks razed and replaced with new housing by 2051.

Officials argue that the buildings, constructed between 1962 and 1975, have reached the end of their useful lives. They claim the towers do not meet modern standards and cost too much to maintain, and that the redevelopment programme will triple housing capacity and improve the quality of homes.
But the policy has proved highly controversial, with critics particularly angry about a lack of transparency or consultation with residents, who are being relocated.

It is now subject to an ongoing legal dispute, has prompted concern from the UN’s special rapporteur on housing, and become a political issue in the build-up to the Victorian state election later this month.
Among the voices leading calls for a change of course is Melbourne not-for-profit research and design practice Office.

Office has worked pro bono to make the case for refurbishing the towers, after learning from residents that the government has not published feasibility studies for keeping any of the condemned estates.
“We thought that was pretty odd that you wouldn’t do a refurbishment study on these estates,” Office director Simon Robinson told Dezeen.
“So we took it upon ourselves to start to do these feasibility studies, along with public housing residents.”

“We’re not saying that they’re in perfect condition,” he added. “We’re also not saying that all of them should be refurbished – perhaps some are beyond repair. All we are saying is that these rapprochement studies need to occur.”
In fact, feasibility studies have been conducted by the government but not been made public, despite requests by the Victorian Legislative Council.
By avoiding the relocation of residents, Office estimates that a retrofit and infill approach would cost around $300 million less than demolition and rebuild.

“As all the estates are occupied, the cost of relocating and housing the residents during construction work needs to be included in the project cost; this is consistently excluded and never disclosed,” said Robinson.
“We have estimated that these costs are very significant, with reports indicating that the government is spot purchasing or head-leasing properties from the private market.”
The practice has put together a counter-proposal based on a strategy that it calls Retain Repair Reinvest (RRR).
RRR focuses on retaining buildings without displacing residents, carrying out renovation work to improve housing comfort and energy efficiency while reducing construction waste and carbon impact.

Robinson agrees that most of Victoria’s existing public housing buildings are currently not fit for purpose – buildings are rundown, cold in winter, and sweltering in summer. But he believes comfortable living standards can be achieved through renovations.
Office has applied its RRR strategy to three Melbourne estates in hypothetical case studies – Ascot Vale Estate, Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.
Formerly home to approximately 10,000 people, Flemington Estate’s four towers make up about 10 per cent of Victoria’s public housing stock.
Only about 32 households remain, though an injunction prevents Homes Victoria from serving further eviction notices while legal challenges are pending.
Office has proposed retaining the estate’s 720 dwellings and building an additional 577 infill social housing units to increase density.

New facades and private balconies would be added, with other upgrades including integrated underground parking, a central communal green space, new heating and cooling systems, improved insulation, new kitchens and bathrooms.

Energy efficiency is another key focus. Double-glazed windows, photovoltaic cells, and water conservation systems would provide a 55 percent reduction of global warming potential compared to the demolition approach, according to Office.
Despite the seemingly obvious benefits, the Victorian government has so far been unmoved by the studies presented by the practice.
Robinson believes the reason lies in the fact that the state government no longer wants to manage public housing.
“When the state government manages public housing, they are responsible for maintaining the buildings and organising new tenants – all the admin that comes with owning a building,” he said.
As well as the demolitions, also attracting concern is the type of housing proposed for redevelopment under the HRRP.
Rather than like-for-like public housing, the new homes will be “community housing” – developed by private developers, and split between below-market and market-rate rental homes.
Despite still being classed as social housing by the state government, community housing is slightly more expensive, and the tenancy is less secure from eviction.
Robinson believes the term was created to misdirect the public.
“What they’re building is community housing, not public housing, so there’s no longer any public housing being rebuilt in Victoria,” he said.
“The government is now calling everything social housing, because they don’t want the public to know that it’s no longer public housing,” he continued.
“Victoria has the lowest percentage of public housing stock in Australia, and we’re currently demolishing it all and turning it into private and community housing.”

The issue is particularly charged in the context of Australia‘s housing-affordability crisis. There are currently over 60,000 people on the waitlist for social housing in Victoria, where social housing accounts for three per cent of all dwellings, below the national average of 4.2 per cent and the OECD average of 7 per cent.
“Public housing serves as foundational social infrastructure that treats shelter as an essential human right,” said Robinson.
“By offering rents permanently capped to income and delivering unmatched security of tenure, it provides an unconditional safety net for society’s most vulnerable households.”

Office’s work has gained political attention. In November 2023, the Victorian Legislative Council debated the merits of the RRR approach, with the council’s Legal and Social Issues Committee urging the government to reconsider demolition and explore all refurbishment options.

The team can already claim a small victory. At Ascot Valley Estate, the first RRR case study released by Office, the development was quietly removed from the planned demolitions list on the Homes Victoria website and part of the estate has since been refurbished.

The estate is a collection of 57 three-storey brick housing blocks, built in 1947 and designed by renowned modernist architect and public housing advocate Best Overend during his time with the Housing Commission.
This gave Robinson and his team hope that the government would consider the alternatives if presented with the option.

“We have presented to Homes Victoria, we’ve presented to different ministers as well, and we’ve kind of heard that they are starting to look at retrofit some of their existing building stock,” said Robinson.
“It kind of suggests that perhaps they’re gonna prefer we show all of them. So we released the following studies on Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.”
However, Barak Beacon Estate has since been demolished, and the construction of the redevelopment is due to complete by the end of the year.
Now the fate of Flemington Tower awaits a ruling from the High Court of Australia following a hearing last month.

A class action filed by Inner Melbourne Community Legal on behalf of public housing residents in North Melbourne and Flemington is on its last appeal, after the Supreme Court of Victoria and Victorian Court of Appeal ruled in favour of demolition.
Meanwhile, the Liberal opposition has pledged to pause the HRRP if it wins office at the upcoming state election.
Robinson hopes he and his team have done enough, and continue to raise awareness about the issue.
“We’ve gotten to a point where we feel we can’t just keep putting out these reports,” he said.

“The papers we produced are quite dense and not for the general public. So what we’re now doing is translating that work into a series of publications, putting it in bookshops, and making it more accessible for the general public.”

“We continue interviews with different residents, different advocates, different professionals, speaking with journalists and doing lectures. The idea is to bring awareness to what’s occurring, rather than us doing more reports.”
He is also calling for a frank discussion in the architecture community about the redevelopment projects, which many of Australia’s prominent studios are working on.

“All the big-name architects are working on these estate renewals, some have even won awards as exemplar projects for these architects to promote their practice in terms of doing public good,” said Robinson.
“It’s really hard to find anyone who’s willing to talk about why they’re doing it, or is it good, the displacement and environmental issues. We’re alone.”
Dezeen put Robinson’s claims to the Victorian state government, but was told it could not respond in the lead-up to the election.

If you enjoy reading Dezeen’s interviews, opinions and features, subscribe to Dezeen In Depth. Sent on the last Friday of each month, this newsletter provides a single place to read about the design and architecture stories behind the headlines.

items.title: William and Kate celebrate Earthshot Prize winners in Mumbai
paragraphs: The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize.
Five award-winners were named at a ceremony in Mumbai, India, and will each receive £1m to scale up their projects.
One of the winners was a country - with Bhutan being recognised for its environmental policies that help to safeguard water supplies for nearly a fifth of the world's population.

Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actor Rami Malek and Bollywood stars Alia Bhatt and Sonam Kapoor were among those who attended the ceremony, which saw performances from Take That and Bridgerton's Simone Ashley.
The annual event, founded by Prince William and now in its sixth year, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.

Prince William was joined by Catherine at the ceremony as the royal couple continued their first official overseas trip together in four years. Catherine's cancer treatment has limited the amount she has travelled internationally.
They arrived on the event's green carpet wearing outfits celebrating Indian fashion.

Prince William wore a bespoke Bandhgala, a classic Indian formal jacket, while Catherine was dressed in an Anarkali dress by Mahima Mahajan made from handwoven silk Georgette with traditional Banarasi gold detailing.

During his speech, Prince William said this decade was the moment when positive change becomes irreversible" and remarked that history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.
He added that "around the world, we are witnessing human ingenuity on a remarkable scale".
Separately, Catherine highlighted the "hope" represented by entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis.
The princess, who presented an award, also said: "Just as the natural world finds ways to adapt and flourish, so too can we, when we nurture new ideas and give them the opportunity to grow.
"The people we're celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come."

items.title: Perron shapes Quebec kitchen around tea collection
paragraphs: A dedicated space for preparing tea has been placed at the heart of this Canadian house’s renovated kitchen, designed by local studio Perron.
Perron overhauled the kitchen for a longstanding client, with whom the studio has worked on several professional and personal projects over the years.
Her residence sits along the south shore of the St Lawrence River, overlooking Quebec City on the opposite bank.
The view across the water, and the client’s love of tea, were the primary guiding elements for the renovation project.
“For this house, we were not simply working from a checklist of requirements,” said Perron founder Nathalie Perron.
“We already knew about our client’s lifestyle, energy and the things that are most important to her.”
The kitchen space was divided into three zones: a space for tea, a central cooking area and a counter overlooking the river.
At the entrance, a small counter wrapped in glossy oxblood red tiles and a partition of burgundy steel bars form a niche that the client has nicknamed her “teahouse”.
Custom lacquered MDF wall shelves store and display cups, saucers, mugs and teapots that she has collected during her travels over the years.
“Each one evokes a specific memory and now has a place in her daily life,” said Perron.
An on-demand hot water tap is also installed within this niche, creating a dedicated space for the tea-making ritual.
The main kitchen area revolves around an angular island, which has space for a bar stool and incorporates a built-in electric stove.
Above, a cylindrical burgundy-hued range hood is framed within more steel bars, suspended from the ceiling to support shelves.
Rows of glass blocks are stacked between the upper and lower cabinets, which are both faced in stained white oak.
Ultra-thin steel shelves hang from the upper millwork, adding extra storage without blocking the light through the translucent bricks.
Opposite, a long counter faces the river through a large window, allowing the homeowner to witness passing ships and changing light conditions as she stands working or washing dishes.
Cristallo quartzite from Brazil forms the countertop and a backsplash.
Long, narrow Cotto Manetti terracotta tiles cover the floor, echoing the shapes of the matte and gloss pink Farblok ceramic tiles by Quintessenza that run up the wall in stripes.
A Mousse wall fixture by Quebec lighting brand JETA adds another feminine touch to the kitchen.
“It is a house that reflects a woman who enjoys going on adventures, but who has created a home that she loves returning to,” said the studio.
Perron has offices in Montreal and Quebec, the latter in an early 20th-century building renovated to house a studio, showroom and Nathalie Perron’s home.
See more innovative kitchens in our Dezeen Lookbooks series, including examples with striking islands, open storage, natural wood finishes and no wall cabinets.

items.title: Jensen Huang to testify before Congress on ‘potential breach of national security’
paragraphs: Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang will testify before several congressional committees on 1 December, setting the stage for a high-stakes hearing in the wake of his resignation following an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, has also agreed to appear for a closed-door transcribed interview the following day, 2 December.

“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, who chair the committees, said in a press release. “The American people need answers on Mr Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous [People’s Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal.”

The three congressmen chair the foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party, and the intelligence committee of the House of Representatives, respectively. On 12 November, they had signed a letter warning Huang that he could face a subpoena if he did not agree to the closed-door meeting.
Nvidia chips are key to powering the artificial intelligence boom. The Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China.
Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO after allegations of extramarital relationships with the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees surfaced.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been Megaspeed International’s executive director. The Singapore-based cloud computing company has bought nearly $5bn in AI chips and advanced hardware. The company said Alice Huang stepped down in 2025.

Megaspeed ultimately facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, in violation of US export controls. On Friday, Malaysia stated that they were investigating whether the company diverted advanced AI ships to other countries.

A recent joint Department of Commerce and Department of Justice letter, stated that the Department of Commerce, under its secretary, Howard Lutnick, first started an investigation in Megaspeed on 2024 for potential export control violations. The justice department, led by the attorney general, Todd Blanche, took over in 2025.

In his first remarks since his resignation, Jensen Huang said on Thursday he would be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO. Elon Musk and other Silicon Valley tech giants, along with 165,000 signatories to an open letter, have called for his reinstatement. Trump has also signaled his openness for the disgraced tech CEO’s return.

items.title: Hunger Games prequel splits opinion: 'Surreally awful' or 'surprisingly strong'
paragraphs: Joseph Zada plays Haymitch Abernathy at the age of 16

Reviews of the latest Hunger Games film have seen it dismissed as a "surreally awful prequel" and "a tortuous, costly mess" by some critics - but called "surprisingly strong" and "one of the best films in the series" by others.
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth movie in the franchise, and tells the origin story of a teenage Haymitch Abernathy - who was played as an adult by Woody Harrelson.

In a one-star review, the Guardian called the film, external "overwrought and boring", and said it "has no actual interest and no authentic reason to exist, other than to gouge an income stream out of its fanbase".
But the Wrap praised its, external "memorable performances, intoxicating style and horrifying commentary", adding: "When the dust settles it may even be the Hunger Games that holds up best."
Sunrise on the Reaping is set 24 years before the first Hunger Games film, and 40 years after the previous prequel, 2023's The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.
"This prequel lands at some mid-point between Ballad and Hunger Games, which puts it on an immediately odd footing," Empire said in a three-star review, external.
"It can't escape the sense of feeling supplementary. It's an enjoyable-enough diversion, but essentially a footnote with aspirations."
Screen Daily called it, external an "underwhelming prequel", which "suffers from a lack of compelling characters" and "feels oddly incidental - a drab afterthought rather than a crucial new chapter".
Kieran Culkin plays Hunger Games host Caesar Flickerman
The film's all-star cast includes Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace and Maya Hawke alongside Joseph Zada as the 16-year-old Abernathy.
IndieWire, external said Zada's performance is "charming enough", but "his character lacks the gravitational charisma or arc that, say, Jennifer Lawrence brought to the original films".
The movie feels "a little bit like a cold cash grab rather than a necessary deepening of the series' lore" and is "a dreary slog", IndieWire's critic wrote.

The New York Times, external also used the word "slog", adding: "One really misses the guiding presence of Jennifer Lawrence, who had the raw pathos to both ground and expand a world in a way many younger stars often can't.
"In Sunrise, we're instead left with fleeting moments in which Plemons or Ralph Fiennes (playing the evil President Snow) briefly elevate the film. They seem to be trapped in this dystopia too."
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping will be released this weekend
However, the Hollywood Reporter, external was more enthusiastic about both the film and Zada's performance, calling it a "star-making turn".
Its critic concluded: "Sunrise on the Reaping is a return, after the disappointing Songbirds and Snakes, to the spirit of the first movies."
And Time Out's four-star review, external said the film is "as strong as any" of the other movies, and "certainly a major step up from 2023's drab prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes".

items.title: Huang says he'd be "honored" to return to Nvidia as he agrees to testify to Congress
paragraphs: A pedestrian walks in front of a Nvidia sign outside the company's headquarters on Nov. 12, 2026 in Santa Clara, Calif. after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO. Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images hide caption

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said Tuesday he would return to lead the company he cofounded if Nvidia's board of directors allowed him to. Huang also agreed to appear before Congress to answer questions about the national security scandals swirling around the company.

"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," wrote Huang in a statement posted on social media. "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."

Huang stepped down from the company last week after acknowledging that he had been unfaithful to his wife. News reports have tied him to a woman who U.S. intelligence officials say was recruited by China's spy agency, as well as with another woman who is an executive at Nvidia. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.

Huang said he would be "honored" to return to the company if Nvidia's board agreed. His comments come as some in Silicon Valley have tried to argue that Huang was pushed out of the company too quickly, and circulated a petition to "stand with Jensen."

"We don't want rushes to judgment. We don't want political pressure from the left or the right to force a board into action before we've even taken the time to turn over the cards and learn what was done," said Brad Gerstner, the founder and CEO of Altimeter Capital, an investor in Nvidia, at Semafor's Silicon Valley and the World conference on Monday.

Huang and Nvidia's general counsel Tim Teter will answer questions behind closed doors from the House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence Committees and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party on Dec. 1st and 2nd.

Lawmakers say they want answers about Nvidia's role in alleged chip smuggling and efforts to evade export controls meant to block China from accessing the most advanced U.S. AI chips. They will also ask Huang about his involvement with Alice Huang, who was an executive with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that was a major customer for Nvidia's chips. In a statement emailed to NPR, Megaspeed said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business," and that Alice Huang left the company in 2025, but that it is conducting an internal investigation.
Nvidia's board said on Tuesday it had formed a committee to oversee the company's national security policies, compliance with U.S. export controls, and risk management of global trade.

On Monday, the U.S. Commerce Department announced new rules to prevent remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and servers, closing a loophole that may have let Chinese companies remotely access advanced Nvidia chips through overseas data centers. The Commerce Department and Justice Department also announced Monday that the DOJ is conducting a criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
Later Tuesday, investors will hear directly for the first time from Nvidia's new acting CEO, Colette Kress, when the company announces its quarterly earnings after markets close for the day.

items.title: How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule
paragraphs: At 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south.

Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions.

“We knew what the target was. Everyone was enthusiastic and excited,” one person who took part in the special operation, using the pseudonym “Leon”, told the Guardian. His 7th Deep Strike Centre is part of “Magyar’s Birds”, a brigade named after the call sign of its founder, Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces. Leon said: “Nobody gets excited any more about oil refineries. This was different.”
The soldiers got ready to launch, then watched the biplane-like drone, laden with explosives, disappear across the southern Ukrainian steppe.

Over the next four hours, hundreds of attack drones followed the same linear path, flying first over land and then over the Black Sea. In the early hours of the morning they arrived at their destination: the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia. Putin opened the monumental road and rail crossing in 2018, driving across it in a Kamaz truck. This was four years after his undercover troops – known as little green men – seized the peninsula.

Russian propagandists had described the bridge as impregnable. It was, they said, an edifice as strong and unyielding as their country’s iron leader. For Ukraine, by contrast, it was a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Also, officials pointed out, it was illegal. Twice Kyiv had tried to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.

On this occasion, the Ukrainian military’s careful, multi-stage plan worked perfectly. “It was a well-coordinated operation. Waves of drones started from different locations. The goal was to overwhelm Russia’s well-organised air defence system, rather than the bridge itself,” Leon explained.

As expected, the initial salvo tied up Russia’s local defences. According to insiders, Ukraine then launched a second drone wave. Its function was crucial and different: to act as a relay system for radio signals. Previously, Ukrainian units had used Starshield, the military equivalent of Starlink, for mid-range strikes on occupied territory. Elon Musk’s SpaceX owns the satellite internet network, which is overseen by the Pentagon and the Trump administration.

Ten days ago, however, limits were mysteriously imposed on Ukrainian drones, so they could no longer fly at above 161 km/h (100 mph). SpaceX insists there is no slowdown – a statement Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says is untrue. On Monday night, it appears Kyiv bypassed US restrictions by setting up its own extraordinary and innovative real-time video and radio connection.

Once the relay was in place, a third wave of attacks could begin. This time they featured Flamingos, a potent Ukrainian-made cruise missile capable of carrying 1,000kg of explosives – enough to seriously damage the bridge. An unknown number of missiles – some reports say at least four – were launched from southern Ukraine and sent towards Crimea.

A video from one of the Flamingos shows it drawing inexorably towards the target. The onboard camera captures a ghostly night-time scene. The crossing looms into view against a grisaille background. Suddenly a gigantic steel arch appears. The feed cuts out. Other footage shows the moment of impact: an orange fireball, pricking the surrounding blackness.

Photos taken on Tuesday morning in the aftermath of the attack show a scene of watery devastation. A massive arch had tumbled overnight into the Kerch straight, with a large concrete chunk of the road crossing. Nobody will be driving across the bridge anytime soon. The adjacent railway arch span was also damaged. “We were very happy, swapping messages all night,” Leon said.

One source in Ukraine’s armed forces said the timing of the operation – hailed by Zelenskyy as “unprecedented” – was deliberate. It was conducted ahead of a meeting on Thursday between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of an Apec summit. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” the person said.

They added: “We understand that what we did shows the world that the king is nude. Putin is weak and vulnerable and we just proved it. The operation was purposefully designed for this specific historic moment. Putin’s plan was to bluff at the summit about how powerful he is. In reality, he can’t even protect the most important and symbolic pillars of his regime.”

In addition to Putin’s political embarrassment before his peers, the disabling of the Kerch bridge has practical consequences. Since annexing Crimea, Russia has militarised the peninsula, effectively turning it into a giant and fortified army base. Since 2022 it has been used as a launch platform for drone and missile attacks on the port of Odesa, and other Ukrainian cities in the region.

Russia’s occupying southern army has relied on the bridge for regular deliveries of ammunition, equipment and fuel. With the crossing partially closed – rail travel reportedly reopened on Tuesday – Russia will have to use an under fire land corridor instead, connecting its Rostov oblast with the Moscow-controlled parts of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia and Kherson provinces.

“We have disrupted their logistics to Crimea. There will be a lot of problems for Russia’s army in the south,” Leon predicted. Debris from the bridge strike is obstructing the narrow shipping corridor through the Kerch strait, linking the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. The Azov sea now resembles a lake. Passenger ferries are unable to move, with the occupied ports of Mariupol and Berdyansk cut off.

The soldiers returned from their mission jubilant and elated. Back at their headquarters, they gathered as usual for a minute’s silence, in memory of those killed in Russia’s bloody war. “We had our daily ritual as usual. Then there were congratulations on a very successful and important operation,” Leon said. Then he added: “We are paying them back.”

items.title: Costa Rican journalist shot dead in first such killing in 25 years
paragraphs: The Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodríguez, who gained prominence for publishing allegations against ⁠suspected drug traffickers and politicians, was shot dead on Monday, authorities said.

The first known killing of a journalist ⁠in Costa Rica in ⁠25 years, ​Rodriguez’s death comes as the country grapples with a surge in drug violence driven by international trafficking groups, despite long ⁠being regarded as one of Central America’s most peaceful and stable democracies.
Rodriguez, 51, was attacked at about 3.20pm local ⁠time amid heavy traffic on a main highway on the outskirts of the capital ​San José, the Red Cross ‌reported.
President Laura Fernández condemned ‌the attack in a video message.

“I am filled with indignation and outrage over ‌the cowardly murder of communicator Camilo Rodríguez. Regardless of the content of his communications, what happened today in our country is a stain on freedom of expression,” Fernández said.

The attorney general, Carlo Díaz, told the local news outlet Extra Noticias that investigators found multiple bullet impacts and a crime scene resembling a contract ‌killing, probably linked to the allegations Rodríguez had published. He gave no further evidence and did not name suspects.
“We know he ​was a communicator who publicly identified people for alleged links to drug trafficking,” Díaz said, adding that Rodríguez had previously reported threats but had declined protection.
“Silencing someone who reports on drug trafficking or corruption, in this case a communicator, is a ⁠signal we cannot tolerate in a democratic society.“
Díaz pledged efforts to ​hold those responsible ​for the murder accountable.

The last such ​attack on a media worker happened in July 2001 when the radio ​producer Parmenio ‌Medina was gunned ​down on a ​Santo Domingo highway, in roughly the same area as Rodríguez’s attack took place.
Costa Rica’s homicide rate doubled between 2013 and 2023 and has only eased slightly since then.

items.title: With up to 31% off karaoke machines for Black Friday, you’ll be singing this Christmas

items.title: Brad Pitt and Florence Pugh pitch for James Bond villain role
paragraphs: Meanwhile, Florence Pugh, who stars alongside Pattinson in Villeneuve's forthcoming Dune: Part Three, said she had thrown her hat in the ring to be in the new Bond film upon hearing the casting news.

Speaking at Elle's Women in Hollywood event on Monday, Pugh said she had sent a message to the director saying: "Congratulations on finding your Bond, nice catch. Any villains the size of a 5ft 4in female?"
In fact, it was Villeneuve presenting Pugh with an honour at the event - so he's now heard her plea twice.
Meanwhile, Pitt also told reporters at the premiere of The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth in Los Angeles that he was delighted to hear the news about Pattinson's recruitment as 007.
"Is that right?! You know what, I love this idea," Pitt told Extra TV.
"I love what he's been doing. I love his choices, I think he's the real deal. That's great, good call."
Bond villains over the years have included Rami Malek, Jonathan Pryce, Christoph Waltz and Christopher Walken.
Several other actors have indicated they would like a shot at being a Bond baddie ahead of Pattinson's casting announcement, including Bill Skarsgård, Saoirse Ronan and Barry Keoghan.

items.title: TV pundit put hand up woman's skirt, jury told
paragraphs: A former England rugby league player and TV pundit is accused of sexually assaulting a woman by putting her hand up her skirt and grabbing her underwear, a jury has been told.
Danika Priim, 42, is said to have committed the alleged offence in the toilets at Horsforth Cricket Club in Leeds on 22 July 2022.

Opening the case at Leeds Crown Court earlier, prosecutor Chloe Hudson told jurors the complainant had done nothing to "encourage, ask for, or imply that she wanted to be sexually assaulted by this defendant".
Priim, from Keighley, West Yorkshire, denies one count of sexual assault. The trial continues.
Giving evidence from behind a screen, the complainant told the jury she had just used the toilet and was applying lipstick while chatting to two friends when the incident happened.
She said Priim "walked straight up to me and put her hand up my skirt and grabbed hold of my pants and my private parts".
She said she had challenged Priim before the defendant put her hand up her skirt for a second time, grinned and walked out.
A witness told the court she thought Priim laughed and said something like "wahey" before she left.
When asked by the prosecutor about the defendant's body language, the complainant said: "She was cold. There was no emotion. She was just staring at me."
She told the jury she had felt "a bit shocked and violated", adding: "My reaction was, 'What on earth has she done? Why did she think it was OK to do that?'."
She said her friends had said "I can't believe she's done that" and "Who does she think she is?".
The woman said: "I just froze. I didn't know what to do."
The jury heard how the woman and one of her friends had discussed the incident on WhatsApp the following day.
In the messages, her friend encouraged her to report it, which she did in November 2022.
Hudson said Priim was interviewed by police, but denied the incident ever happened.
Chloe Fairley, defending, asked the complainant: "She wasn't in the toilet at all with you, was she?"
To which the woman replied: "Yes. She was."
Priim played for Bradford Bulls, Leeds Rhinos and represented England, including at the 2017 World Cup.
She retired from the game in 2021 and has worked as a pundit for the BBC and Sky on a freelance basis, including during the BBC's coverage of the 2022 Rugby League World Cup.
The trial, which is expected to last three days, continues.

items.title: SOM completes first phase of Philadelphia train station restoration
paragraphs: Architecture studio SOM has completed the first phase of the renovation of the William H Gray III 30th Street Station in Philadelphia, USA, “breathing new life” into the 1930s beaux arts main train hall.

The project saw the renovation of the main train hall, a beaux arts Graham, Anderson, Probst & White building completed in 1931 with a grand limestone facade and Corinthian columns. It serves as a major transit hub for the Northeastern United States.
The hall is on the National Register of Historic Places, greatly restricting the changes that can be made to the structure and its interiors.

Keeping to the historic details, including the art deco chandeliers that hang from the tall ceilings, SOM restored the space with builder Gilbane through renovation and a series of specific interventions.
Chief among these was the moving of ticketing, bag drop-off, and other facilities that had been placed in the main train hall into a little-used northern wing of the building.
“Our restoration and repositioning presents an extraordinary opportunity to leverage the station’s strengths, while breathing new life into this beloved building,” said SOM Partner Colin Koop.
This move freed up more room for seating and through traffic in the main hall.
Working with retail partner Nelson Worldwide, SOM also revamped the concessions in the south concourse.
SOM worked closely with US rail system operator Amtrak on the project, which includes offices for Amtrak in the upper levels of the building.
It is part of a wider renovation SOM announced for the station and surrounding areas in Philadelphia in 2016, which included a number of tall buildings. The status of these new structures is unclear.
SOM noted the efforts in preserving the character of the structure.
“We are preserving its historic character while positioning the station for the next generation of travelers to come,” said SOM Principal Phil Wessell.
“As part of our broader work along Amtrak’s Northeast Corridor, this revitalization reinforces the station’s role as both a vital transportation hub and a defining civic space for Philadelphia.”
SOM also led the renovation of Daniel Patrick Moynihan Train Hall in New York in 2021, with plans for a Penn Station renovation released earlier this year by PAU.

items.title: I tried the Funbox kids' 3D printer with my daughter – but would I recommend it?
paragraphs: A truly kids-focused 3D printer, which is accessible and simple to use. It's built fairly well, but comes with some key compromises in regard to size and build complexity. It's a fun toy, and a good introduction to 3D printing for younger children.
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

I was captivated by the idea of a 3D printer designed for children, so I jumped at the chance to let my nine-year-old try the Funbox. She’s wanted a 3D printer for ages. I’ve held out, partly because of the cost and partly because of the inevitable tide of tiny plastic things that would end up around the house.

The Funbox is a compact, good-looking printer made by Ugee. It's fully enclosed for safety, has a clean air filter, is anti-scald and you can create with just a tap via the app. With Christmas coming up, plenty of parents will be hunting for the right option for their kids, so I want to be honest about whether this is it. Does this compare to the best 3D printers?

The external design is delightful. Ugee has nailed the look for kids: it’s cute, it has minimal buttons and fuss, and mine arrived in baby blue. A pack of stickers in the box lets your child decorate it themselves.

The inside is just as accessible. The build plate is easy to put in place and everything is clearly marked to show you how to get started (although we did make a wrong turn by not actually putting the plate in the first time around as you can see above – oops!).

Loading filament is simple, though it can be a bit fiddly for small fingers. It is pretty much plug and play – setup took me about 20 minutes, and my daughter was able to manage the first print pretty much independently with minimal interference, only some instruction. Bear in mind, the build space is small, so this printer is best for smaller prints. You can keep an eye on your print via the camera, which links to the app – my daughter was fascinated by this part.

Designs come from a marketplace in the Funbox app, available for mobile or tablet. It should be simple to use, but it’s glitchy. On our Huion tablet, the ‘start’ button was hidden behind the notch and there was no way to scroll or move the screen to reach it. That forced us onto the mobile app, which wasn’t ideal when I wanted my daughter to use the printer independently, without borrowing my phone.
For the most part, the Funbox worked as expected. My daughter could pick a print and start it herself, and she really enjoyed the process.

The small build volume is the main constraint. Many designs have to be printed in parts and assembled, which is fine if you stick to small prints. For anything more complex, you’ll need to be ready to help with sticking or putting pieces together. It also prints in a single colour at a time.

Most of the toys we printed turned out well, especially single-piece prints with no moving parts. The detail was good, and the results matched what the marketplace listings promised. Highlights include a cat hair comb, a skull and crossbones hair slide and a phone holder, which would hold my phone if it was the right size (note: must check next time).

Functional toys were a different story. We made a couple of fidget toys that couldn’t do their job without breaking. That could be down to the third-party design, or to the filament being too brittle for the purpose. We couldn’t tell which.
That fits what this printer is: a starter machine built for fun, not one that delivers polished, fully functional prints every time.
We haven’t yet tested the AI 3D model builder, which turns your child’s drawing into a printable 3D model. We’ll cover our experience of it in a separate piece.
The Funbox costs $299/£318 but is often on sale for $279/£289. Whether that’s reasonable depends on who you're buying it for.

For my nine-year-old, I’d rather take on the steeper learning curve of a basic ‘grown-up’ printer like the Bambu Lab A1, which I’d expect to give better-quality prints for similar money. It’s less approachable for a child to use alone, but the results would be worth it for her. For a younger child, though, the Funbox’s ease of use and friendly design make a stronger case, and I think they justify the price.
If you want a genuinely child-focused printer, this is a good option. Just be aware you’re trading away print size and complexity.
Choose your designs carefully. Ugee’s own are reliable, but third-party designs from the marketplace are hit and miss.
If your child is at the upper end of the age range (nine to 12), consider a basic printer from one of the adult-focused brands instead. For younger children, the Funbox is the easier fit.

items.title: Nvidia boss ends – level 1
paragraphs: Nvidia is a big tech company. Its boss, Jensen Huang, leaves his job suddenly. The company’s stock price falls.

Huang leaves after news about his relationship with a woman who may be a spy for China. Nvidia chooses another boss for some time. So the business stays safe. Experts say that it will be very hard to find a new leader. Huang is the boss for 33 years.
Now, US officials want to check if Nvidia breaks any rules. The company sells computer parts to China. This big problem may make trade between the US and China more difficult.

Difficult words: suddenly (quickly, without a plan), stock price (how much one part of a company costs), spy (a person who gets information about other people or countries and they do not know about it).

items.title: Nvidia boss ends – level 2
paragraphs: Nvidia’s share price dropped quickly after its CEO and co-founder, Jensen Huang, suddenly resigned.
He left the company after facing serious investigations over a personal affair with a woman who was a suspected Chinese spy, as well as a second affair with a company manager.

To keep business running smoothly, Nvidia named its finance boss as temporary leader. Experts say replacing Huang will be very difficult because he led the company for 33 years and was very important to its success in AI.

US officials plan to investigate what the company knew about the spying and whether Nvidia broke rules by selling computer chips to China. This problem could lead to stricter US trade laws and increased tension between America and China.

Difficult words: spy (a person secretly collecting and reporting sensitive information for a foreign government or competitor), temporary (when something lasts for only some time), tension (a state of difficult relations between countries or people).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Nvidia boss ends – level 3
paragraphs: Nvidia’s share price dropped sharply after its co-founder and longtime boss, Jensen Huang, suddenly resigned. His decision followed growing pressure and a company investigation into his secret relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China.

Media reports also revealed a second affair with an executive inside Nvidia. To keep the business stable during this difficult change, the company appointed its finance chief as interim CEO to reassure investors and maintain stability during the unexpected leadership change. However, business experts warn that replacing Huang will be very hard, because he led Nvidia for 33 years and had no clear plan for a successor.

Beyond problems inside the company, the scandal raises serious questions about whether Nvidia broke US rules by selling advanced computer chips to China. Experts expect US politicians and police to investigate the company closely. They warn that Nvidia’s weaker influence in Washington could lead to stricter trade limits and increase political tension between the US and China.

Difficult words: executive (a person with senior managerial responsibility in a business organization), interim (temporary), successor (a person who takes over a job, office, or position after someone else leaves).

items.title: ‘We don’t want our city to lose its storytellers’: Sydney artists given $25k in Australian first – no strings attached
paragraphs: Julian Hamman feels as if a “great weight” has been lifted from his shoulders. On Monday the 26-year-old film-maker from Sydney was calculating how many more casual shifts he would need to pick up as a gallery host and paramedic assistant in order to finance his creative work.

But on Tuesday night, Hamman found out he is one of 40 creatives to receive an “artist living grant”, a new initiative from the City of Sydney which awards him a catch-free lump sum of $25,000 to simply continue living and working as a creative.

“From my casual jobs I’ve made around $25,000 [this year] and a lot of that goes towards groceries and having to fit my schedule around my work,” he says. “The brain task-switching you do when you work freelance and two jobs is exhausting … Having a base income will allow me to focus on my practice and have some brain space.”

Totalling $1m, the 40 new grants were approved by the council on Monday night, awarding no-strings-attached direct payments not tied to specific projects, based on a successful basic income for artists introduced in Ireland three years ago. Ireland’s pilot scheme was made permanent in February 2026, giving 2,000 creative workers €325 a week.

“Our research shows artists are leaving Sydney due to low incomes, rising costs and limited resources,” Sydney’s lord mayor, Clover Moore, said in a statement. “We don’t want our city to lose its local storytellers and creative soul.
“While it’s not a cure all, these grants will boost 40 Sydney artists working across a range of artforms at different points in their careers, with many from under-represented communities.”

According to Creative Australia’s most recent report, practising professional artists in Australia earned average gross incomes of $54,500 in the 2021–2022 financial year, comprising $23,200 in creative income, $15,300 in arts-related income and $16,000 in non-arts income.
The first of its kind in the country, Sydney’s $25,000 grant is open to artists of all disciplines, from all over the city – not only those who live in the City of Sydney catchment.

Kamilaroi and Tongan musician David Leha, who makes music as Radical Son, is another recipient. He applied for the grant in August and says the money will help with living costs, touring costs and promoting his music.

“It won’t pay for one thing, but it will help with all things,” says the 50-year-old, who is based in Liverpool. “I have been in the arts now for 25 years and it hasn’t been easy, especially in the last decade. There’s a saying that you often have to pay to play and in some cases we’re losing money to perform, so to be able to get this support is really helpful. The costs go on and on.”

Leha splits his time between writing, recording and touring new music and studying for a PhD in creative studies at the University of Newcastle. Along with the rising cost of living, he says the particular challenges he faces as a First Nations musician make it difficult to make enough money from music alone.

“We are expected to have a social media presence and unfortunately some venues are booking based on your following rather than the quality of the music itself, and as First Nations artists our stories are so diverse, but it might not necessarily translate to getting bums on seats.”
Morgan Hogg, a multidisciplinary artist of Cook Island Māori (Ngāti Tāne), Tahitian and English descent, is another recipient of the inaugural grant.
“It’s such a pivotal time in my career,” she says. “I’m about five years into my career as a professional artist and it’ll mean having more time to dedicate to my practice. I’m very grateful.”

The 26-year-old, based in Ashfield, supports her career with a casual job at the Sydney College of the Arts. “Some weeks I’ll work an eight-hour shift, and some days I’ll work 20 hours a week. It depends on how much work they have for me and how much time I need to spend on art projects.”

Hogg estimates she spends 80% of her time as an artist on admin, including identifying and applying for arts grants. “For a project for next year alone I have applied for seven different grants, and I write them all myself … it probably takes me two to three weeks outside of my normal job and I don’t necessarily get paid for it.”

The $25,000 grant, which is expected to be paid to all 40 artists by the end of the year, will help fund Hogg’s travel to the Cook Islands, Tahiti and Rapa Nui (Easter Island) for two video works, which involve working with traditional knowledge holders in the region.
The City of Sydney says it will not dictate how the grant money is spent. It can fund any aspect of creative practice, living expenses and the costs of producing new work.

“There are no specific requirements to ‘create’, or restrictions on other work, meaning the money can be spent on … whatever the artist needs,” said City of Sydney Greens councillor Sylvie Ellsmore in a statement. Ellsmore put forward a motion for an artist’s basic income three years ago, which led to this new grant.

“Sydney is losing more artists than any other capital city, because it’s so expensive to live here. Meanwhile too much arts funding is still being allocated to big name, commercial festivals, who often don’t pay artists enough – or at all,” she said.
“Basic income models are how we should be funding the arts – with money going directly to artists, musicians, writers and creators, no strings attached.”

items.title: Channel 4 admits it doesn't know number of Married At First Sight UK sex abuse complaints
paragraphs: Married at First Sight UK, known as MAFS UK, had been running for 10 seasons and was one of Channel 4's biggest shows, with audience figures often topping three million.
The Panorama investigation in May heard from three women who made allegations about the men they were partnered with - claims the men deny:
One woman said her on-screen husband raped her and threatened her with an acid attack.
A second woman told both Channel 4 and production company CPL, before broadcast, about being allegedly raped by her on-screen husband. Her episodes were still aired.
A third woman accused her on-screen husband of sexual misconduct.
All three women accused the show of not doing enough to protect them.
A review was commissioned into MAFS UK by Channel 4 shortly after the BBC first contacted the broadcaster with details of the allegations.
Earlier this month, the completed review recommended extra safeguards on the show. But Channel 4 said the programme had "run its course" and apologised to the women involved in the investigation.

Speaking to MPs on the House of Commons culture and media committee on Tuesday, Dogra was repeatedly asked if she knew how many allegations Channel 4 and CPL had received over the years that MAFS UK was on air.

"I looked specifically into those instances [the three women], I did not do a broad sweep of every episode or every season of the show. That is not what the terms of reference for the show were," she responded.
"If there are others, we would take them seriously and look into them on the same basis."
Channel 4's bosses were also questioned at length about Brand by MPs in the hearing.

Brand's work on Channel 4 included hosting Big Brother sister show Big Brother's Big Mouth and its celebrity equivalent from 2004 to 2007, a chat show in 2006, and appearing on Big Fat Quiz of the Year.
Addressing Dogra and Channel 4's chairman Geoff Cooper, MPs said the member of staff who made two complaints about Brand "fell through the cracks".
In response, Dogra said: "I'm not sure we can apologise enough as an organisation for putting her through that twice. We have apologised in public in the past and in private."
She accepted that the woman's complaints were "not handled properly" and added that "it's almost unforgivable that happened twice".
When asked by the committee if junior members of staff could raise complaints against a star without fear of losing their job, Dogra replied she "can't say 100%" that that would be the case.
Woman who accuses Russell Brand of rape says prison message 'upsetting'

"What I can do is set the standard, set the tone, make sure that the facilities are available, make sure that my staff and the production companies understand the repercussions of not complying, and understand the kind of culture that I'm trying to set, and we're trying to set as an industry."
She also said she found the "cultural personality" around Brand "horrendous".
"I find it distasteful, and I look at the jokes... that is the lowest form of humour, because these are jokes that are made at the expense of someone else's physical safety.
"I don't believe it should have been acceptable then, and I certainly don't think it's acceptable now."
During the session, Dame Caroline also put to Channel 4 bosses that in both the MAFS UK and Brand cases, the broadcaster appeared like "a child with their hand in the cookie jar".

The committee chairwoman asked: "To what extent can you reassure us that Channel 4's priority is genuinely the welfare of the staff who work there, the staff who have worked there, and the people who take part in your shows - rather than purely when the world is looking at you and you suddenly feel that you've got a reputational reason to take a look at these shows?"
Dogra responded by saying that when Channel 4 commissioned the review, "we didn't even know whether the Panorama programme would be made".
She added: "We had received a right-to-reply letter and the programme came out six weeks later, but it equally it could not have been made. We always intended to do the review."
In the instance of the woman who tried to complain about Brand, she added: "I'm not sure there are more apologies we can give. Because none of those things should've happened."
If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.uk

items.title: I gasped at the new Tin Can phone – I’ve been looking for a solution like this for months
paragraphs: Yes, I genuinely gasped when the Tin Can press release landed in my inbox this morning, as it is exactly the product I've been searching for.

While I'm committed to a smartphone-free childhood for my children, I empathise with my children's need to communicate with their friends outside of school. They're also a bit young for the best dumbphones, but I still gatekeep my phone, only allowing occasional texting to other parent's phones in order to reach their pals. And I suddenly realised how unfair this is.

When I was nine, as my daughter is now, I was using our landline to call friends every day, honing valuable communication skills, and the lack of a home phone in my house means that my daughter is unable to do the same. As a new product, it's filling a very real gap in family life – and it's beautifully designed as well.

The Tin Can is already available in the US and Canada, and it's now making it to the UK. It runs on Wi-Fi, so no costly extra landline charges on your broadband (the route I was all set to go down), it looks simple to use, is crucially screen-free, and comes in a variety of delicious colours. It also has helpful parent controls, including restrictions like 'quiet time', you can only call other Tin Can handsets (for free), as well as parent-approved numbers (as part of a monthly subscription), and emergency numbers.
Of course, for best results, your children's friends also need to have a Tin Can – so I'm off to convince the parents I know to put it on their Christmas lists.
Pre orders are open for the UK, and it will arrive with you from 30 November.

items.title: Batman to James Bond: The clues about what to expect from Robert Pattinson's 007
paragraphs: He has been in big-budget blockbusters like Twilight, Tenet and The Batman, as well as a string of quirky arthouse films - so what clues can Robert Pattinson's past roles give us about what he might be like as James Bond?
Every actor creates a new James Bond, and Pattinson is one of the best in the business at crafting a memorable character.
The British actor can be an action man or an anti-hero, a romantic lead or a comic fool. He can be granite-faced or goofy, and everything in between.
"I was thinking about what the aspects of James Bond are, and he's done all of those throughout his career," says Paul Tweddle, host of the Heavy Spoilers film podcast, external.

He cites Pattinson's performance as a brooding heartthrob in teen vampire franchise Twilight, his suave and quick-witted secret agent in Christopher Nolan's Tenet, the withdrawn and focused title character in The Batman, and the ruthless and manipulative Antinous in Nolan's The Odyssey.
Pattinson has "often been drawn to really dark fare", says Anna Smith, film critic and host of the Girls on Film podcast, external.

"Wouldn't it be interesting to see Bond go a little bit darker?" she suggested to the BBC's World Service. "But also what he's got, and I'd like him to do more of, is comedy. And goodness knows, we need a Bond who can handle humour."
Unusually for a James Bond actor, one word that has cropped up frequently is "weird".
Earlier this month, Pattinson was described as "the weirdest guy in Hollywood" by the Celebrating Cinema podcast, external.
"Pattinson is an actor who makes bold, interesting, risky choices. For such a handsome guy, he can bring the weird, and then some," wrote Chris Hewitt in Empire, external.
"About 0.07 seconds after the announcement, people were already anticipating the weird with his Bond. And they may well get their wish."
Pattinson (right) starred with Willem Dafoe in The Lighthouse in 2019

Variety's chief critic Guy Lodge said, external Pattinson's reputation as an actor "has been considerably enriched by his predilection for playing, frankly, losers and weirdos", such as in more offbeat films like Good Time, The Lighthouse, Primetime and Mickey 17.

"Even his blockbuster assignments are more interesting when he lets his inner freak out to play," Lodge added. "His big, heightened, leeringly villainous turn in The Odyssey is off on its own beam entirely."
Associated Press film critic Jake Coyle said, external smaller films like The Lighthouse and High Life show "Pattinson's proclivity for pushing boundaries".

"He's certainly the funniest and quickest to laugh James Bond we've had in decades," Coyle continued. "It will be interesting to see how much of his personality bleeds into Bond, or how much the tux stifles it."
So what do Pattinson's performances in some of his biggest films tell us about what to expect?
Pattinson in Tenet with Himesh Patel (left) and John David Washington (right)
Pattinson plays a dapper and enigmatic British agent in Christopher Nolan's time-bending 2020 thriller, as adept at bungeeing off an arms dealer's tower as he is delivering some deliciously dry wit.
"He's very suave, he's thinking on his feet," Tweddle says. "He's someone who's holding his cards close to his chest and not necessarily giving the game away.
"Tenet is the obvious one where Nolan's basically doing a kind of James Bond movie."

The Times' chief critic Kevin Maher agrees, external: "Pattinson has effectively played Bond already, when he effortlessly inhabited the role of the suave yet nonetheless lethal British spy Neil in Tenet.
"For many observers (including this one) that was the role. That was the audition. There was no turning back after Neil."

New York Times critic Alissa Wilkinson noted that Pattinson has picked up other "Bond-adjacent" roles. "The most obvious is Bruce Wayne, a.k.a. Batman, the wealthy playboy with a lair of tech toys and his own gussied-up automobile," she wrote, external.
"Wayne and Bond have a lot in common on paper, but in Pattinson's hands Wayne becomes emo, reclusive, awkward, with the hair of a '90s grunge rocker."

The Guardian's Peter Bradshaw also pointed out, external parallels with how Pattinson played "the darkly conflicted caped crusader Batman in Matt Reeves's 2022 film, lurking athletically in the shadows - like Bond, used to working in secret".
Like Tenet, The Batman proved Pattinson is an expert at action scenes, whether that be jumping off a building or being involved in an explosive car chase with The Penguin.
"Batman is a really good example of where he's a withdrawn figure, someone who has his mind focused solely on a task, and I think that's a big part of what James Bond needs to be," Tweddle says.
However, Pattinson's 007 should be a little less brooding and aloof than his stony-faced Batman and Bruce Wayne.
Although Pattinson plays the villain in Nolan's Greek epic, Antinous's menace and ruthlessness could come in handy when playing Bond, according to Tweddle.
"I think Robert Pattinson also has quite a psychotic side to him, which a lot of the James Bond books delve into - how he's a killer, and he needs to have that side to him," he says.
"What he's done in The Odyssey shows he can be manipulative, and connive and make certain plans, which is what a spy needs to do."
Collider's Collier Jennings named, external The Odyssey, along with Tenet and The Batman, as films that show Pattinson is "the perfect" fit for Bond.
"All three roles carry an element that makes James Bond work," Jennings wrote.
"Batman has the combat skills and subterfuge you'd need to be a spy of Bond's caliber, not to mention the cutting edge hardware.
"Neil has a great grasp on the intricacies of pulling off complex covert operations.
"Antonius walks with a swagger and arrogance that either makes you love him or hate him."
Pattinson's current film sees him play real-life NBC journalist Chris Hansen, who carried out sting operations on suspected paedophiles for TV show To Catch a Predator.
It again demonstrates Pattinson's range as an actor and his ability to take on complex roles - he balances the portrayal of Hansen not as a villain but equally not as a hero.
"He's very much face-to-face with the predators in the room, and he's controlling the situation," Tweddle explains.

"It's very confrontational and demands a certain amount of power. Being able to control the room like that is also quite transferable to James Bond, and interrogations are a big part of what he does."
Pattinson will next be seen playing shape-shifting villain Scytale in the forthcoming third instalment of the epic sci-fi series - directed by Denis Villeneuve.
The pair's reunion for the next Bond movie is not a coincidence. Villeneuve's experience of working with Pattinson on the film may have been the deciding factor when casting James Bond.

"The thing I adore with Robert Pattinson is that when you roll cameras, there's always a certain moment where you have no idea what will happen. He is an explosion in front of the camera," the director told Time, external before the Bond casting was announced.
"He has an incredible imagination and is a very playful actor, and a very creative actor, always trying to bring new ways of expressing himself and always trying to surprise me."
Surprising, bold, weird? One thing is for certain, Pattinson's James Bond is going to be interesting.

items.title: Anthropic IPO: how can I buy shares, and is it worth it?
paragraphs: The technology company Anthropic is heading for a blockbuster stock market listing this week in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history.

The company is a leader in artificial intelligence, and is best known for its chatbot Claude. The float, which is expected to value the business at $1.4tn (£1tn), comes at a volatile time for tech stocks, yet it has been reported that the shares could be six times oversubscribed.
When a company floats it issues a prospectus for would-be investors that details its activities and lays out the share offering, including an estimated price.

Anthropic’s prospectus explains that the shares on sale will be 825m of class A common stock, and that the initial public offering (IPO) price will between $70 and $78 a share. However, the final price will be set on Wednesday.

The shares will come with voting rights, but, if all the shares’ votes are combined they will only represent 49.9% of the total vote available, so will not allow buyers to be able to force any changes in the way the company is run.
The shares will be listed on the Nasdaq in New York on Thursday, and will be available to individual investors alongside big institutions.

In the UK, several investment platforms are offering customers the chance to subscribe to shares, including AJ Bell, Hargreaves Lansdown, Robinhood and eToro. At Robinhood and eToro the minimum investment is $250 (£189), at Hargreaves Lansdown the minimum investment is £250, and at AJ Bell investors will need at least £1,000 to apply. AJ Bell is closing applications at 1pm on Wednesday, while Hargreaves Lansdown and Robinhood will close at 3pm. All say they could close the doors early without notice.
Once the IPO has happened and the shares have been listed they can be bought at any point, and through platforms that have not been involved in the IPO.

Yes – in fact, there are already funds which own stakes in the company. In the UK they include the Baillie Gifford US Growth and Scottish Mortgage investment trusts, while Fidelity has investments held in funds available to US investors.

Once the IPO is over, the stock will ultimately find its way into some tracker funds – although some will be quicker than others – and managers of actively invested funds could also choose to buy shares. That means people might well end up investing in Anthropic even if they do not attempt to buy any shares directly.
Anthropic’s prospectus includes 92 pages on potential risks to the company and its industry, so it is not an investment for the faint-hearted.
Recent weeks have highlighted the fragility of the US markets, and tech stocks in particular, so this is one to consider very carefully.

Nils Pratley, the Guardian’s financial editor, has raised questions about the company’s governance structure, saying it “represents an extraordinary concentration of power in the hands of a few individuals”.
Jason Hollands, the managing director of the investment platform Bestinvest by Evelyn Partners – which is not participating in the IPO – highlights some other things investors need to consider.

“Anthropic would give most retail investors the first opportunity to have a direct stake in a frontier AI developer. But it remains a capital-intensive business, and it has yet to establish a consistent path to profitability,” he says. “Investors will need to judge whether the company can turn demand for its models into durable earnings.”
Hollands says if demand for shares exceeds the limited supply, “that could support the price initially with a ‘pop’, but it does not guarantee a strong debut or lasting gains over the coming months”.

He adds the SpaceX listing in June “is a reminder that a hotly anticipated IPO and early enthusiasm can quickly be followed by volatility: its shares have traded below their IPO price at points since listing”.

When we asked Claude whether to buy shares in Anthropic it was upfront about why it is not a great source of investment advice: “I can’t tell you whether you should buy. I’m not a financial adviser, and I’m also made by Anthropic, so I have an obvious conflict of interest here.”

It went on to present a few facts about the IPO, and some useful questions that any investor should be considering before buying an individual share in an IPO. Can you cope with a loss if it goes down in value? How much of your portfolio will an investment in it represent? Will you already have exposure to the share through a tracker fund?

items.title: Dezeen launches 20x20 project to identify the architects and designers to watch over the next 20 years
paragraphs: Today is Dezeen’s 20th birthday, and to celebrate we launch our 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler. For the series we’ve asked 20 architects and designers who have had a major impact over the past 20 years to each select an architect or designer that they believe will have the biggest impact over the next 20 years.
Called 20×20, the project aims to celebrate the past 20 years of Dezeen while looking forward to the names and faces we’ll be seeing much more of in the next 20 years.
We’ll be revealing the selected architects and designers on Dezeen over the next four weeks, getting to know them and their work in a series of interviews.
The series launches today with a profile of Russian-born, Paris-based designer Harry Nuriev, who was selected by Danish architect Bjarke Ingels.

He will be followed by the selections of Es Devlin, Faye Toogood, Francine Houbine, Frida Escobedo, Huberto Campana, Iris van herpen, Jeanne Gang, Kelly Wearstler, Lesley Lokko, Ma Yansong, Marc Newson, Mariam Kamara, Marina Tabassum, Nendo, Neri&Hu, Patricia Urquiola, Philippe Starck, Sabine Marcelis, Sou Fujimoto and Yasmeen Lari.
All of the interviews will be listed below as they are published:

items.title: ‘She set out to buy a painting a day’: on the trail of Peggy Guggenheim’s legendary shopping spree
paragraphs: Peggy Guggenheim, art enthusiast and socialite born into a wealthy New York family, was often photographed outside her palazzo in Venice with a handbag dog and outré sunglasses. The Peggy Guggenheim Collection as we now know it, however, was nearly not in her Venice palazzo but London, evidenced by a short-lived and largely overlooked period between January 1938 and June 1939 when she ran Guggenheim Jeune in Cork Street. This exhibition posits that this initial gallery’s activities were far more influential in the shaping of contemporary art than previously recognised. Guggenheim Jeune mounted a flurry of 20 exhibitions including such UK firsts as a group show dedicated to collage, and solo exhibitions by Wassily Kandinsky, Jean Cocteau and Yves Tanguy.

How to demonstrate the pioneering qualities of a gallery that is now a ghost? With reassembling and contextual padding, it appears. The catalogue states that at least 60% of the artworks in this exhibition were originally shown at Guggenheim Jeune, though only a handful of captions list definitive instances. Does this imply that where not stated, they are included for illustrative purposes?
