items.title: Ministers to end Palantir’s contract with NHS in England in 2029
paragraphs: Ministers will end the NHS’s contract with the controversial tech firm Palantir – but not until 2029, to allow time to line up British companies to replace it.

The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) has decided to extend Palantir’s contract to provide the federated data platform (FDP) – the software that links different healthcare providers – for two more years rather than exercise a break clause that would have let them axe it next spring.
Ministers have come under growing pressure to end the NHS in England’s relationship with Palantir, which is run by the Donald Trump-supporting US tech billionaire Peter Thiel.

James Frith, a health minister, said Palantir’s role would end in 2029 to boost public trust in NHS tech, end its “over-dependence” on one supplier and let UK companies start providing crucial digital infrastructure. The DHSC will in the meantime select UK tech firms to replace it.
However, Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs criticised Palantir being given a further two years.

“My committee has repeatedly called on the government to exercise the 2027 break clause in Palantir’s federated data platform contract with the NHS,” said Chi Onwurah, the chair of the Commons science and technology select committee.
“It’s deeply disappointing to hear that it won’t do so and is instead choosing to extend the contract for two years, during which time it says it will procure a UK-based supplier.
Martin Wrigley, a Liberal Democrat MP, said: “After months of campaigning by the Liberal Democrats, the government has finally admitted that the Palantir contract has to end.

“However, ministers have kicked the can down the road to March 2029. That leaves a company co-founded by Trump ally Peter Thiel, and criticised by human rights groups over its work with ICE [the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency], holding the keys to our health data for years to come.”
Campaign groups such as Amnesty International and Just Treatment have been urging ministers to activate the break clause in February in the contract that NHS England agreed with Palantir in 2023.

Many NHS care trusts have declined to use the FDP, amid widespread doubts in the service that it is as good as Palantir insists. NHS England last week deleted a claim from its website that 137 trusts were benefiting from the FDP after the Guardian disclosed that 29 were using it never or rarely.

“The current contract will remain for two years, before coming to an end,” Frith told MPs. The DHSC will soon invite British tech outfits to bid to be part of whoever replaces Palantir. “A process this important must command public trust as well as clinical confidence,” Frith added in a tacit admission that many hospital bosses and doctors are sceptical about Palantir’s claimed benefits.

Ben Coleman, a Labour member of the Commons health select committee, who last week urged ministers to replace Palantir with a group of British firms, said: “I’m glad the government is ending reliance on a single supplier and shaking off the Palantir albatross. This must be done without disrupting patient care or creating new dependence [on a new single supplier]”.
Amnesty International said the decision was “a victory for healthcare workers, patients and campaigners who refused to give up”.
“Doctors and nurses … should never have to work in a health service that partners with a company supporting a military committing genocide.

“Palantir has openly acknowledged supporting Israel’s military in ‘war-related missions’, while Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. ‘First, do no harm’ should apply not just to NHS staff, but to the companies the NHS contracts with,” said Tom Guha, its crisis campaigner.

items.title: Manila media center for ASEAN summit showcases Filipino hospitality to 2,000 registered journalists from 20 countries, organizer tells VOA
paragraphs: President Donald Trump is set to meet Southeast Asian leaders in Manila at the conclusion of their annual ASEAN summit on Tuesday. Hundreds of journalists covering the summit have been working at a nearby International Media Center run by the Philippine government. VOA's Michael Lipin reports.

items.title: Robert Pattinson as James Bond says a lot about Amazon's plans for 007
paragraphs: As rumours about the casting of the next James Bond began to hot up this week, my phone has been busy. Most of my friends (hello, both!) know me as a huge James Bond fan, and have wanted to know who I thought was going to get the role. Well, one thing's for sure, I told them all. It won't be Pattinson. Mark my words. He's just too famous.

So you can imagine my surprise when Robert Pattinson was indeed announced as the new James Bond this afternoon. Everything about the news feels bizarre to me, including the lack of press release and associated fanfare (whereas Daniel Craig rode down the Thames on a speedboat, Pattinson was announced via a simple social media post). But the biggest shock is that Pattinson is by far the most famous person to be cast in the role. He's the first bonafide A-lister to pick up the Walther PPK. He's Batman, for God's sake. For better or worse, the Bond brand changed forever today. And it's thanks to one name: Amazon.

It perhaps isn't surprising that Blofeld's—sorry, Bezos's—company has opted for such a bankable star. The company paid billions to acquire MGM (which owned the rights to Bond), and will want a return on its investment. But the whole thing seems so at odds with the ethos of the previous Bond custodians. "I felt I had to have an unknown actor, not a star," producer Cubby Broccoli said of the search for the very first Bond. "Above all, a man you’d believe could be James Bond."

For decades, Bond has been one of the most carefully controlled brands in entertainment. The gun barrel sequence, the theme tune, the 007 logo, the Aston Martin; every element is instantly recognisable, and has been meticulously protected by the Broccoli family. Bond films have always felt like events, partly because they don't come along very often. But Amazon doesn't do scarcity, it does content. And with the company now in creative control of the franchise, it's hard not to wonder how long it will be before 007 becomes less of a cinematic institution and more of an endlessly expandable IP. I'm not sure I'm ready for the 'Young Q' spin-off.

There are, of course, opportunities here. Bond has arguably been in need of a shake-up for some time, and Pattinson is a genuinely exciting actor, capable of bringing something strange, unpredictable and perhaps even uncomfortable to a character that has occasionally felt trapped by his own iconography. But the choice also feels like a statement of intent from Amazon. Where previous Bond actors were largely blank canvases onto which the 007 identity could be projected, Pattinson arrives with a huge, established brand of his own. Rather than making a star out of Bond, Amazon has bought a star to sell Bond. It's a subtle distinction, but a significant one. Am I going to be able to look up at the screen and see James Bond, rather than Robert Pattinson in a suit?

But while it'll be Pattinson's name that hogs the headlines, the bigger question isn't simply what kind of Bond Pattinson will be, but what kind of brand Amazon wants Bond to become. Will the company recognise that Bond's enduring appeal lies partly in his exclusivity, his mystique, and his ability to remain just a little out of reach? For all of his reinventions, 007 has always felt bigger than the actor playing him. Until today.

Daniel John is Design Editor at Creative Bloq. He reports on the worlds of design, branding and lifestyle tech, and has covered several industry events including Milan Design Week, OFFF Barcelona and Adobe Max in Los Angeles. He has interviewed leaders and designers at brands including Apple, Microsoft and Adobe. Daniel's debut book of short stories and poems was published in 2018, and his comedy newsletter is a Substack Bestseller.

items.title: Photos reveal scale of Trump’s White House ballroom, drawing criticism
paragraphs: Earlier this month, Trump’s White House ballroom and military bunker laid its final structural steel beam, with politicians and critics weighing in on the scale of the project.

Recently taken images of the extension, which show the structure with massive concrete shear walls, steel beams, and columns, along with a partially enclosed roof structure, have drawn attention to the scale of the building.
No sign of its planned neoclassical ornamentation has yet been implemented.
Officially called the East Wing Modernization Project, the structure dwarfs the Executive Residence and West Wing.
Trump announced the laying of the last steel beam in the superstructure on 4 November, the day after the national midterm elections.

“This is a special structure,” Trump said on a tour on 4 November, according to NBC News. “It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world, and they’ve been trying to get it for 150 years.”
Since then, there has been a renewed wave of criticism online over the project, ranging from outrage to humour.
Former senator and presidential candidate Hillary Clinton wrote on X (formerly Twitter), commenting on the size of the structure and noting the midterm election’s “repudiation” of Trump.

“It says everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People’s House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday,” wrote Clinton.
Congressman Jim Clyburn took a similar stance in a statement on Facebook, noting that the ballroom was “much bigger” than the rest of the White House.

Architecture critic Kate Wagner took a more humorous approach, noting that the ballroom is not neoclassical in construction. Wagner compared it to a Ramada Inn, a chain of hotels in the US, that they will “glue pediments to”.
“[It’s] an outcome designed in a lab to make everyone angry. possibly the most trump building ever built,” wrote Wagner on X.com.
The ballroom has been controversial since Trump demolished the White House’s West Wing in October 2025. The National Capital Planning Commission approved the project in April.
It has faced legal challenges, with US District Judge Leon issuing a stay in response to a lawsuit led by the National Trust for Historic Preservation.
the fact that trump's ballroom is clearly not neoclassical in any way shape or form is possibly the funniest moment in architectural history
In August, the Supreme Court allowed the project to continue, though the dissenting opinion said it was “likely unlawful”.
Despite the legal challenges, construction has continued, with Trump’s team leaning on the national security aspects of the underground bunker.
The administration has also floated plans to add a screening facility at Sherman Park – a small park to the southwest of the White House. Trump also installed a paved helipad on the White House lawn.

items.title: Quel head trip! Failed postcards, scrapping poets and germ-ridden film rock Paris Photo – review
paragraphs: No one at the three-day Paris Photo fair seemed worried about being a target for protesters – the fate of fellow art fair Art Basel Paris, which closed two days early. “Photography isn’t expensive enough,” joked one gallerist.

This 29th edition coincided with celebrations across France of the bicentenary of photography, and as such looked back at photography’s origins and the questions that have preoccupied photographers from the beginning. One example was a 19th-century portrait that is thought to be an extremely rare depiction of Rimbaud with a black eye – the poet was a known ruffian who often got physical over literary squabbles. Whether the photograph is really Rimbaud or not begs the question: what matters more, the truth, or what we believe the truth to be? After 200 years, photography hasn’t resolved the issue. The strongest thread running through Paris Photo is the uncertainty and instability of photography: as evidence that collapses into fiction and performance.

Lara Tabet’s Vitreous Body, developed with curator Yasmine Chemali, was among the fair’s most conceptually adventurous projects. Tabet, who trained as a medical biologist, collected water samples from canals, natural sources and waterways around Marseille, then mixed them with photographic film. The bacteria in the samples eat away at the film and transform it into brightly coloured abstract compositions, portraits of the city of sorts, a way of representing the landscape through microorganisms invisible to the naked eye. The works on agar bioplastics are the most interesting – the bacteria continue actively to transform the material, so that the work will continue to be alive, and changing. They are both beautiful and disquieting. Nature is not just depicted, but a collaborator in the image.

A different but equally intriguing interrogation of representation came from the young Colombian artist Felipe Romero Beltrán, who has frequently collaborated with African migrants in Europe, especially dancers. In his carefully constructed black-and-white photographs, his collaborators re-enact the positions used by police to subdue someone they’re arresting; yet without the uniforms or weapons, the aggression and hostility, the hierarchy and power, the choreographed movements become surprisingly tender and soft, institutional control becomes intimacy. The bodies carry the narrative without directly showing the violence those same bodies are regularly subjected to by the state.

Kourtney Roy showed works from her Failed Postcards series, taking another kind of vernacular visual language, travel photography, and turning it into something more ambiguous, strange and at times hilarious – saturated colours, theatrical poses and awkward fails, as she constructs scenarios in front of the kind of picturesque views tourists are prone to photograph. Beneath these polished shiny pictures, there’s also a darker rumination on the way experience is commodified.

Silina Syan brings a different understanding of the relationship between image and place. Her Made in Bangladesh series is rooted in Bidyakut, her father’s village in Bangladesh, and the architectural transformations that result from migration. The elaborate mansions financed by family members living abroad stand in striking contrast to the surrounding vernacular architecture; these buildings become visual markers of economic aspiration, family obligation and belonging. Some of her photographs are encased in their own architecture, carved wooden frames or sculptural elements framing the image. The architecture becomes a portrait of people who are absent.

One of the fair’s big draws was the chance to see Ponte City by Patrick Waterhouse and Mikhael Subotzky. Developed over 15 years, the project examines Johannesburg’s famous 54-storey residential tower through an extraordinary accumulation of photographs, documents, objects and residents’ stories. A new addition is their Ponte City book box presentation, which turned this archive into a modular installation of mobile towers, books, images and archival material. Photographs of doors, windows and television screens become fragments of a collective portrait of the tower, revealing the complexity of a building that embodies South Africa’s contested social and architectural history. It raises questions about the ethics of documenting a community, about how to preserve residents and honour their lives without reducing them to an art object. It’s a richly layered and absorbing story – enough to make you forget you’re at a fair.

Ultimately, Paris Photo 2026 was at its most convincing when it moved beyond the familiar. The bicentennial resulted in a load of nostalgic booths, not only at the fair but at institutions across the city, but does anyone really care about the anniversary? The best bits were about photography’s future – its capacity to be porous, to absorb other references and disciplines, to challenge reality as we know it. Two hundred years after its invention, photography’s most interesting question may no longer be what it can show us, but what it can make visible that we have previously been unable, or unwilling, to see.

items.title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
paragraphs: Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.

In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.

Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.

In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.
Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.

The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.
The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.
Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.

The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”

Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”

Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.

The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”

Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.
“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.
Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.

Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.

items.title: This clever art frame makes your images look like real prints – and today you save £77
paragraphs: Want to display your photos or artwork digitally, but in a way that looks like they've actually been printed? The Fraimic Smart e-ink Canvas pulls off just this clever trick. That's because while most digital art frames are built around standard, glowing screens, the Fraimic is built around a full-colour e-ink panel that reflects light like paper. It looks great, and is one of our top e-ink art frames.
Now the Smart e-ink Canvas is down from £385 to £308, direct from Fraimic. That’s a saving of £77, or 20%: pretty great for a device that only went on general sale at the start of this year.

You can use this smart frame to display both your own photos and public domain art from the Met. It also has a neat party trick called Voice-to-Vision. You tap the corner of the frame, describe what you’d like to see, then tap again. Your prompt goes to an OpenAI image model, and a couple of minutes later the new artwork appears on your wall.

The E Ink display is what makes the Fraimic canvas so special. There’s no backlight, so from a normal viewing distance, paintings and illustrations look convincingly like prints. E Ink only uses power when the image changes, so you don’t need a cable trailing down the wall. You can also pop the canvas out of its walnut frame and into any standard 14x18-inch frame, which is a nice touch.
It’s not perfect. Because it has no light of its own, it needs a bright spot without harsh overhead glare, and images change slowly. There’s no app either, so everything runs through a website.

It's also worth noting that Fraimic isn’t the only colour E Ink frame out there, as our guide to the best e-ink art frames shows, and the SwitchBot AI Art Frame on that list creates AI images too. However the app you need for the latter pushes a $3.99 monthly subscription, while Fraimic gives you 100 free generations a year.

items.title: James Bond: What we know so far about the next 007 film
paragraphs: When a bartender asked James Bond in 2006's Casino Royale whether he'd like his vodka martini shaken or stirred, the irritated spy replied: "Do I look like I give a damn?"
Such throwaway lines were a clever way of signalling to the audience that this was a new era for 007 - and that the film series launched in 1962 was being overhauled with the arrival of Daniel Craig.

Over the next few films, producers struck a balance between nodding to the past while also moving away from some of the cheesier elements of the series, no longer sticking rigidly to all of the tradition and tropes of Bond.
"Were you expecting an exploding pen?" Ben Whishaw's Q later asked the secret service agent in Skyfall. "We don't really go in for that anymore."

Two decades on from Craig's debut, the series is about to be rebooted once again, with a new actor and new creative team. It's an exciting time for Bond fans as they wait to see what shape the next era will take. Here's what we know so far.
Pattinson is known for films including Twilight, The Batman and Tenet
British actor Robert Pattinson has been confirmed as the next actor to play James Bond.
He shot to fame as Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, and went on to star in Twilight.
Pattinson appeared opposite Kristen Stewart in the series of five films based on Stephenie Meyers' vampire novels.
He has gone on to star in other major films and franchises including The Batman and Christopher Nolan's recent adaptation of The Odyssey.
But Pattinson is also respected within the industry for his unusual choice of roles, often appearing in independent, arthouse and experimental films.
His other credits include The Lighthouse, Mickey 17, Life, The Drama, Good Time, Primetime, The Rover, Bel Ami, Tenet and The Lost City of Z.
L-R: Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Jack Barton are all thought to have auditioned for the role
A handful of actors were thought to have made it to the final screen tests before Pattinson scored Britain's biggest film role. They included:
Jack Lowden, 36 - whose credits include Slow Horses and Pride and Prejudice
Josh O'Connor, 36 - The Crown, Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery
Callum Turner, 36 - Masters of the Air, The Capture
Jack Barton, 31 - Heartstopper, SAS: Rogue Heroes
Nicholas Hoult, 36 - About A Boy, Superman
Paul Mescal, 30 - Normal People, Gladiator II
But while many of the names are seen as hot, up-and-coming actors, Pattinson was arguably the most bankable movie star.
The film is expected to go into production in 2027, before its release in 2028. No exact dates have been announced.
Film schedules can be notoriously fluid, but it's clear that development is well under way, with the director and writer already in place.
It will be the 26th film in the official film series, but the title has not yet been confirmed.
Steven Knight (left) will write the script, while Denis Villeneuve will direct the film
The movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, known for Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival, Blade Runner 2049 and the recent Dune trilogy starring Timothée Chalamet.

"Some of my earliest movie-going memories are connected to 007," the French-Canadian director said last year. "I grew up watching James Bond films with my father, ever since Dr. No with Sean Connery. I'm a die-hard Bond fan. To me, he's sacred territory."
He added: "I intend to honour the tradition and open the path for many new missions to come. This is a massive responsibility, but also, incredibly exciting for me and a huge honour."
Bond 26 will be written by Steven Knight, known for TV series such as Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer, Locke and The Girl in the Spider's Web.
Knight has said it had always been on his "bucket list" to write a Bond film, adding that he felt he was "doing my duty for King and country" by joining the franchise.
He told the BBC he planned to "write the character, not the actor", adding: "The thing with Bond is it's its own universe and franchise. So there are certain rules.
"Obviously you have to move it along, but I love where it sits. I love that it's British. I love that it's not DC or Marvel... So I feel a responsibility to the text."
Irish actor Pierce Brosnan starred in four Bond films, including 1999's The World Is Not Enough
Sean Connery starred in six official Bond films between 1962 and 1971
George Lazenby starred in just one Bond film, in 1969
Roger Moore starred in seven Bond films between 1973 and 1985
Timothy Dalton starred in two Bond films, in 1987 and 1989
Pierce Brosnan starred in four Bond films, between 1995 and 2002
Daniel Craig starred in five Bond films between 2006 and 2021
You might have noticed some overlap in the above dates.
That's because Connery returned to the lead role for 1971's Diamonds Are Forever, after Lazenby took his place for 1969's On Her Majesty's Secret Service.
Connery also later appeared in 1983's Never Say Never Again, a Bond film produced by a different studio and not part of the official film series.
Roger Moore pictured filming 1985's A View To A Kill
If you discount the films not in the official series, there have been 25 Bond films in total. In order, they are:
Daniel Craig (pictured with co-star Léa Seydoux) stepped down as Bond with 2021's No Time To Die
With the change in ownership and a new creative team now in place, the new Bond film is likely to make a fresh start.
It would be difficult to continue the story chronologically given the ending of 2021's No Time To Die, but that still leaves producers with plenty of options.

A different version of James Bond, who exists in a different universe, would be easily pulled off in an era where audiences are used to major film franchises restarting in a different world or timeline.

Bond 26 could even be set in a significantly earlier era - an idea that gained more popularity after Tony Gilroy revealed he and fellow director Steven Soderbergh previously pitched a 1960s version, external of Bond.

Separately, actor Ralph Fiennes recently said, external he had once been in talks to play Bond, and had suggested producers make a "black and white and very sort of film noir-y" version set in the 1950s.
Neither idea materialised, but the suggestion went down well with some Bond fans, who noted a period piece would help make the film truer to Ian Fleming's original character and books.
Exactly what shape the next film takes will become clear at a later stage. For now, Christmas has come early for fans who have been waiting for years to find out who the next 007 will be.
In Robert Pattinson, producers have finally found their spy.

items.title: From Batman to Bond - how Robert Pattinson landed the role of 007
paragraphs: Robert Pattinson has starred in films including the Twilight franchise and The Batman

Robert Pattinson's career is already flying high with roles in films including the Twilight series, The Batman and The Odyssey, so signing up to play James Bond will propel his profile into the stratosphere.
He's already established himself as a leading man, action star and character actor, which is clearly why he is about to play the suave, British secret agent 007.

At 40, he is slightly older than some of the other men reportedly lined up for the role, but he's also the most famous - something the new Bond studio Amazon-MGM may have favoured, with an eye on the box office.
His recent work has garnered both critical and box office success, including Christopher Nolan's summer blockbuster The Odyssey, in which he played the villainous Antinous.
Pattinson was also called "Oscar-worthy" by the Independent and "superb" by The Times, for his performance in November's Primetime, as the real-life host of US TV show To Catch a Predator.

He also helped lead 2022's The Batman to the second-biggest North American opening of the Covid-19 pandemic behind Spider-Man: No Way Home. The Guardian said he played the "brooding" role with "appealing vulnerability, external".

Meanwhile in dark romantic comedy The Drama, he and his co-star gave a "career-highlight performance", external. It's one of three films he appeared in with Zendaya this year, along with The Odyssey and Dune: Part Three.
Robert Pattinson starred in 2022's The Batman, which was described by critics as a grim, gritty, and gripping super-noir
Born in Barnes, south-west London, Pattinson grew up with his father, a classic car trader and mother, who worked at a modelling agency, and two elder sisters.
His interest in acting started while he was still at school, when he joined the Barnes Theatre Club.
"I wouldn't be acting if it wasn't for that little club," he told Your Local Guardian in 2008, external.
"I went originally because a lot of pretty girls went there," he said. "I worked backstage and I started acting when all the good people left and I was the only one tall enough to play the lead.
"In a weird sort of way, that stuff was probably the best I've done and the stuff I am most proud of."
He landed his first big film role more than two decades ago, playing Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire. A relatively minor character, but it was enough to get him noticed.
Robert Pattinson and Kristen Stewart starred in five Twilight films from 2005 to 2012

Three years later, he had a starring role in the first of five Twilight films, along with Kristen Stewart, in which they played star-crossed lovers - vampire Edward Cullen and mortal-turned vampire Kristen Stewart.
Based on Stephanie Meyer's hugely popular young adult books, the films globally grossed more than $3bn (£2.2bn) by 2012, and established Pattinson as a heartthrob.
He spoke in his early career of finding his often adoring, screaming fans hard to deal with.
"Although is part of the job, it feels like they have been paid to turn up and scream at me at 7.30pm," he said.
"Nothing I don't think can prepare you for the fans. I don't know why I'm not getting used to it but I'm completely overwhelmed every time."
Pattinson and Zendaya have appeared in three films together this year - The Drama, The Odyssey and Dune: Part Three

The following year though, he was back in big-studio territory, with Odyssey director Christopher Nolan, in sci-fi thriller Tenet, and again in 2022 with The Batman, directed by Matt Reeves and co-starring Zoe Kravitz and Paul Dano.
Pattinson told Screen Daily why he returned to big-budget films, explaining: "I guess I was trying to do the opposite of what I've been doing. I started thinking, 'I really want to do a big thing.'
"I hadn't done something with a massive budget for ages. But you approach it exactly the same way."
The Batman got generally positive reviews, re-establishing Pattinson with a broader range of fans.
By 2025, when he was on the red carpet for Parasite director Bong Joon Ho's sci-fi black comedy, Mickey 17, he said it was "quite strange" to have a fanbase that was now dominated by men, external.
"There's like a bunch of guys, which is a new one for me!" he told the Associated Press.
Pattinson's private life has often created interest in the press, not least his previous relationships with Stewart, and then the singer FKA Twigs.
Since 2018, he has been in a relationship with model Suki Waterhouse. They got engaged in December 2023 and had their first child, a daughter, in March.
Robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse have been a couple since 2018
With his latest role as James Bond, Pattinson will be extremely busy, not least because the forthcoming Batman sequel is reportedly due out in 2028.
But the actor will have a head start as 007, having already worked with Bond 26 director Denis Villeneuve, who also helmed Dune: Part Three.
Pattinson was full of praise for him on their most recent film, despite the strain of working in the furnace-like heat of the desert.

"The scale of this stuff is just unbelievable, you're having your own Dune theme park, where the gimbal is going upside down and flying, and this is not like work at all," he told the New York Times, external.
"There are no negatives. Apart from having your sweat drained out of the top of your head, and getting like bulbous sweat bubbles. But even then, I didn't even really notice them.
"He's so easy to work with, Denis, it's never really a stress."
Sounds like Pattinson will have the cool head needed to juggle his forthcoming roles - including James Bond. You could even say he may end up being shaken, but not stirred.

items.title: Motion North 2027 reveals speakers for two days of talks, workshops and more
paragraphs: Manchester-based design and creative festival Motion North has announced the line up for Motion North 2027, which is to be held on 10th and 11th March at Freight Island, Manchester.

The two day festival is known as the industry event for international big name speakers, but with an intimate feel. Packed with over 20 speakers across three stages, and creative workshops to get stuck into, the festival hosts a schedule of content that promises diversity of thought and creative excellence. The aim of the talks are to inspire and challenge the next generation of creatives, and offer fresh insight for those working in the creative industries.

Highlights of the speaker line up from the world of motion design, animation, branding and design includes industry leaders in high end 3D product and brand films, Found, multi award winning artist Lucas Zanotto who blends his product design roots with playful artistry; infamous illustration and animation maestros, Nice Shit,; Emmy award winning animation director, Margherita Premuroso and Oscar winning VFX studio DNEG.
The current line up is here, with more speakers to be announced in the run up to the festival.

Excitingly, in addition to the talks, is a new place to hang out – The Marketplace: a curated showcase where independent artists have been invited to present and sell their unique crafts, graphic prints and books. In addition to this, there will also be a programme of social mixers, including an event hosted by Creative Brunch, with more announcements to come.

Established in Manchester in 2010 as a space for the creative community to meet and share ideas and experiences, Motion North is brought to the creative community by MightyGiant studio, which aims to champion the industry and bring a leading professional event to the city of Manchester.

Georgia has worked on Creative Bloq since 2018, and has been the site's Editor since 2023. With a specialism in branding and design, Georgia is also Programme Director of CB's award scheme – the Brand Impact Awards. As well as immersing herself with the industry through attending events like Adobe Max and the D&AD Awards and steering the site's content streams, Georgia has an eye on new commercial opportunities and ensuring they reflect the needs and interests of creatives.

items.title: The first scene from the new Harry Potter series just dropped – and it's sparked a fierce filmmaking debate
paragraphs: It seems fair to say that HBO's new Harry Potter series has a lot to live up to. Will it do justice to the books? Can it recapture the (ahem) magic of the movies? Will it step outside of the shadow of the controversies surrounding its author? But most importantly, won't somebody think of the blocking?

Yes, blocking—the staging and positioning of actors on screen—has become a buzzword after HBO dropped the very first piece of footage from the show, depicting a feast in the grand hall of Hogwarts. Fans are naturally comparing the scene to its 2001 movie counterpart, and not favourably.
Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone | The Start-of-Term Banquet Clip | HBO Max - YouTube

Viewers have been lamenting for years the move towards dark and washed out colour grading in modern movies and TV shows, and it seems not even Hogwarts is immune to the gloom. Compare this grand hall scene to the same one from the movie version of Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone and difference is night and day. HBO's offering looks like somebody at Hogwarts forgot to top up the electricity meter.
But it's the staging that's raising the most eyebrows.

Remove the color and focus on the composition and blocking. Even in black and white, the remake looks flat. The 2001 clip contained so much more exposition: house ghosts, Snape, student backstories. Every square inch of the frame is used. The new Dumbledore and McGonagall look botoxed and appear in vanity makeup, everything is center frame so that it can be shared on social media in vertical videos.November 15, 2026
A Great feast banquet hall scene Harry potter HBO (2026)/Harry potter and Philosopher's stone (2001) https://t.co/86bQoRP5IRNovember 15, 2026

Indeed, many individual shots from the 2001 original tell a story through the simple fact of their composition. When Harry spots Snape through the crowd, the framing of the two characters creates instant intrigue and drama. But here, the individual shots look much duller and less vibrant.

Overall, the whole looks rather like a recession indictor. From the darker palette to what looks like a vastly reduced food offering at the so-called 'feast', the whole thing looks, to quite Ryanair, "cheaper than a Ryanair flight". And given the recent response to the new posters for the series, the whole thing has a long way to go to win round fans.

Daniel John is Design Editor at Creative Bloq. He reports on the worlds of design, branding and lifestyle tech, and has covered several industry events including Milan Design Week, OFFF Barcelona and Adobe Max in Los Angeles. He has interviewed leaders and designers at brands including Apple, Microsoft and Adobe. Daniel's debut book of short stories and poems was published in 2018, and his comedy newsletter is a Substack Bestseller.

items.title: Nike Tuned Air "a huge stride forward" in air-filled trainer design says innovation lead
paragraphs: Sportswear brand Nike has unveiled the 3D-printed air bags that will be used for its next generation of air-filled trainers. In this interview, the brand’s chief innovation, design & product officer Phil McCartney explains why it is a technological and performance advance.
“I see it personally as a revolution, not an evolution,” McCartney told Dezeen from the LeBron James Innovation Center in Oregon. “It’s a huge stride forward.”

Tuned Air was designed to give Nike much greater control of how air is used within the midsole to provide cushioning and support. Using a combination of proprietary 3D printing and “selective lamination” allows Nike to create midsoles that perform in different ways under different parts of the foot.
Informed by the raised vibrant colours on magazine covers, the airbag is built up from layers of ink.
“We can engineer the structure and tune the structure in the heel differently to the forefoot,” said McCartney.
“We can also tune the height, so you can have a variety of different heights, and we can tune the structure inside.”
Nike unveiled the technology and concept images for a running shoe today, and is planning for the first Nike Tuned Air trainer to be launched next year.

The trainers will be the first in what Nike sees as a third major generation of its air-filled shoes, since Nike CEO Phil Knight worked with inventor Frank Rudy to use a cushioning system filled with gas in the late 1970s.
Following the Nike Air Tailwind in 1978, Nike developed Air Max in the 1980s and Air Zoom in the 1990s.

“At its core, Air, for 50 years, has been this magical combination of lightweight, cushioned and resilient – it doesn’t break down over time,” said McCartney. “That’s why from day one when Phil [Knight] struck the deal with Frank Rudy, we’ve been so committed to it – it just delivers a really unique benefit.”

“If Max Air is about maximal cushioning and impact protection, Zoom Air is more about responsiveness and snappiness,” he continued. “Tuned Air, because of this proprietary ink and selective lamination process, allows us to literally tune the sensation within the airbag, which enables us to sort of move free from the constraints of typical geometry and shape.”
According to McCartney, this change in how the airbags are manufactured opens up possibilities, especially in customisation.

“It is the first step in exploring all the different places that this will go,” said McCartney. “The capability and what we’re able to do with this proprietary ink and the selective lamination allows us to really unlock the real potential of air.”
“It also creates this canvas for all the design explorations that we’ve always wanted to do, but the limitations of the manufacturing process didn’t allow,” he continued.

“So now the handcuffs are off in terms of it being a canvas – what expressions do we want to explore? What different visuals, geometries, and different ways to articulate the benefit can we explore? We’re looking at all of that. “
While the air-filled midsole has been manufactured, the trainer is still in development. However, McCartney expects the shoe to look close to the concept render that was revealed today.

“There’ll be a few modifications,” he said. “Knowing where the design is going to go. It’s pretty representative as an illustration, but it isn’t the final design.” He noted that the final air bag design will be close to the prototype.
“What we’re exploring now is how do we take the idea of lightweight cushioning and this idea of tuned [and find] what that looks like in an expression and an experience on the upper.”

One key design element that will feature in the commercial release next year will be the full-length, visible air bag, which McCartney said is an “important part of the design and important part of this platform”.

The midsoles are the latest innovation in Nike’s exploration of using air within footwear and apparel. While it has made millions of shoes containing air, it has also recently unveiled the inflating Air Milano Jacket at 2026 Winter Olympics and its Radical AirFlow t-shirts that counterintuitively use more material to make a wearer cooler.
In all the areas of innovation that McCartney oversees at Nike, air is where he sees the most potential.

“There’s a number of areas, but if I had to pick one, I think that [air] is the platform that intrigues us most, that drives our creativity the most, that also translates into the biggest athlete benefit. And I mean athlete in the broadest sense of the term – if you’ve got a body, you’re an athlete.”

“We’re really intrigued and fascinated by the notion of being able to harness what’s all around us to further performance,” said McCartney. “That started in footwear, obviously. This is the next revolution.”

items.title: Are squishy toys safe? – level 1
paragraphs: Many kids love playing with squishy toys. Scientists test some of these toys to see if they are safe. They find that one toy has too much of one chemical. This chemical can hurt children.
Also, if squishies stay in a hot car for a long time, they can break. Hot liquid may come out. This can hurt a child’s skin.
The store takes the bad toy away. They give money back to parents. Experts tell families to check toy labels and keep the toys away from hot places like cars.
Difficult words: squishy (soft, not hard when you touch it), liquid (a substance which flows, like water or gel), label (a piece of paper on a product which gives information about it).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.
