items.title: I built a powerful new web design tool that focuses on craft, not automation – try a live demo now
paragraphs: As creative software races toward increased automation, are we as designers asking the right questions?
Over the years, I’ve watched the conversations of web developers and designers shift increasingly toward technology, and further away from something we once took great pride in: Craft.

The 20th century was an extraordinary period for graphic design, particularly typography and print. By the 1990s we had inherited an astonishingly mature digital toolbox: QuarkXPress, Photoshop, PostScript typography and all the precision that came with them.

Those tools were deeply rooted in the crafts they replaced. Photoshop borrowed directly from the photographic darkroom – dodge, burn and all. Quark brought centuries of typographic practice into the digital workspace, giving designers extraordinarily precise control over type and composition.

Then we moved communications to the web – and somehow left much of that toolbox behind. Our web platforms never came close to giving designers the same depth of control. Many creatives simply accepted the loss and said, “Well, that’s just the web.”
I never quite bought into that. Instead I started making notes for what would become Design Studio for Gutenberg (DSG), a powerful designer-first plugin for WordPress Gutenberg.
And at this moment, an inflection point when creative software makers increasingly want to automate design itself, we need to ask: Could better tools offer another way forward?
Web typography has always been a particular sore point for me.
I’ll admit my standards may be unusually high. I cut my typography chops as a Type Director at J. Walter Type, part of the legendary JWT ad agency, and such training is hard to shake.

So I found workarounds for maintaining the quality my clients expected. For example, for important headlines I would often set the type in Illustrator, kern it properly, export it as SVG artwork and bring that into a website as art.
Ridiculous? Perhaps. But my clients included brands like American Express, Merck and Lincoln Center. They expected high-quality work, and I delivered. But there had to be a better way.

As each new web-design platform arrived, I would look to see whether somebody had finally built one from a designer’s point of view. A typographer's point of view. Many claimed they had. But mostly they just gave us what programmers thought designers wanted.
Eventually I stopped waiting. A few years ago I sat down with my studio’s programmers and gave them a simple directive:We are going to build what designers need.
WordPress was the obvious foundation. It was open source, mature and unlikely to disappear like so many web-dev programs before it.

My other directive: Design Studio could not be another heavy page-builder sitting on top of WordPress. It needed to live inside Gutenberg and thus benefit from WordPress’ lighter weight and faster core.
We even created our own mantra: WordPress Builds Webpages. DSG Designs Them.
We methodically broke down what was missing. The list grew fast.
We ultimately ended up creating a system with THREE BLOCKS, one custom TEMPLATE, and more UI additions and tools than I could count.
Let’s start with the three blocks, which contain tools you simply will not find in other web-development systems:

This text block is unique. It has every major type control that you might have found in Quark or InDesign. Powerful tools like KERNING, without which we can never hope to produce professional grade typography.

Font choices in TDB are not tied to any template. Instead they allow full font and style selections just like a desktop app. And it works directly with our font management system found in the DESIGNER DASH backend (more on that later).

Another earmark of a professional toolset is system-wide keyboard commands that make work dramatically faster. Imagine masterfully kerning your headline, sliding in a copyright icon, scaling and tucking it perfectly. Try that with your current web system!
It also allows mixed type, font, style and more, all within a single text container.
A friend testing DSG at a major ad agency said it best: “Composite layers in WP? Mind blown.”

Import multilayer Photoshop or Krita files (see my comparison of those two here), then treat each layer independently with blur, invert, halftone, sepia and full BLEND settings. Then each layer can be easily scaled, rotated, and even placed anywhere on the page.
This tool is simply fun. Go play with it in our LIVE DEMO.
This full-width block offers real freedom. Starting with a HEIGHT CONTROL slider, so no more needing to wedge in spacers or scaffolding.
Within the Composition Block, TDB and ADB can be placed freely anywhere you want. Even overlapping each other, or hanging off the CB. (Our website is the perfect example.)
Some early testers had to look twice to make sure they were still in WordPress.

We knew just what they meant: Rulers, Guides, Grid, device-specific Visibility icons across every object in the List View. We include a very special BLANK CANVAS template, better page controls, and a backend DESIGNER DASH with tabs for Font.
My goal here isn’t to catalog every Design Studio for Gutenberg feature. I mention these to make a larger point: Web designers deserve better tools. And that feels particularly important now.
AI has an enormous role to play in our future creative work. Let it remove drudgery, generate first passes, organise assets and automate anything that doesn’t benefit from human judgment.
But craft begins where the default answer ends. “Craft” has always been, and shall always remain a very human thing.

Craft is deciding that two letters need to be kerned tighter. That an image needs to move three pixels down. That this composition should deliberately break the grid. That the mobile version shouldn’t simply be a smaller copy of the desktop.
Those are precisely the kinds of decisions that only professional designers should make. And it requires precision tools like those in DSG that allow such decisions to be executed.
After reading the DSG manual, I asked ChatGPT how its own web-building abilities compared with those of a competent designer using DSG. Its answer was spot-on:
“A surprising amount of what DSG enables is still awkward to get from AI.” — ChatGPT
In my mind it is not a question of human vs. AI. But instead, how to use the best tools for each part of your job.

We built a live demo so you can come kick the tires. And because we are very big on sharing in general, and the open source, free and affordable software movements, we are releasing Design Studio for Gutenberg, with everything we have talked about and so much more for just $39. Including per-person unlimited use (right, that means no more counting websites), and a license that never expires.
With the release of Design Studio 1.0 we hope to contribute to the goal of building a better web. This is step one.
Visit Design Studio for Gutenberg, try the DEMO: https://openstudiony.com

Lance Evans is creative director of Graphlink Media (graphlink.com), a boutique creative marketing agency in NYC, with clients like Olive Garden, Miller Beer and AMEX. Lance recently launched "OPEN STUDIO | NY", a YouTube channel looking at production techniques for advertising and publishing shops. Visit it at youtube.com/@OpenStudioNY

items.title: US basketball player arrested with 75lb of marijuana at Nigerian airport, say authorities
paragraphs: An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country.

Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said a 28-year-old player named as Greene Da’monte Khiree from the state of Georgia was arrested at Lagos’s main airport last Wednesday after he arrived on a flight from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.

The NDLEA said the player told them he had come to Nigeria to “build networks” for his basketball career. The agency said evidence on his phone suggested he had “knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity”. The NDLEA said it detained the player when he attempted to leave the airport with his hand luggage after abandoning two checked-in bags. The agency said those two bags were found to contain 32 parcels of marijuana, and a tracking device.
Nigeria has strict drug laws, and trafficking carries a sentence of life in prison.

A basketball player by the name of Damonte Greene is listed on the roster of the Pattani Raptors in the Thai Premier Men’s League. Greene, a Georgia native, played college basketball for Reinhardt University and South Georgia Technical College. He played semi-professional basketball in the US before representing a number of teams in Thailand.

WNBA star Brittney Griner and former Utah State player Jarred Shaw were imprisoned in Russia and Indonesia respectively for marijuana offenses. Griner was released in December 2022, while Shaw remains in prison.

items.title: The Scouse actor reaching new heights in Liverpool drama This City Is Ours
paragraphs: With millions of viewers and a major role in a Bafta-nominated series, you might not expect Adam Abbou to know much about feeling self-conscious.
"When we were kids it wasn't so cool to be from Liverpool," the This City Is Ours actor says.
"I'd be in these rooms with people who were really posh and I always felt out of place."
The Liverpool-based BBC series has become a hit, with Abbou, who plays Freddie, stepping into a prominent role for its second season.
But it's not just the storylines on drugs, gangs and murders hooking audiences - it's the setting too, and the Scouse actors bringing it to life.
Created by Liverpudlian writer Stephen Butchard, This City Is Ours recruited heavily from Merseyside.
Lead actors James Nelson-Joyce, Jack McMullen and Mike Noble were all born in Liverpool, as was Abbou, who grew up in Anfield.
But like many young and aspiring actors, for a long time he thought where he came from could hold him back.
"I didn't see a lot of [Liverpudlian accents] on TV when I was a kid," the 23-year-old says.
As a result, acting "always felt really out of reach".
Abbou played the title role in a touring production of Billy Elliot the Musical in 2015, and has since appeared in dramas like Casualty, Time and Waterloo Road.
He says he wasn't expecting his latest gig, where he plays Freddie, gangster Banksey's son, to become so significant.
"If you would have asked me 10 years ago, I would have said you probably need to move to London," he says.
"So for me to be able to do a show like this in Liverpool, it just further proves that you can do it from anywhere."
From the reaction he's had locally, Abbou thinks the series has been a boost for Liverpool overall.

The reaction has been "quite crazy" in the city, he says, "but of course it would be because people love to see themselves and their accent reflected on TV and when it is, you almost feel like you know the person".
"It has truly been incredible to see the rise of the Scouse accent," he adds, crediting the Netflix series Adolescence, starring and co-created by Stephen Graham, with accelerating the change.
"Stephen Graham really was the one who started the wave for Scouse actors," he says.
"And then the likes of Jodie Comer and now you've got your Mike Nobles, your James Nelson-Joyces... and now your Adam Abbous.
"We're making waves for young Scouse talent."
As for what's next, Abbou says the series has helped push his career forward and he has some "exciting projects lined up" which he can't speak about just yet.
"I just want to do things that make me feel creatively fulfilled and mean something and have a voice."
- The last episode of The City Is Ours season two airs on BBC One at 21:00 GMT.

items.title: Shisuo Design Office creates "surreal" rural house in China using salvaged steel
paragraphs: Jiang Deng Lu is a house in rural Anhui designed by Chinese studio Shisuo Design Office using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.
Described by Shisuo Design Office as a “surreal rural house”, the compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site.
It sits beside the client’s ancestral home and serves as both a memorial for his late father and a separate dwelling where his elderly mother can host visiting relatives.

“The client wanted to build a house beside the old family home, providing a comfortable place for his mother and relatives to gather and share meals during holidays,” Shisuo Design Office told Dezeen.

“But beyond this practical need, there was a deeper emotional connection. The old house was left by his father, while the new one represented his own way of creating new memories for the family,” it continued.
“We hoped the house would bring the family together more often, beyond just festive occasions.”
Jiang Deng Lu’s proportions were determined by the recycled stainless steel offcuts and unused windows salvaged for the project by the client, who is the owner of a stainless steel factory.
“The building’s geometry was strictly reverse-engineered from these salvaged materials,” said Shisuo Design Office.

“Instead of imposing a predetermined architectural form, we meticulously measured and mapped these specific surplus components. The building’s precise dimensions, roof pitches, and structural envelope were entirely reverse-engineered from this salvaged inventory,” added the studio.

“The resulting structure starkly contrasts the client’s modern, lightweight metal industry with the heavy, rooted legacy of his father’s masonry, translating familial love into a rigorous tectonic language,” the studio said.

Externally, the house is wrapped in a full stainless-steel facade, which the studio said deliberately contrasts with “traditional rural vernacular”. This is punctured by the salvaged windows, positioned to frame views of the river.
It has a rectangular plan, with a balcony that is suspended over the river on one side.
Inside is a living space, which sits raised above a dining area accessed directly from the foyer. A bathroom and shower room sit off this dining space.

Interior finishes are pared-back, with stone flooring and white walls complementing the cool-toned exterior of the home. Wooden furnishings and greenery seen through the windows add warmth to the space.
According to Shisuo Design Office, the highlight of the interior is a nine-metre-long window that cantilevers 2.2 metres outward, providing shelter for the terrace below.
“The most distinctive feature is a nine-metre-long horizontal window facing east, overlooking a grove of trees planted by the client’s late father,” said the studio.
“For the client, these trees are more than a landscape; they hold personal memories of his father. We wanted to bring the grove into everyday life, rather than simply frame it as a view.”
Jiang Deng Lu is shortlisted in the rural house category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Casa Plaj by Extrastudio and Hata-Mazanka Guesthouses by YOD Group.
Another house featured on Dezeen with a distinctive metal facade is Bondi House, a two-storey, two-bedroom dwelling by Nick Kent Design in Sydney.

items.title: How Playstation nailed its iconic startup screen
paragraphs: There’s a short ritual that plays out every time someone switches on a PlayStation. You press the power button and, before the dashboard appears, movement and sound take over, building through a sequence before the console hands you over to play. It lasts only seconds, but those seconds have a beginning, a build, a pause and a release. They are designed as an experience in their own right.

For more than thirty years, every generation of PlayStation has opened with its own version of this sequence. The motion, visual language and sound have changed but the decision to design that transition has remained. What could easily be functional downtime has instead become part of the PlayStation experience. It rivals the best motion in logo design, but it also has its own function as well.
All PlayStation Startups (PS1, PS2, PSX, PSP, PS3, PS Vita, PS4, PS5) - YouTube

That intent goes back to the beginning. When Manabu Sakamoto designed the original PlayStation logo, he wanted it to capture one of the console’s defining promises: 3D. The interlocking P and S created a sense of depth and space rather than simply sitting flat on a 2D screen. By spring 1994, that identity had been turned into an animation, handed to sound designer Takafumi Fujisawa as what the team called a “motion logo.”

Fujisawa was given little direction beyond that animation and had to set the tone himself, working within tight technical limits. He wanted the startup to feel like walking into a cinema. That particular hush where you sense something is about to begin.

A straight cut from power-on to interface would give you a change of state and nothing else. Motion gives those few seconds structure; sound and visual design give them character. They are all working together, but motion is what determines how the experience unfolds through time.

The startup’s primary job isn’t just to create an ‘atmosphere’, as it also helps organise the experience of entering the console itself. The sequence tells the player that something is happening, creates a sense of progression, and makes the eventual handoff into play feel deliberate.

On the original PlayStation, it took on a more practical role. The startup sound helped confirm that the hardware was running correctly and that the disc had been read. If it hadn’t, part of the sound was designed to loop to signal that something was wrong.
The important point is that the startup was not simply decoration sitting on top of a technical process. Motion, sound and visual design were part of how that process was communicated and felt.
That is where motion becomes especially useful. It can signal change, control pace, create anticipation and prepare someone for what comes next.

Over time, the original function of that startup changed. Hardware changed, interfaces changed, and the need to tell a player that a disc had been successfully read stopped mattering. Yet, PlayStation kept designing the transition.

Five generations on, those startups have looked, moved and sounded very different. What has survived through that time is the expectation that switching on any PlayStation from PS1 to PS5 deserves an authored beginning.

That consistency does not always come from repeating the same expression. It sometimes (and in this case) comes from recognising which moments are the most valuable. PlayStation could change the way those seconds looked and felt because the thing it had established beforehand went beyond the mere execution of it.

Brands spend enormous amounts of time designing the things people see, whether it be the best logos, typefaces, colours, layouts or interfaces. But experiences are also full of moments between those things.

When an app opens, or a payment completes, an audience waits for something to begin. These transitions are easy to treat as functional gaps, especially when the instinct is to get people to the next thing as quickly as possible. The point, though, is not to add friction; it is to recognise that these moments already exist, and that repeated transitions can become part of the brand experience when they are deliberately designed.

Motion matters disproportionately in those spaces because it works in the same material the moment is made of: time. It determines how one state becomes another, and how that change is experienced along the way. PlayStation was able to make that transition worth designing and returning to in its own right.

Andrew Vucko merges a lifelong interest in motion and design with a passion for brand building. As the founder of Vucko, he leads a global motion studio that transforms brands like Google, Meta, and Spotify through award-winning motion identities, systems, and guidelines.

items.title: Casa Mouda opens Lagos gallery to promote design in Nigeria
paragraphs: Papa Omotayo, Gemma Sfeir and Nifemi Marcus-Bello have helped design two spaces in Lagos for the local creative studio Casa Mouda to host exhibitions that promote design in West Africa.
Casa Mouda’s initiative includes the launch of an exhibition to mark the opening of two spaces in Lagos – aiMe Gallery at Eko Hotel and aiMe Concept on Eko Atlantic.

AiMe Gallery was redesigned by Lagos-based architect Omotayo at the entrance to the hotel’s conference centre, while aiMe Concept was designed with interior designer Sfeir and designer Marcus-Bello in a storefront in the larger Eko Atlantic development.
Both spaces feature exposed concrete walls and columns with touches of warmth, including an earthen bar and screen in aiMe Gallery.
Casa Mouda founder Caline Chagoury Moudaber said that the spaces, together, were designed to highlight the work done by designers in Lagos.
“As we began to conceive our first chapter of Casa Mouda, we knew we needed to start by recognizing some of the people who had already built so much of its foundation,” said Chagoury Moudaber.
“There are incredible designers producing on the continent that have done extraordinary work, often taking on alone what usually takes an entire industry elsewhere.”
The inaugural exhibitions include designers from Lagos, but also those who have chosen to work in the city from abroad.

Among the latter group is American designer Germane Barnes, who showcased his wooden Corona Chair, which features inverted pyramidal legs, and his take on a peacock chair, both produced in Lagos in collaboration with Casa Mouda.

Beyond his contribution to the interior layout, which includes permanent seating for the hospitality at aiMe Concept, Marcus-Bello showcased his LM stools and M2 shelves. The works showcase the production possible in Lagos, but also a more modern, minimalist angle for Marcus-Bello, who is known for his massive metal collectible design pieces.
“Nifemi Marcus-Bello has been quietly doing the legwork to set up real pathways for production for years,” said Chagoury Moudaber.
On the more craft-oriented side, the collection showcased works in bronze and wood by craftsman Jean Servais Somian, also produced in collaboration with Casa Mouda.

Servais Somian’s work includes an armoire with gridded screen wooden doors, a console with stacked oval shelves, stools in wood with painted recesses that have a graphic appearance and textural cast bronze stools and side tables. It is an impressive array showcasing the craftsman’s range.
French studio Hall Haus showcased its metal basketball hoops and chairs, a blend of African aesthetics with Parisian urban ephemera, reflecting the cross-cultural background of the studio’s members.
Meanwhile, Moroccan designer Hajar Daide showcased a mix of delicate Nigerian woven wood techniques with lush blue Moroccan fabrics for her Friction Bench.

Atmosphere was top of mind for the designers, and Casa Mouda worked with US musician Malloy James to create custom speakers at the entryway for aiMe Gallery, while aiMe Concept features a listening station.
The spaces have also been set up to further promote craft in the region through display and retail, such as textiles, bags and other smaller items such as jewellery.

“The designers who have forged the way are sharing information on what they have learned; the ones new to this area of production are bringing new techniques and perspectives,” said Chagoury Moudaber.
“It has been an incredibly collaborative, generous, and inspiring process – and we are only just beginning.”
Other recent design showcases include the inaugural Walker Design Triennial in Minnesota and Danish design initiative The Mindcraft Project, curated by Christian + Jade.

items.title: Eight highlights from this year's Sharjah Architecture Triennial
paragraphs: The third Sharjah Architecture Triennial focuses on the myriad ways architecture can be understood through the lens of anthropology. Here are our highlights from the event, including installations and exhibitions.
Curated by anthropologist Vyjayanthi Rao, this year’s edition was centred on the theme Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures.
Rao said the 2026 Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which takes place over five months, will invite discourse about the different ways cities and urban life can be imagined.
“Though I’m not an architect, I’m literally talking to students day in and day out about how they see the world, and how that translates into the practice,” Rao told Dezeen.
“Being an academic, you’re always asked to define yourself in terms of your discipline,” she continued. “It doesn’t make sense to limit yourself, especially when you are in the practice of life.”

“You’re learning from people about the ways in which they live – that’s what I do as an anthropologist, and I think that’s what a lot of architects do because they’re inspired to build for people and the places that they inhabit and thrive in.”
Read on for eight highlights from this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial.

Artist Curry J Hackett created this draping shelter spanning the width of the Old Al Jubail Vegetable Market in homage to the Black community in Virginia’s Prince Edward County, which created improvised learning spaces when schools closed during the Civil Rights Movement.

Videos play in the former stalls at either end of the fabric enclosure, screening archival images of the period, as well as images of Rosenwald Schools – the community-building initiative that established thousands of schools for Black children in the South.

“Rather than integrate, schools closed for five years, and leading up to that, schools were dealing with a lot of overcrowding,” Hackett told Dezeen. “The county begrudgingly funded ‘tar paper shacks’, which were shoddy, demoralising structures, to ease overcrowding, and that’s what you’re seeing interpreted here,” he continued.

“Interspersed sonically and visually throughout the installation is a mashing up of the local story of my home town in Virginia with the regional story of the Rosenwald Schools in the South – their architectural rethinking of materials and retelling the history.”
Research and construction studio Abari showcased a tent-like structure made from a bamboo frame, which was limited in size due to difficulties with material regulations.
The structure is one module of a larger pavilion that was constructed in Nepal, designed as a travelling venue to host bamboo weaving workshops.

“We were not able to create an installation here in the UAE, partly because Abari’s work is based on building with bamboo, and the difficulty with this project was that the global supply chain and its regulations could not be met within the timeframe,” said Rao.

“What you see here is one repeatable module of a pavilion that is currently moving within different communities in Nepal – we improvised and decided Sharjah would travel to Nepal, and we’d just have a piece of it here in this exhibition.”
Drawing upon her fieldwork in Sharjah, Palestinian architect Samar Halloum designed a brick pavilion that was shaded overhead by a draping fabric canopy.
In reference to the historical public drinking-water structures in the Gulf region, Sabeel Negotiated features a water fountain and wooden stools for people to gather around.
According to Rao, the strikes by Iran on countries in the Middle East in February disrupted brick supply in the United Arab Emirates, so Halloum redesigned the pavilion with cloth-filled bricks.

“One of the shortages was bricks because they come from Saudi Arabia, and the factory stopped producing bricks,” said Rao. “There were some leftover bales of cloth from another installation, so Halloum used those bales and cast them in resin, so you’ll see some of the bricks in the installation are actually made of cloth.”
History as Repair: Documenting Karachi by Kishwar Rizvi

This exhibition by art historian Kishwar Rizvi explores how colonised communities in Karachi, Pakistan, took ownership of their urban environment by adapting architectural styles, from European classicism to Mughal-inspired ornament.
Through maps, photographs, sketches and interviews, it aims to shine a light on an architectural history at risk of being forgotten.
The exhibition argues for the protection of colonial-era buildings in Karachi, which are under threat of demolition due to neglect.
Patch-Time by Hiba Bou Akar, Mohamad Hafeda and Nathalie Harb

The Patch-Time installation is a collaboration between researchers Hiba Bou Akar and Mohamad Hafeda and artist Nathalie Harb that explores the displacement of people in Lebanon, from the 1970s to the present day, through the materials used to protect and repair homes.

In workshops organised by Lebanese non-profit Ahla Fawda, displaced women crocheted tarpaulin, sand-bag cloth and sheeting into panels that form a canopy displayed in a courtyard at the triennial’s Al Qasimiyah School venue.
Underneath the canopy, a table made from breeze blocks, wood and a central mirror displays fabric artwork and the stories of women and children affected by war.

“We worked on two levels: one that is the collective, and one that is more of the individual, looking at how people shelter their home through war adversity and displacement,” said Harb. “We asked [the women] what their relationship to their home was, and in the pieces, you see how it changes from generation to generation with their relationship to material.”
After Night There is Nothing by Mohamad Nahleh and Ozayr Saloojee

Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee designed a giant globe of the night sky and split it into three parts, which were scattered across different locations at the triennale.

The outer shells of the curved structures are wrapped in thatch, while the interiors feature vinyl surfaces with designs showing man-made military objects in the sky reimagined as creature-like constellations.

“This is ‘night sky optimism’ – optimism through catastrophe,” said Nahleh. “The night sky we are talking about in this project is not the sky of beautiful stars and constellations, but the contemporary sky filled with drones, satellites, rockets and missiles that are changing the way we understand the sky above us.”

“We have noticed in our research that, especially in geographies witnessing prolonged violence, these objects are producing new mythical creatures,” he continued. “We think of these creatures as ones that attempt to tame the military brightness that is populating the sky around us.”
Kuwaiti designer Badriyah Alsalem plotted 41 medieval Arabic poetic names for the sun as cut-outs on the astronomical graph that forms a circular canopy over her pavilion, As the Sun Rests.

Forming patterns of shadow in the sand below, three of the suns were embroidered in red, depicting the sharaq rising sun, saqa’a noon sun and gharab setting sun, while markers on the ground show where these canopy highlights will fall on different dates during the triennial.
“If you look up, you see the static data visualisation, and if you look down, it is animated by the sun itself, so it becomes an analogue device to read this historical data,” said Alsalem.
Lalla Alwyia Khalwa by Ziad Jamaleddine, Makram el Kadi, Iheb Guermazi and Beya Othmani
Situated on Sharjah’s Al Khan Open Beach, Lalla Alwyia Khalwa is an installation designed as a place for reflection away from the busy city, dedicated to the saint Lalla Alwyia Kasserine.

Dried plants form a grid of columns on a raised platform for visitors to walk through. Stone slabs on the floor mark places of pause, and a metal stool provides a reflective space to listen to the accompanying sound installation.
“We chose the beach because it is already a space for retreat, so this is a retreat inside a retreat,” said the design team, Ziad Jamaleddine, Makram el Kadi, Iheb Guermazi and Beya Othmani.
“We carved a series of spaces – one for prayer, one for sitting, and a courtyard to enjoy the sky.”

Sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026 takes place from 14 November 2026 to 14 April 2027 at various locations across Sharjah, UAE. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

items.title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
paragraphs: The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.

The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.

The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. Some animal rights activists have compared authorities’ baboon management to apartheid.
During Friday’s relocation, outraged protesters tried to stop vehicles taking the baboons away. One person sprayed a fire extinguisher, according to the Daily Maverick, a local news outlet.

After the confrontation, the local Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals branch urged those opposed to the baboons’ capture not to try to stop the vehicles. “Capture and transport are already stressful for the baboons,” it said in a statement. “Delaying their arrival prolongs their time in crates and risks adding to that stress – this is not fair on the baboons.”
It said it remained opposed to the baboon’s relocation, adding: “Our presence did not imply support … our inspectors are present because the animals need someone looking out for them.”

On Sunday, dozens of people sat outside the wildlife centre in a silent protest, some tying flowers to the fence. Baboons from a different troop also gathered at the boundary, calling to the newly captive animals, the Daily Maverick reported.

“We stand together for the Seaforth and Waterfall troops, for their freedom, their dignity and their right to live as wild animals,” Mandy Neal, the administrator of the Save Kogelfontein Baboons Facebook group, posted on Monday, calling for weekly Sunday silent protests. “ Our message is simple: CAPTIVITY IS NOT CONSERVATION.”

The City of Cape Town said in a statement on Sunday that the relocation had been successful, with the baboons being monitored 24/7 after being checked by vets and the females receiving contraceptive implants.

It said: “The Waterfall troop has been relocated due to the severity and persistence of human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment, the limited available natural low-lying habitat, the increasing risk to the baboons’ welfare, and public safety concerns … [and] as a very last resort after other interventions were evaluated and deemed ineffective, and as an alternative to culling.”

Prof Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town, said the baboon management plan had undergone two years of public consultations. “It has thus been disappointing watching members of the public and select NGOs, many which did not engage in the stakeholder process, now compromising the safety and welfare of the baboons and people through violent actions directed at staff and baboons in transit.”

items.title: B2 Architecture turns North Korean defector testimonies into Prague exhibition
paragraphs: B2 Architecture has created the Life Behind the Walls exhibition in Prague, using a maze of red timber frames and translucent fabric to explore life in North Korea.

The 1,500-square-metre exhibition takes visitors from a bright, interactive installation designed around a children’s book to a darkened gallery featuring portraits and testimonies from North Korean defectors.

B2 Architecture divided the installation into two contrasting environments. The first features a grid of red-painted timber beams, with large sheets of red and pink fabric suspended between the frames to create semi-transparent walls.
The structure forms a maze that visitors can explore, with glimpses of other rooms and activities visible through the fabric.
Illustrated panels, games and interactive activities are fitted into the structure, while photographs by photographer Michal Huniewicz show North Korea as it is presented to the outside world.
Children are encouraged to navigate the maze independently and stop to draw, write and complete activities as they move through the installation.

The displays are based on Tota lítá, a children’s book by North Korean studies scholar and writer Nina Špitálníková, which explains the principles of totalitarianism in language that is accessible to younger readers.
“Children are often given very little space within exhibition formats,” B2 Architecture told Dezeen. “This project consciously challenges that convention.”
The atmosphere changes as visitors pass between two walls displaying photographs of the border between North Korea and China by photographer Tim Franco.

Beyond this threshold, the playful red maze gives way to a dark gallery. This contains black display structures with portraits and personal accounts of people who escaped North Korea, alongside stories of those who did not survive its regime.
Tall, translucent fabric panels printed with shadowy human figures were arranged throughout the space, creating silhouettes that overlap with the portraits displayed behind them.
In a central room, a monumental statue of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un stands on a raised plinth, surrounded by spotlights and theatrical mist.
The temporary installation was constructed using lightweight, modular timber beams and stretched textiles, allowing it to be assembled and dismantled efficiently.
The timber structure was retained for use in another project, while the textiles and flooring were passed on to several theatres for reuse.
Prague-based B2 Architecture was founded by architect Barbara Bencová in 2012 and works across residential and commercial architecture, interiors and public spaces.

Other projects by the studio featured on Dezeen include the DDB Prague office, which features an anamorphic optical illusion that makes the advertising agency’s logo appear complete from a particular viewpoint.

items.title: Why Dispatch's creators said no to '10,000 endings'
paragraphs: Every interactive story faces the same temptation: give the player more. More branches, more endings, more ways to bend the script until it snaps. Dispatch, AdHoc Studio's episodic superhero workplace comedy, went the other way. It stars Breaking Bad's Aaron Paul as former hero Robert Robertson, who now sends a team of reformed villains out on call-outs.

As the breakout indie game celebrates its one-year anniversary with the Dispatch Deluxe Edition, which lets you play the storyboard art, I caught up with the team. We've heard how Four video tracks and a doughnut shop got it started and how AdHoc made Dispatch feel like an animated TV series, so now I want to know how a choice-driven game gets that far by holding choices back. We put the question to AdHoc co-founders Nick Herman and Dennis Lenart, the studio's COO and CTO and both co-creative directors.

AdHoc starts with the belief that most developers get the equation backwards. "When folks set out to make an interactive narrative game, they incorrectly assume that it's all about the branching narrative that makes it exciting," Herman says. "We believe it's about the quality of that narrative at the core, and then you have to branch that quality narrative."

That's easy to say and hard to do, he admits, and harder still when you have to write multiple good stories at once, which is what the team signed up for. So the development team works from the story's spine and its characters, then figure out what choice space could believably exist alongside them.

Robert Robertson arrives with a backstory and a personality, so options that betray him are off the table. Herman sees that as a gift: it "eliminates blue sky" and lets the team concentrate on a believable character. It's also why he's wary when people ask for thousands of endings. Would 10,000 of them really be as compelling as a six or seven that the team has made as satisfying as possible?

Lenart describes the whole process as "almost an exercise in restraint at times". Picture 10 developers in a room discussing a scene where a character is aggressive towards you. A couple of them will say they wish you could just punch him. "The thing we have to filter that through is, 'Would Robert conceivably punch him in this situation?'" says Lenart. "A lot of times the answer is no."

It isn't a flat ban. If everyone agrees that punching him would be thrilling but there's no motivation for it, Herman says the conversation becomes how to make it a viable choice. Lenart says you go back into the scene and the story and set it up "so that that choice feels like it's a payoff to something that exists".

Skip that groundwork and the cost is steep. "The more you do that, the more you start diluting your character and then they kind of become a little bit faceless," Lenart warns. Herman puts it more bluntly: the story starts to feel like "a narrative toy" and less like one with believable characters.

So how do you make a choice feel weighty without animating an entirely new story? Lenart says, "A lot of the magic in these types of games is the story that people are telling in their heads". The most effective choices, he says, are the ones where "you're affecting how another character in the story thinks about you".

Treat someone a certain way in front of the group, and players will assume that character's later behaviour is motivated by it. Every glance in a later scene gets read as payback for what you said earlier, which Lenart compares to real life. AdHoc builds on that expectation on purpose.

Herman calls it "the grease between the major cogs of choices". Players carry a decision forward for an hour or so, until the grease runs out and they need an injection of new stuff. If a scene doesn't land that way, he says, "it's probably because something's broken". Contrivance, or a sense of being guided, are the signs to go back and fix.

There's a hard budget reason for the discipline too. "It's also just so expensive to do it the way we're doing it," says Herman, with a vision for cinematic quality and animation that makes 30 different endings impossible.

Lenart gives an example of a branch the team could have offered. Imagine letting players choose at the start whether Robert works as a dispatcher or makes a new suit and heads off to be a hero in another city. It sounds great on a flowchart, but "you'd end up animating an entirely different game", with two separate stories, and Robert's arc would stop being about redemption.

Herman is generous about other approaches. He points to Slay the Princess, The Stanley Parable, and Detroit: Become Human as games where their branchiness and reactivity are major selling points. "Interactive narrative games are not one thing," he says. "The beauty of the medium is that everyone finds ways to express it in different ways."

Where does the line fall between what the player controls and what stays with the writers and developers? Lenart says it comes down to how much agency AdHoc is willing to hand over in order to tell a story it believes in. The more it gives up, the greater the risk of versions that aren't great. "Our goal was always to make it so that any path you play through is compelling and satisfying."
There's a cost, and AdHoc accepts it. Herman says some players will end up on a path that isn't their preference, and with stories it gets personal: "this isn't how I wanted it to go."

Lenart has seen the other side of the argument. On earlier games, multiple endings were mandated as a studio priority, and the takeaway was that "some of them worked". Some people had good playthroughs, others got endings they weren't satisfied with, and some were upset they didn't get the endings their friends did.

He doesn't count loose ends as a failure, either. "Not every story or movie you watch ends with you thinking everything is perfect and wrapped up," he says, and the threads people talk about afterwards are part of the experience. But "it can get out of hand if you don't keep it under control".

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

items.title: This artist is building a world inspired by swashbuckling novels and his own city, Montpellier
paragraphs: Léo Gouvert is a concept artist based in France who specialises in environments. His interest in drawing began back in the playground, copying Pokemon artwork when he was six years old. After other kids admired his work, he never stopped

Below, he tells us about four examples of personal work made using Photoshop and Blender. See our guides to the best drawing tablets and the best laptops for 3D modelling if you need new hardware for your own projects.

“The goal with this was to capture an atmosphere that evokes the disappearance of a great civilisation, somewhere between melancholy and magic.”

items.title: Yellow weather warnings issued for snow and ice as temperatures plummet
paragraphs: A spell of cold and wintry weather is set to grip northern areas of the UK early this week, bringing the threat of ice and hill snow.
A yellow weather warning for ice is in effect until 10:00 GMT on Monday after Arctic air pushing across the UK on Sunday night caused temperatures to plummet.
Cold health alerts for parts northern England also remain in force from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) until 21:00 GMT on Thursday.

Some snow is forecast over the hills and mountains in the north over the coming days but the wintry chill will be fairly short-lived in the south, where temperatures will rebound to above average by midweek.
Injuries from slips and falls on icy surfaces are possible as well as difficult driving conditions on Monday morning
Monday morning will start on a chilly note for all parts, although the coldest conditions will be across the northern half of the UK.

Whilst temperatures in the south will generally be a few degrees above freezing, northern England, Scotland and Northern Ireland will wake up to a sharp frost with some wintry flurries over the hills.
A Met Office weather warning for ice is in place until 10:00 GMT on Monday for northern and eastern Scotland as well as part of Cumbria, Northumberland and Durham.
In these regions, showers of rain, sleet or hill snow are likely to fall onto sub-zero surfaces, bringing a risk of icy stretches on untreated roads, pavements and cycle paths.
Cold health alerts, issued by the UKHSA, are also in force across north-west England, north-east England, Yorkshire and the Humber until 21:00 GMT on Thursday.
These alerts are only issued in England and are aimed at health and social care professionals.
Though Monday will be dry and bright for many places, wintry showers will affect some eastern parts of England and Scotland, with these falling as sleet or snow over high ground.
Afternoon maximum temperatures will be a chilly 4-8C in most places - a few degrees below the seasonal average.
Later in the day, the next front will approach from the south-west bringing milder air and some heavy and persistent rain.
As this band of rain then moves northwards overnight into Tuesday, a further spell of hill snow may develop.

A yellow weather warning for snow is set to come into effect on Tuesday from midnight until 12:00 GMT, covering the Midlands, north-east and north-west England, Yorkshire and the Humber and parts of south-west Scotland.
Where snow does accumulate, depths of 1-5cm are likely, although some locations above 300-400m could see 5-15cm.
Some roads and railways are likely to be affected, resulting in longer travel times by road, bus and train services. Power cuts are also possible.
Further south, Tuesday will be a very different day with blustery conditions and some heavy showers.
This battleground of colder, drier conditions in the north and milder, wetter weather in the south will continue into the middle of the week.
You can keep up to date with your local forecast by checking BBC Weather online and on the app.

items.title: Apple MacBook Pro M6 review: probably the last of its generation
paragraphs: Apple’s base-model MacBook Pro gets a solid speed bump, offering most of the features from its top-level siblings but in a design that has just been superseded and may soon be phased out.

It is the starting model in Apple’s popular MacBook Pro line, but that doesn’t make it cheap. Costing from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199) it is £300 or equivalent more than its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to jack up prices. It is, at least, £500 cheaper than the other new MacBook Pros.

The laptop’s solid aluminium body, look and feel are identical to its predecessors, using the design first introduced in 2021. With five generations of the machine having been and gone, it is a bit of a known quantity, but the 120Hz miniLED screen is still brilliant, as are the first-class keyboard and trackpad. The port selection is also solid and the MagSafe charging cable remains a delight.

The M6 model only comes with the smaller 14.2in screen, which is still the sweet spot for portability and productivity. It reaches a sustained 1,000nits brightness for standard content and working – double that of the MacBook Air – and hits 1,600nits to make HDR content pop. It is only really beaten by the OLED screen on the new MacBook Pro design, which costs considerably more.
Screen: 14.2in mini LED (3024x1964; 254 ppi) ProMotion (120Hz)
Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, 3x Thunderbolt 4/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, SDXC, headphones

The M6 is Apple’s latest generation chip and was first used in the Mac mini to great effect. Compared with the M5 generation of chips, including the current MacBook Air, the M6 MacBook Pro is about 11% faster for day-to-day usage and 24% for more intensive multi-core tasks. The extra performance wasn’t that noticeable in day-to-day tasks, but just like the M5 version, it absolutely flies during use.

However, it also has up to 57% faster graphics performance, beating many of Apple’s older M-Pro chips. That makes the M6 quite a leap from older machines with more than enough power for many creative work tasks.

The MacBook Pro also has fantastic battery life, lasting about three days of light work between charges using the browser, messaging, notes and word processing apps. That makes it one of the longest-lasting laptops for general use, but even for more intensive work, developing and editing photos, the battery still lasted about two days.

The MacBook Pro is made of 45% recycled materials, which Apple breaks down in its environmental impact report. The battery should last in excess of 1,000 full-charge cycles and can be replaced for £225 by Apple. Apple makes repair manuals available. The company offers trade-in and free recycling schemes.
The MacBook Pro M6 costs from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199).

For comparison, the 14in M5 Pro MacBook Pro costs £2,499, the 14in OLED MacBook Pro costs from £2,899, the 13in MacBook Air costs £1,299, the Dell XPS 14 costs from £2,038.45 and the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra costs £2,599.
The M6 MacBook Pro is a potent machine for general use that is let down by its high price, mostly thanks to the scourge of RAMageddon.
But it is also likely one of the last iterations of its design, having been superseded by the new thinner, lighter and OLED-equipped MacBook Pro.
The M6 is a great laptop with fantastically long battery life and a quality screen, keyboard and trackpad, built on the foundations of the many great MacBook Pros over the last five years.

But at £1,999 or equivalent it is also a difficult pill to swallow, primarily aimed at Apple buyers who want a nicer screen or more ports than a MacBook Air and are prepared to pay £700 more for it. For everyone else, there are better models available with more grunt or a cheaper price.

Pros: great performance from M6 chip, minimum of 16GB memory and 1TB storage, super-long battery life, great ProMotion screen, great Centre Stage camera, plenty of ports and an SD card slot, great speakers, Touch ID, top-class keyboard and trackpad, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support.
Cons: no Face ID, no USB-A, RAM or SSD cannot be upgraded after purchase, very expensive, not a big upgrade on M5 version, no OLED screen, heavier than newer design.

items.title: Gas starts flowing from Jackdaw after government green light
paragraphs: The Jackdaw platform is located 150 miles east of Aberdeen
Gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field, with the UK energy secretary saying it will help to heat millions of homes and businesses this winter.
Ministers last month announced the Jackdaw field, which lies 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved after years of uncertainty and a court case.
It has now been announced that it has begun producing gas which will start flowing into Britain, according to its operator Adura.
The UK government approved production from the gas field in the North Sea last month, amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.
Jackdaw is operated by Adura under a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.
A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "Last month, I gave Jackdaw the green light and today its gas will start flowing into Britain, thanks to the hard work of the skilled North Sea workers.
"It means homegrown gas from this project will help to heat millions of British homes and businesses this winter and beyond, in a boost for our energy security.
"It also will help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission gas as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear."
Claire Mueller, Jackdaw project director at Adura, said the gas field was "now helping to power Britain".

She added: "At a time of considerable uncertainty around the world, Jackdaw will provide secure energy from our own waters to heat British homes and power our economy, while reducing our reliance on imports with higher emissions.
"Jackdaw also demonstrates what can be achieved when Britain makes pragmatic, evidence-led decisions about the energy it needs, while properly accounting for our climate responsibilities."
Mueller said the decision was a "positive step towards restoring confidence in the North Sea".
She added that Adura was "proud to be producing the oil and gas our country will continue to need for decades".
Why is the Jackdaw gas field approval so controversial?
Adura has said Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand.
The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.
The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.
The decision to green-light Jackdaw drew criticism from some Labour backbenchers and environmentalists, while Conservatives called on the government to also approve the Rosebank oil field.

Both projects were approved for development by the previous Tory government in 2022 and 2023 respectively but these decisions were struck down by the Scottish courts after a challenge from environmental campaigners.
This followed a Supreme Court ruling that developers had to account for the climate impact caused by burning fossil fuels in their planning applications.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to stick to the UK's net zero target despite giving the green light to Jackdaw.
He previously said the decision would "significantly strengthen our energy security by increasing domestic gas production by about 6% and support the UK's energy supply for more than a decade".
A decision on the larger Rosebank oil project is yet to be made.
Protesters gathered outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero in Westminster on Wednesday morning
The co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the Jackdaw approval as "climate vandalism".
He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now."
Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank.
Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.
Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify".
The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.
Jackdaw's operators said its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortages
Jackdaw sits close to the boundary between the British and Norwegian sectors of the North Sea, in an area where Westminster originally granted licences to explore for oil and gas in 1970 and 1989.
The field was discovered in 2005 but it was expensive and technically difficult to exploit.
Shell did not commit to its development until 2022, shortly after the Conservative government had granted consent for production.
But in January 2025, after a challenge by environmentalists, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled that consent for Jackdaw and Rosebank had been granted unlawfully.
The judge, Lord Ericht, said the developers should have provided a more detailed account of the fields' impact on climate change as part of the permitting process.

The judge allowed the companies to continue with preparatory work short of producing oil and gas while they crafted new environmental impact assessments taking into account the eventual effect of actually burning the fossil fuels, not just the emissions which would be created in extracting them.
An inside look at Jackdaw, the UK’s newest and most contested gas platform.
When BBC News visited the platform this summer, Adura CEO Neil McCulloch said its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortages this winter.
However, the UK government has previously suggested that Jackdaw will have little impact on energy security and none on reducing domestic gas and electricity bills.

In August, in an interim response to a consultation on the future of the country's gas supplies, Energy Minister Michael Shanks said the UK would inevitably become more reliant on imports as domestic production declined, external.

"With diminishing output from the North Sea over the past decades, any gas produced from the UK Continental Shelf represents a tiny fraction of global demand and so will not lower prices nor materially boost supply," wrote Shanks.
Labour has previously said it is opposed to the issuing of new exploration licences but it will consider new production projects if they are tied back to existing facilities.
McCulloch described the Jackdaw decision as "an important and positive step forward" - but said attention now turned to Rosebank.
He has urged the UK government to approve production from the field, in which Adura owns an 80% stake. The other 20% is held by London-based Ithaca Energy.
Rosebank contains an estimated 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil.
But while most of Jackdaw's gas is likely to be consumed in the UK, Rosebank's oil will be taken off by tanker and sold on international markets.

items.title: How sensitive data from Centrelink and other Australian agencies may have been fed to Palantir software
paragraphs: The personal information of Centrelink customers, taxpayers and childcare workers is among a trove of sensitive data that may be ending up in Palantir’s surveillance software in Australia, without the departments responsible for the information even knowing about it.

As Guardian Australia reported in September, Palantir’s software is used by the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission (ACIC) as part of the multi-agency fraud fusion taskforce, which was established in 2022 with the goal of targeting fraud in government payments from the national disability insurance scheme, childcare and welfare.

New documents, released under freedom of information requests, reveal the extent to which at least 10 government agencies share sensitive data with the taskforce, which could be fed into Palantir’s software.

The controversial US tech company, co-founded by the Donald Trump-aligned billionaire Peter Thiel, has clients including the Israeli military and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) that use the software to analyse vast amounts of data.

While the company has insisted it has no access to the data clients enter into the software, the Greens leader, David Shoebridge, has led calls for a ban on Palantir contracts with the Australian government.

In April, the company implied some cultures were inferior to others in a 22-point manifesto posted on X and described by one UK MP as the “ramblings of a supervillain”. Shoebridge has said Palantir should not be near Australian data given how the data mining software is used by the IDF and ICE.
The Australian government has spent nearly $80m on Palantir contracts since May.

The taskforce is headed up by the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) and Services Australia. The intelligence program – known as the fraud fusion centre – is led by the ACIC, and brings in “large volumes of information, data and intelligence” held by agencies that could be relevant to the taskforce work, according to the documents released under FoI.

The FoI requests, undertaken by Dr Gabrielle Josling, an independent researcher and data scientist, showed at least 10 federal agencies were sharing data with the ACIC – data that could ultimately be put in Palantir’s software by the commission.
Documents from the Department of Education show the ACIC is “collecting criminal intelligence and analysing and crossmatching data” from sources including:
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (Asic).
The Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre.
The Department of Employment and Workplace Relations.

The personal information authorised by Services Australia to be obtained by the ACIC includes names, date of birth, information about proof of ID, addresses, telephone numbers, Centrelink claims or reviews, itemised income and asset details, employer information, bank account information and “surveillance material” held by the agency.

The collected data is held by the fraud fusion centre and, while a privacy impact assessment noted that the ACIC is not subject to the Privacy Act, the agency’s protocols state it acts in accordance with the Australian privacy principles “wherever reasonably consistent with the effective performance of its statutory functions”.

Services Australia said each disclosure to the ACIC was considered on a case-by-case basis. There had been two disclosures in the financial year to date, compared with 21 in 2025-26 and 47 in 2024-25.

The ATO’s documents do not reveal the extent of the data provided by the agency but state that tax file numbers cannot be provided under law. It made 758 disclosures between November 2022 and July 2026, including 376 to the NDIA and 42 to the ACIC.

A spokesperson for the ATO told Guardian Australia the taxpayer information was disclosed where it was “lawfully able” to do so under the terms of the memorandum of understanding as part of the taskforce, the ATO’s intelligence disclosure governance plan and the Tax Administration Act.
The federal education department has withheld releasing information about what data it has provided to the taskforce but the documents state it is data related to the childcare subsidy scheme.
A spokesperson for the department refused to comment on “detailed operational information-sharing arrangements” and directed questions about Palantir use to the ACIC.

The ACIC said data handling is subject to agreements with the agency supplying the data, and that Palantir was “part of a suite of analytical tools to undertake analysis on specific cases to assist partner agencies to disrupt serious organised crime networks defrauding government programs”.

The agency did not respond to questions from Guardian Australia on whether other federal agencies were informed if the data provided was ingested into Palantir’s software. Neither the ATO nor Centrelink were aware if Palantir was used.
“The use of software by another agency is a question for that agency, and any questions relating to ACIC use of data obtained under the FFT are best directed to the ACIC,” an ATO spokesperson said.

The documents reveal that the memorandum of understanding in 2024 between taskforce agencies originally required the taskforce to develop an ethics and human oversight framework governing the control of the information shared. It was described as “an important part of effective risk management for the FFT”.
Ethical risks were supposed to be assessed and recorded on a risks register.

But correspondence released from September 2025 reveals that it was determined that the process was “too difficult to implement” and the framework instead became an “ethics guide” in October last year.

In a submission to the Australian National Audit Office’s review into the taskforce, Josling said the new model abandoned requirements for defined assessments and reviews of the taskforce. A framework for evaluating and monitoring the performance of the taskforce was also not developed.

“A multi-agency taskforce needs a way to learn from data quality problems, data matching limitations, unproductive referrals, emerging risks, and weaknesses in governance,” Josling said in the submission.

Companies and governments have faced pressure to stop using Palantir, with both Coles and Westpac reportedly deciding against renewing their contracts with the firm. The UK government has also faced pressure to drop its contracts with Palantir, including a contract with the NHS.

Palantir has maintained that it does not have access to the data clients enter into its software. A spokesperson has previously defended the company’s contracts with the Australian government, saying it is just a software company.
“We are committed to supporting Australian government agencies in tackling complex challenges, including serious financial crime and fraud,” they said.

items.title: Art psychotherapists are already regulated | Letters
paragraphs: We welcome the discussion about public protection, professional accountability and the importance of appropriate regulation within counselling and psychotherapy (Letters, 5 November). However, we feel it is important to highlight a distinction that may be helpful to readers.

Art psychotherapists are already a statutorily regulated profession in the UK, regulated by the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC). The HCPC regulates 15 health and care professions, including arts therapists (art psychotherapists, art therapists, drama therapists, music therapists) and the titles art therapist and art psychotherapist are legally protected. Practitioners must meet HCPC registration requirements, standards of proficiency, conduct and ethics, and continuing professional development requirements.
This means that art therapists occupy a different regulatory position from counsellors and psychotherapists, whose professional registration is currently voluntary.

We do recognise the importance of extending statutory protection across professions where it is currently absent, but would appreciate recognition that we, along with drama therapists and music therapists, are a statutory regulated profession. Elizabeth Donnelly Chief executive officer, British Association of Art Therapists

items.title: With up to $300 off, these early MacBook Black Friday deals might be as good as they're going to get
paragraphs: MacBook Black Friday deals couldn't come soon enough this year following the price hikes amid the ongoing component shortage. Happily, the deals are starting to arrive across major retailers, and some of them may already be as good as they're going to get.
The highlights are $200 off the 2026 M5 MacBook Airs at Amazon, while B&H Photo has up to $300 off M5 MacBook Pros.

Could we still see a discount on the brand-new touchscreen PROLED XDR MacBook Pro released this month? It's unlikely, but perhaps a very small one. If it does come up, you'll find it here because we'll be updating the MacBook deals below throughout Black Friday and Cyber Monday.
If you want to shop around rival brands, see our guide to the best laptops for graphic design. And see our iPad Black Friday hub if you're also after an Apple tablet.

MacBook Black Friday deals in previous years have typically ranged from around $200 MacBook Airs to around $300 off MacBook Pros. Higher-configuration MacBook Pros with 2TB SSDs and 36GB+ memory sometimes come in for bigger discounts of up to around $500, particularly on previous-gen models.

Black Friday 2026 takes place amid a slightly different context compared to previous years because of the shortage of components provoked by the boom in AI data centre construction. Apple hiked the starting price of all MacBooks in mid-2026 because of the component crunch, and prices are unlikely to come back down soon. That may also mean that there's less appetite for discounting during the sale season.

Refurbished MacBooks from reputable sellers like Back Market or Apple's own refurbishment programme can offer exceptional value, especially when you're seeing savings of over $800 / £800. These devices are thoroughly tested, come with warranties, and often include replaced batteries and outer shells, so they look and perform like new.

The main consideration is which generation you're buying – an M1 MacBook from 2020 is still perfectly capable for many people's needs, but it won't support all the latest Apple Intelligence features or handle some heavier creative workflows in video or 3D art. We'd recommend refurbished options if you're primarily using your MacBook for web browsing, productivity apps, and light creative work. However, if you need cutting-edge performance or plan to keep the laptop for five or more years, buying new might be the better long-term investment.

The main differences come down to performance, display technology, and connectivity. MacBook Airs are thinner, lighter and fanless, making them silent and incredibly portable, whilst still offering excellent performance for most users. That makes them ideal for students, writers, and casual users who prioritise battery life and portability.

MacBook Pro models feature more powerful chip configurations (like the M5 Pro and M5 Max), active cooling that allows sustained high performance, brighter displays with ProMotion technology, and additional ports including HDMI and SD card slots. They're designed for professionals doing demanding work like 4K video editing, 3D rendering, or software development.

For most people, a MacBook Air provides more than enough power, but if you're regularly pushing your laptop to its limits with intensive creative or technical work, the MacBook Pro's extra capabilities justify the higher price.

What would traditionally be called Black Friday is the Friday after Thanksgiving in the US, so 27 November in 2026. However, most retailers now start their Black Friday sales much earlier than that – as early as the start of November in some cases. As for when it ends, Black Friday now rolls into Cyber Monday, which falls on 30 November this year. That's likely to be the last day for deals before the Christmas holiday period.
Subscribe to the Creative Bloq newsletter for details of curated offers, bringing the tools you need to create – and products perfect for the design-obsessed.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.
